summary: In 1788, the Birmingham physician William Withering was consulted by an apothecary in Wellington, Shropshire, about the case of a woman, Mrs Houlston, whom Erasmus Darwin's son, Robert Darwin, a medical practitioner in Shrewsbury, had attended the day before. Withering thought that Darwin's prescription had been inappropriate and changed it. Robert reacted angrily, and a vituperative correspondence followed. Erasmus, Robert's father, also medically qualified, may have been involved in the affair, by urging his son to attack Withering and by helping him to write his letters. Erasmus may have had good reason for wanting to damage Withering's reputation. Although all three of them were alumni of the Edinburgh Medical School in the latter half of the 18th century, albeit at different times, and although Erasmus had recommended Withering to both a post in Birmingham and membership of the Lunar Society, he may have become jealous of Withering's success as a physician and botanist. The enmity between them had culminated in a dispute over the treatment of a patient in Staffordshire, whom Withering was asked to see after Erasmus had attended her, with little therapeutic success. Withering recommended digitalis, which seemed to have saved her life. Darwin reported the case in 1780, anonymously including it in a posthumous publication credited to another medical son, Charles, and without crediting Withering. In turn, Withering responded by criticising Darwin in his 1785 monograph An Account of the Foxglove The rift between the two seems to have been irreparable.
title: When I use a word . . . Alumni of the Edinburgh Medical School 1726-2026: Erasmus Darwin versus William Withering.

summary:
Objectives

To evaluate the early comparative effectiveness of robotic versus conventional total hip replacement (THR) in the UK.

Design

Target trial emulation study.

Setting

Public and private hospitals using data from the National Joint Registry of England, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Isle of Man, Guernsey, and Jersey.

Participants

666 283 THRs performed between 2018 and 2024; 656 080 were conventional THRs and 10 203 were robotic THRs.

Main outcome measures

Five year THR implant survival (mean 2.5 year follow-up), all cause revision risk, cause specific revision risk, malpositioning revision risk, intraoperative complications, and patient survival up to five years. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, Cox proportional hazards regression, and Fine and Gray models were used. Propensity score matching created comparable treatment groups to estimate the average treatment effect in the treated population.

Results

The five year implant survival of the matched conventional and robotic THR groups was 98.8% (95% confidence interval (CI) 98.6% to 99.0%) and 98.8% (CI 98.3% to 99.1%), respectively, with no difference in revision risk between groups (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.22; P=0.73). Cause specific revision risk and intraoperative complication risks did not differ between groups. However, a significantly lower risk of revisions related to implant malposition (dislocation, leg length discrepancy, and malalignment) was observed in the robotic group (hazard ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.93; P=0.03). The five year patient survival of the matched conventional and robotic THR groups was 96.3% (95% CI 95.8% to 96.8%) and 96.2% (95.2% to 97.0%), respectively, with no difference in all cause mortality risk (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.34; P=0.17).

Conclusions

No significant differences were found in overall THR or patient survival, cause specific revision, or intraoperative complication risks between robotic and conventional groups. Robotic THR was associated with a lower revision risk from causes related to implant malpositioning. However, the possibility of unmeasured and residual confounding cannot be ruled out owing to the observational design. These results highlight the importance of careful evaluation of robotic technology in publicly funded healthcare systems because of the substantially higher capital and procedural costs.
title: Early national comparison of robotic versus conventional hip replacements for arthritis using National Joint Registry data: target trial emulation study.

summary:
Objective

To evaluate the early comparative effectiveness of robotic versus conventional total knee replacement (TKR) and unicompartmental knee replacement (UKR) in the UK.

Design

Target trial emulation study.

Setting

Public and private hospitals using data from the National Joint Registry of England, Wales, Northern Ireland, the Isle of Man, Guernsey, and Jersey.

Participants

697 145 knee replacement surgeries between 2018 and 2024: 675 034 were conventional (TKRs and UKRs) and 22 111 were robotic.

Main outcome measures

The main outcome was five year knee replacement survival (mean 2.5 years follow-up); all cause revision risk; cause specific revision risk; intraoperative complications; and revision complexity of robotic versus conventional (TKR and UKR) knee replacement. Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses were used to compare implant survival and indications for revision surgery. Propensity score matching using target trial emulation framework was used to estimate the average treatment effect in the treated population.

Results

The five year implant survival of the matched conventional and robotic TKR groups was 98.5% (95% confidence interval (CI) 98.3% to 98.7%) and 98.6% (98.2% to 99.0%), respectively, with no between group difference in revision risk (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.26; P=0.71). The five year implant survival of the matched conventional and robotic UKR groups was 97.8% (95% CI 97.2% to 98.3%) and 96.4% (92.4% to 98.3%), respectively, with no between group difference in revision risk (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.42; P=0.86). Cause specific revision risk and intraoperative complication risks did not differ between groups for either TKR or UKR.

Conclusions

No statistically significant differences were detected in revision risk, cause specific risk, or intraoperative complication risk between the robotic and conventional groups. This was consistent for both TKR and UKR. The possibility of unmeasured and residual confounding cannot be ruled out, however, owing to the observational design of the study. These results highlight the importance of careful evaluation of robotic technology in publicly funded healthcare systems, given the substantially higher capital and procedural costs involved.
title: Early national comparison of robotic versus conventional knee replacements for arthritis using National Joint Registry data: target trial emulation study.

summary: Medicare Improvement Fund Premium Rebate Frequently Asked Questions Q: What will the Medicare Improvement Fund do for Medicare beneficiaries? A: The Administration is making a $90 Premium Rebate available for Part B premiums to certain Medicare beneficiaries because the best way to improve Medicare is to put healthcare dollars back where they belong – in the hands of our Medicare beneficiaries – and make coverage more affordable. Q: How much is the Medicare Improvement Fund Premium Rebate and when will beneficiaries receive it? A: Eligible beneficiaries will receive one $90 rebate in October 2026. Most beneficiaries will receive a direct deposit for $90 on or around October 8 th followed by an email or a letter from the President in mid-October. Some beneficiaries will receive a paper check for $90 from the U.S. Department of the Treasury later in October with the following accompanying message “Medicare Improvement Fund Payment; $90 Payment to Offset October Premium.” Q: Who will receive the Medicare Improvement Fund Premium Rebate? A: The 20.8 million Americans in Original Medicare Part B who are: (1) Living in the United States, are (2) not receiving premium assistance from Medicaid; or, (3) not paying an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount. Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage are not eligible. Q: How will eligible Medicare beneficiaries receive the Medicare Improvement Fund Premium Rebate? A: The vast majority of eligible Medicare beneficiaries will receive the Medicare Improvement Fund Premium Rebate via direct deposit from the Social Security Administration. Those without direct deposit will receive a check to the mailing address they have registered with Medicare. Q: How can I check if I am eligible for the Medicare Improvement Fund Premium Rebate or if the Premium Rebate has been delivered? A: Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Part B who are not receiving premium assistance through Medicaid or do not pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount can call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to check on their eligibility for the premium rebate. Beneficiaries who want to check on the status of their payment should call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213 beginning on October 15, 2026. Q: What is the Medicare Improvement Fund? A: The Medicare Improvement Fund was created by Sec. 7002 of the Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2008 “to make improvements under the original fee-for-service program under parts A and B for individuals entitled to, or enrolled for, benefits under part A or enrolled under part B.”[1] Q: How has the Medicare Improvement Fund been used in the past? A: President Trump is the first president to actually use the Medicare Improvement Fund to improve Medicare by making the program more affordable for enrollees. In the past, Congress has repeatedly withdrawn from the fund to “offset” new spending around 20 times.[2] For instance, President Obama worked with Congress to take $20.7 billion from the Medicare Improvement Fund to help pay for Obamacare in 2010.[3] ### ^ https://www.cbo.gov/publication/59115#footnote-005 ^ https://www.cbo.gov/publication/59115#footnote-005 ^ https://www.cbo.gov/sites/default/files/111th-congress-2009-2010/costestimate/amendreconprop.pdf CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145
title: Medicare Improvement Fund Premium Rebate Frequently Asked Questions

summary: Transparency in Coverage Final Rules (CMS 9882-F) Introduction Consistent with the President’s Executive Order 14221 , “Making America Healthy Again by Empowering Patients with Clear, Accurate, and Actionable Healthcare Pricing Information,” on October 5, 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services (through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services), in partnership with the Departments of Labor and the Department of the Treasury (collectively, the Departments) jointly finalized changes to the Transparency in Coverage regulations to improve the accessibility of pricing disclosures to participants, beneficiaries, and enrollees, and the standardization and reliability of the public pricing disclosures from non-grandfathered group health plans and health insurance issuers offering non-grandfathered group or individual health insurance coverage. These changes build on the historic disclosure requirements the Departments issued in the Transparency in Coverage final rules on Nov. 12, 2020 (the 2020 final rules) in line with the President’s June 24, 2019, Executive Order (EO) 13877, “Improving Price and Quality Transparency in American Healthcare to Put Patients First” and EO 14221, “Making America Healthy Again by Empowering Patients with Clear, Accurate, and Actionable Healthcare Pricing Information.” This fact sheet discusses the provisions of the Transparency in Coverage final rules (CMS-9882-F) that amend the 2020 final rules. You can access the final rules in the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/2026-20447/transparency-in-coverage Under the 2020 final rules, non-grandfathered group health plans and health insurance issuers offering non-grandfathered group or individual health insurance coverage are required to post machine-readable files monthly for each plan or coverage they offer — an in-network rate file disclosing in-network rates for all covered items and services, an allowed amount file disclosing out-of-network allowed amounts and the associated billed charges for covered items and services, and a prescription drug file disclosing in-network rates and historical net prices for covered prescription drugs. These requirements became applicable in July 2022. 1 Improved Standardization, Accuracy, and Accessibility of the In-Network Rate and Out-of-Network Allowed Amount Machine-Readable Files Based on internal assessment and external stakeholder feedback received since implementation began, the Departments have identified three main barriers to fully achieving the goals of the 2020 final rules: inaccessibility due to the large size of the machine-readable files, data ambiguity due to lack of contextual information alongside the raw data, and areas of misalignment with the Hospital Price Transparency rule that make comparing data across disclosures challenging. Reducing the Number and Size of Machine-Readable Files and Increasing Accessibility to Make Data More Meaningful A major driver of large in-network rate file sizes involves including provider-negotiated rates for items or services the provider is unlikely to furnish because of their specialty and the nature of the item or service (e.g., rates for podiatrists to perform heart surgery). This occurs because payer-provider contracts often negotiate rates at the provider organization level for every provider who is a member of the organization, regardless of clinical specialty. To address these unlikely provider-rate combinations, the final rules include amendments to: Require group health plans and health insurance issuers to exclude from their In-network Rate Files provider-rate combinations for items and services that providers would be unlikely to be reimbursed for given that provider’s specialty area. The provision requires plans and issuers to determine which provider-rate combinations to exclude by using their internal provider taxonomies or other internal rules used during the claims adjudication process to determine if the provider should be reimbursed for the item or service given that provider's specialty; Post the internal provider taxonomy mapping or other rules they used to prepare each In-network Rate File in a new file called the Taxonomy File; and Post a new file called a Utilization File for each In-network Rate File, which will include all providers who have submitted and received reimbursement for at least one claim for a covered item or service for the most recent plan or policy year ending six months before the posting of the file. To reduce duplicative data, the Departments finalized a change to the level at which group health plans and health insurance issuers must report data in the In-network Rate File. Under this provision, plans and issuers must prepare one In-network Rate File for each provider network they maintain or contract with, rather than for each plan or policy they offer, as required by the 2020 final rules. Because it is very common for multiple plans offered by the same issuer or administered by the same service provider to leverage the same provider networks with the same negotiated rates, requiring network-level reporting will streamline how rates are reported, reducing both the number and the size of In-network Rate Files. Further, reporting in-network rates at the network level also aligns with how the Hospital Price Transparency data is typically reported. Aligning payer and hospital data reporting will help normalize data across different systems, improve consistency, and make comparisons between the payer and hospital machine-readable files easier for file users. Improving Data Availability The Departments have received feedback and observed that many group health plans and health insurance issuers include limited or no data in their Out-of-network Allowed Amount Files, which may be due, in part, to the current 20-claims threshold for reporting. This has limited the transparency of out-of-network pricing information to the public and, in turn, limited what researchers, academics, and developers can analyze. The Departments include three amendments for the Out-of-network Allowed Amount Files to address insufficient data: 1) require payers to aggregate their Allowed Amount Files by insurance market type (large group, small group, individual, and self-insured); 2) lower the claims threshold for reporting payment of out-of-network allowed amounts from 20 to 11 claims; and 3) increase the amount of out-of-network data disclosed to the public to better position researchers and academics to conduct analyses to inform the public. Taken together, the Departments expect these amendments will significantly increase the amount of out-of-network data disclosed to the public. The barrier to meeting the 11-claim threshold will be lower, particularly when data is aggregated by market type and the reporting period is more than twice as long. Further, the Departments understand from stakeholder feedback that out-of-network allowed amounts across plans and policies are most aligned by market type. Providing this data at the market-type level will allow users to compare allowed amounts for plans within the same market, which, based on feedback, the Departments anticipate will better position researchers and academics to conduct analyses to inform the public. The final rules also require additional data elements to provide context around the reported data. Group health plans and health insurance issuers will be required to report the plan’s or policy’s product type (e.g., HMO, PPO) for each plan or policy represented in an In-network Rate File and Out-of-network Allowed Amount File, as well as the common provider network name and network identifier associated with the provider network represented in the In-network Rate File. Making Data Easier to Locate The final rules include two provisions to help users locate the machine-readable files. First, plans and issuers will be required to publish a plain text file (.txt file) located in the root folder of the plan’s or issuer’s website (or under certain circumstances, for another party to publish the file on its public website on the plan’s or issuer’s behalf) with information on the specific location of the machine-readable files. This file must also include contact information, including a monitored email address for an individual or group dedicated to receiving and responding to inquiries and issues related to the machine-readable files. In addition, plans and issuers will be required to add a link in the footer of the homepage of their website titled “Price Transparency” or “Transparency in Coverage” that routes directly to the publicly available web page that hosts the machine-readable files. This will allow for a standardized and predictable navigation path for users trying to find the files. Together, these requirements will help automate locating and downloading the machine-readable files and provide a point of contact for questions about or clarification on the data within the files. These requirements will also apply to the prescription drug machine-readable file. These provisions align with current requirements under the Hospital Price Transparency rules. Reducing Stakeholder Burden Beginning in the second year of implementation and continuing thereafter, these final rules are expected to generate a net cost savings to plans and issuers of approximately $174.5 million annually, due in part to the reduced reporting cadence for certain machine-readable files. The Departments are requiring plans and issuers to update and post the In-network Rate and Out-of-network Allowed Amount Files quarterly rather than monthly to help lower data storage and hosting costs, decrease bandwidth needs, and reduce ongoing maintenance expenses. Plans, issuers, and researchers have indicated that, since provider networks and rates do not change significantly from month to month, switching to a quarterly reporting cadence will not lead to a significant reduction in meaningful data. This reduced reporting cadence will also provide more time for file users to analyze the data, as some file users have informed the Departments that they have difficulty keeping up with the pace of downloading and ingesting the file data monthly. This change in reporting cadence along with the reduction of both the size and number of machine-readable files will reduce the current burden associated with preparing, ingesting, analyzing, and storing the public disclosures. Adopting a Single File Format in Technical Implementation Guidance Currently, the 2020 final rules require group health plans and health insurance issuers to publish their machine-readable files in “any non-proprietary, open format,” such as JSON, XML, or CSV, as specified through technical implementation guidance, which allows the Departments flexibility to adapt file formats to new and emerging technologies. To promote standardization across payers’ files and remain consistent with current industry practice, the final rules require plans and issuers to use a single format. The Departments intend to specify the JSON format in guidance for all machine-readable files other than the text file, which is required to be published as a plain text (.txt) file. Increasing Accuracy and Accountability Through Attestation To improve the accuracy, reliability, and accountability of the disclosures in the machine-readable files, the Departments are requiring plans and issuers to attest, in each In-network Rate, Out-of-network Allowed Amount, Taxonomy, and Utilization machine-readable file, that to the best of its knowledge and belief, the plan or issuer has included all applicable information in accordance with the requirements, and the information encoded is true, accurate, and complete as of the date in the file. Plans and issuers must also encode, in each In-network Rate, Out-of-network Allowed Amount, Prescription Drug, Taxonomy, and Utilization machine-readable file, the name of t

summary:
Background

Postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (long COVID) presents a therapeutic challenge, with fatigue being a common, debilitating symptom.

Objective

To assess the efficacy of fluvoxamine and metformin to treat long COVID fatigue.

Design

Randomized, placebo-controlled, adaptive trial. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06128967).

Setting

Outpatient sites in Brazil.

Participants

399 adults with fatigue 90 days to 24 months after confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Intervention

Participants were randomly assigned to fluvoxamine (100 mg twice daily [BID]), extended-release metformin (750 mg BID [n = 71] from October 2023 to April 2024; reduced to 500 mg BID [n = 40] in May 2024 after a protocol amendment until the group was stopped for futility in September 2024), or a matching placebo, each for 60 days with follow-up to day 90.

Measurements

Change in Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) score.

Results

Median baseline FSS scores ranged from 5.6 to 5.9 across all study groups. The treatment effect on FSS score for fluvoxamine versus placebo showed a mean difference of -0.43 at day 60 and -0.58 at day 90; both had a posterior probability of superiority of 99%. Fluvoxamine also improved quality-of-life scores with a high posterior probability of superiority. Findings for metformin were inconclusive. Incidence of adverse events was lower for fluvoxamine (24.0%) than for metformin, 750 mg BID (45.1%); metformin, 500 mg BID (42.5%); and placebo (35.5%). Grade 3 or higher adverse events were rare (≤2.7%), with no treatment-related deaths.

Limitations

The results were inconclusive for metformin because of a dose change recommended by the data safety and monitoring committee due to adverse effects causing study withdrawal and early termination. The benefit of fluvoxamine after 90 days is unknown. The trial did not address other long COVID symptoms.

Conclusion

Fluvoxamine shows potential for improving long COVID-associated fatigue and quality of life.

Primary funding source

The Latona Foundation.
title: Effect of Fluvoxamine and Metformin for Fatigue in Patients With Long COVID : An Adaptive Randomized Trial.

summary:
Objective

To evaluate the association between quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and subsequent risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes.

Design

Nationwide, population based matched case-control study.

Setting

Population of Sweden, from 1 January 2006 to 31 December 2023.

Participants

624 713 singleton births among nulliparous women aged 16-35 years in Sweden between 2006 and 2023; 92 620 (14.8%) women had received quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy.

Main outcome measures

Risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination, with preterm birth (<37 weeks), including its subtypes, and spontaneous preterm birth as primary outcomes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, prelabour rupture of membranes, small for gestational age infant (<10th centile), severe small for gestational age infant (<3rd centile), stillbirth, and neonatal mortality as secondary outcomes. Effect modification by age at human papillomavirus vaccination was assessed. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios and adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results

After adjustment for confounders, quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination was associated with lower odds of all included adverse pregnancy outcomes. Statistically significant associations were observed for preterm birth (<37 weeks) (adjusted odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.91 to 0.99), very preterm birth (28 weeks to 31 weeks) (0.85, 0.75 to 0.97), spontaneous preterm birth (0.95, 0.91 to 0.99), preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (0.93, 0.87 to 1.00), and severe small for gestational age infant (0.92, 0.87 to 0.97). Risk reduction was generally more pronounced among women vaccinated at younger ages.

Conclusions

Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy was associated with a lower risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, particularly among women vaccinated at earlier ages, extending benefits of human papillomavirus vaccination beyond cancer prevention.
title: Quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccination before pregnancy and pregnancy outcomes: nationwide, population based case-control study.

summary: 2027 Medicare Advantage and Part D Star Ratings Note: The information included in this Fact Sheet is based on the 2027 Medicare Advantage (MA) and Part D Star Ratings published on the Medicare Plan Finder on Oct. 8, 2026. For details on the methodology of the MA and Part D Star Ratings, please refer to the 2027 Part C & D Star Ratings Technical Notes available at http://go.cms.gov/partcanddstarratings . Ensuring that Medicare works for seniors and people with disabilities and that people with Medicare have access to robust, stable, high-quality, and affordable options for the coverage they need are top priorities for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). CMS continues to implement enhancements to the Medicare Advantage (MA) and Medicare Part D Star Ratings programs to incentivize plans to strive for ongoing quality improvement and to help ensure that Medicare enrollees receive high-quality care. CMS publishes the MA (Medicare Part C) and Part D Star Ratings each year to measure the quality of health and prescription drug services received by consumers enrolled in MA and Part D prescription drug plans (PDPs or Part D plans). An important component of the Star Ratings is to provide people with Medicare and their caregivers with meaningful information about the quality of plans in Medicare Plan Finder, alongside information about benefits and costs, to assist them in comparing Medicare health and drug plans and choosing the Medicare coverage option that best fits their health needs. The 2027 Star Ratings announced today appear on Medicare Plan Finder for 2027 Open Enrollment, which begins on October 15, 2026 and runs through December 7, 2026, and will impact 2028 MA quality bonus payments. Highlights of Contract Performance in 2027 Star Ratings MA Prescription Drug (MA-PD) contracts are rated on up to 43 unique quality and performance measures; MA-only contracts (without Part D coverage) are rated on up to 32 measures; and standalone PDP contracts are rated on up to 13 measures. For each measure, CMS establishes thresholds called “cut points” that are used to determine whether each contract’s performance for that measure receives a one, two, three, four, or five-star rating. Changes in the Methodology for the 2027 Star Ratings CMS made changes to the methodology for the 2027 Star Ratings through previous notice and comment rulemaking. There are two new measures added beginning with the 2027 Star Ratings: Concurrent Use of Opioids and Benzodiazepines (COB) and Polypharmacy: Use of Multiple Anticholinergic Medications in Older Adults (Poly-ACH). i The Care for Older Adults — Functional Status Assessment measure is returning to the 2027 Star Ratings after substantive specification changes. i The respecified Colorectal Cancer Screening measure was moved into the 2027 Star Ratings as a new measure, replacing the legacy Colorectal Cancer Screening measure. i All of these measures are process measures developed from evidence-based clinical treatment guidelines, each with a weight of one. These clinical process measures are critical for measuring healthcare and medication use quality, ensuring that care is delivered effectively, and preventing long-term health consequences by addressing potential health concerns early in the beneficiary’s care. summary:
Background

Artificial intelligence (AI)-based systems show promise for assisting primary care providers (PCPs) with patient care. We aimed to evaluate the safety and quality of clinical conversations of a patient-facing conversational AI system, which engaged in real-world urgent primary care appointments.

Methods

In this prospective, single-centre, single-arm feasibility study, English-speaking patients aged at least 18 years interacted with the Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE) up to 5 days before a single-complaint urgent primary care appointment. Physician safety supervisors monitored all interactions and were trained to intervene on the basis of predefined safety criteria. AMIE transcripts and summaries were shared with PCPs before the visit. Primary outcomes were the number of supervised conversation safety stops, AMIE's conversation quality assessed by clinical evaluators, and patient and PCP experiences per surveys. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06911398).

Findings

From April to November, 2025, 114 patients were enrolled with 98 completing both the AMIE interaction and the PCP appointment. Zero conversation safety stops were required on the basis of prespecified criteria. Safety supervisors noted one hallucination and added clinical information in five interactions. AMIE's conversations were rated favourably in 87-100% of cases (17 criteria) by clinical evaluators, and 48-96% (16 criteria) by patients. Patient attitudes towards AI improved after interacting with AMIE and remained elevated after the patient's visit with their physician. PCPs completed post-surveys in 60 of 98 cases, including 44 cases in which they reviewed the AMIE transcript before the visit. PCPs found AMIE helpful for visit preparation in 33 of 44 cases and reported that it might have changed their behaviour in 25 of 44 cases.

Interpretation

Although further research is needed, this study shows the initial feasibility of conversational AI in a real-world setting-assessed via conversation safety and quality, as well as user acceptance-and represents a crucial step towards clinical translation.

Funding

Alphabet.
title: Conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence in ambulatory primary care: a prospective feasibility study.

summary: Our decisions today can support or threaten future human health. Insofar as we protect the planet or invest in fruitful research on pandemic countermeasures, we promote future wellbeing and health, sometimes at the present generation's expense. As we warm the planet, accelerate antibiotic resistance, or consume finite natural resources, we might serve present-day wellbeing or health at the expense of future generations. To decide which such trade-offs are legitimate or advisable, we need to know how to balance the health interests of future generations against each other and against our own. Should concerns for future health be confined to the 21st century as per the stated mission of the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health? If not, how far into the future should they extend, and why? Population ethics is a branch of ethics that considers future populations' wellbeing. This Review, a part of the Lancet Commission on 21st century global threats to health, applies general insights from population ethics to future populations' health, and shows why that application is more complex than meets the eye.
title: Addressing threats to future global health-what is the right timeframe?

summary: By 2050, almost 1 billion people are expected to live with osteoarthritis-a disabling musculoskeletal condition with currently no cure. Despite its burden and costs, osteoarthritis remains largely invisible in national and global health agendas, is poorly integrated within service models for other chronic health conditions, and is frequently perceived as inevitable with ageing and associated with limited therapeutic options. This context drives an osteoarthritis identity problem that fuels frustration among those living with the disease and health-care professionals, perpetuates stigma and inequities, undermines access to effective interventions, and crucially, deprioritises osteoarthritis in health policy. How can health systems be strengthened to mitigate the burden of disease and prioritise the prevention and control of osteoarthritis? We outline a co-created, globally relevant roadmap for health policy responses for osteoarthritis prevention and care that extend beyond the UN's Agenda 2030 targets. The intended audience for the roadmap includes health policy makers, health services managers, clinicians, and civil society organisations. The roadmap anchors to three strategic priorities underpinned by guiding principles of a life course approach, prioritising health equity, and ensuring that responses are affordable and sustainable across economies. Priority 1: recognise and respond to osteoarthritis with capacity building in national surveillance of burden, cost, and modifiable risk factors, and explicitly embedding musculoskeletal health within national and subnational health policies. Priority 2: scale up high-value, person-centred, equitable care for approximately 600 million people living with osteoarthritis. This priority requires reframing of societal narratives around osteoarthritis and reconfiguring service models to integrate osteoarthritis into primary and chronic disease care while also addressing social, environmental, and commercial determinants of musculoskeletal health. Priority 3: slow the osteoarthritis trajectory via primary and secondary prevention targeted at excess bodyweight and joint injury, enabled by cross-sectoral and cross-disease cooperation. These priorities are supported by accelerators requiring global collaboration, within and outside the osteoarthritis community.
title: Strengthening health systems to prioritise, provide care, and prevent osteoarthritis: a roadmap for global health policy.

summary:
Background

Existing data on malformations associated with benzodiazepine use in pregnancy are conflicting.

Objective

To assess the risk for major congenital malformations from first-trimester exposure to benzodiazepines.

Design

Population-based U.S. cohort study.

Setting

Medicaid (2000-2018) and Merative MarketScan (2003-2020) databases.

Participants

Pregnant persons enrolled from 90 days before pregnancy to 30 days after delivery, and their live-born infants enrolled for 90 days after birth.

Measurements

Exposure was defined as at least 1 fill of a benzodiazepine in the first trimester. Primary outcomes were any major congenital malformation and organ-specific malformations previously associated with benzodiazepine exposure. The investigators estimated relative risks (RRs) comparing exposed versus unexposed pregnancies with propensity score fine stratification weights to control for confounders. An RR of 1.3 or higher was prespecified as clinically significant.

Results

In total, 51 339 of 2 478 434 (2.1%) publicly insured and 27 779 of 1 750 721 (1.6%) commercially insured pregnancies had benzodiazepine exposure. The adjusted absolute risks for any malformation in exposed versus unexposed pregnancies were 4.0% versus 4.1% for Medicaid and 4.9% versus 4.8% for MarketScan. The pooled adjusted RR was 0.99 (95% CI, 0.96 to 1.03). Associations with organ-specific malformations were not consistently observed in sensitivity analyses, nor was a dose-response relationship observed. Analyses of different benzodiazepines yielded similar results. The risk for selected organ-specific malformations was increased in some analyses of coexposure to benzodiazepines and other psychoactive medications, but a consistent pattern did not emerge.

Limitations

Potential nondifferential exposure and outcome misclassification; analyses restricted to malformations prevalent at birth.

Conclusion

No substantial increase in the risk for malformations was consistently identified across data sources. Findings from coexposure analyses were inconsistent and warrant further study.

Primary funding source

National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.
title: Benzodiazepine Use Early in Pregnancy and Risk for Congenital Malformations.

summary: Delirium is a common, acute confusional state that is associated with adverse patient, caregiver, and health system outcomes. All patients are at risk for delirium, although those with advanced age or acute infection and those taking sedatives and anticholinergics are at greater risk. The pathophysiology of delirium is complex and includes neuronal injury, inflammation, metabolic imbalance, and blood-brain barrier disruption. It is important to note that delirium is preventable; recognizing people at risk and identifying and addressing predisposing and precipitating factors is paramount. No single intervention or medication has been shown to be effective in treating delirium; therefore, standard-of-care treatments rely on multifaceted strategies to address contributing factors.
title: Delirium.

summary: Machine-learning networks can learn without detailed instructions from a designer. Those that do may offer insight into how the brain reorganizes itself during learning.
title: How artificial neural networks build their own learning machinery

summary: Cervical cancer is the third most common gynecologic cancer, with more than 13 000 new cases diagnosed in 2025. The incidence of and mortality from cervical cancer vary across racial and ethnic groups and in persons living in medically underserved or geographically isolated areas, with half of all cervical cancers occurring in women who are underscreened or have never been screened. Persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most important risk factor for cervical cancer and is associated with nearly all cases. Although genital tract HPV infection is common, most HPV infections are transient, and cervical cancer occurs in only a small portion of patients with HPV. For decades, cervical cancer screening relied on annual cytologic assessment. A growing understanding of the role of HPV infection in the natural progression of cervical cancer has led to updated screening recommendations from the American Cancer Society and the Women's Preventive Services Initiative, as well as a draft update from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. These recommendations include primary HPV testing as a preferred screening strategy and include an option for self-collected specimens for HPV testing. Here, 2 experts in this field, a primary care physician and an obstetrics and gynecology physician, debate how to apply these guidelines when screening a patient for cervical cancer. They discuss a range of screening options and consider the challenges of applying these guidelines across different age groups and in patients at increased risk.
title: How Would You Screen This 26-Year-Old Woman for Cervical Cancer? Grand Rounds Discussion From Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.

summary:
Objective

To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines.

Design

Systematic review and meta-research analysis.

Data sources

Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025.

Eligibility criteria

Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome.

Main outcome measures

Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis-LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness.

Results

The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations. Trial reports were predominantly small sample, single site randomised studies published between 2024 and 2025, spanning diverse clinical specialties and primarily targeting patient facing education and management recommendations. Mean reporting completeness was modest across eligible trial reports (TRIPOD-LLM 40%, CONSORT 2025 44%, CONSORT-AI 59%, CHART 52%), trial protocols (SPIRIT 2025 51%, SPIRIT-AI 57%), and trial registrations (WHO Trial Registration Dataset 61%). Clinical trial reports of LLM interventions prioritise narrative framing and commentary over the methodological detail needed for replication, risk-of-bias assessment, and governance of model performance over time. Critical methodological elements for reproducibility, including data and intervention provenance, input preprocessing, model versioning and access modality, inference parameters, output postprocessing, as well as protocol, data, and code access, were inconsistently reported. Harms planning, monitoring, and reporting were often incompletely reported, limiting the critical appraisal of the safety of LLM interventions in healthcare.

Conclusion

Clinical trials of LLM interventions show modest adherence to established reporting guidelines, with persistent underreporting of LLM specific methodological details, reproducibility artefacts (protocols, data, code), and harms reporting required to support reproducibility and confident appraisal of safety risks before their clinical translation.
title: Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review.

summary: Climate change and biodiversity loss are global environmental crises driving emerging infectious diseases, including bat-borne pathogens of public health significance: Ebola, Marburg, Nipah, Hendra, classic rabies virus, and Australian bat lyssavirus, as well as the fungus Histoplasma This review presents the evidence on the mechanisms of transmission, impact, and prevention and management strategies relevant to each of these pathogens. Transmission pathways vary between pathogens but often involve exposure to body fluids or excreta of a bat or other infected animal or human. The diseases associated with these infections have high mortality rates, and survivors may continue to experience a range of long term effects, including neurological and neuropsychiatric signs and symptoms. Prevention strategies may be implemented to reduce the risk of zoonotic spillover and human-to-human transmission of these pathogens, including better ecological stewardship, reducing exposure of domestic animals and humans to bats, isolation of infected people, and, where possible, vaccination of humans and animals. The mainstay of treatment for these conditions is supportive care; however, specific drugs are now available for histoplasmosis and Ebolavirus infection. In the face of climate change and further loss of biodiversity, developing more effective strategies to prevent and manage these conditions will be critical.
title: Bat-borne zoonoses: transmission, impact, prevention, and management.

summary:
Objectives

To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of adverse event summary reports for medical devices and compliance of the reports with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requirements.

Design

Cross sectional study.

Setting

The FDA manufacturer and user facility device experience (MAUDE) database.

Participants

All adverse event summary reports filed in MAUDE from July 2019 to June 2025.

Main outcome measures

Identification of device problem codes, appropriate identification as summary reports in the submission form, concordance between the number of events data field and the report narrative, and compliance with FDA reporting deadlines.

Results

6308 summary reports were submitted to MAUDE containing 159 503 adverse events. Use of summary reports increased from 808 to 1757 between 2020 and 2024, a factor of 1.21 per year (P<0.001). Most (91%) adverse events in summary reports were for class 3 high risk devices. Summary reports lacked descriptions of potential device related problems: 57% of reports denoted an "adverse event without identified device or use problem" and 38% of reports selected "insufficient information" in the device problem code data field. Manufacturers incorrectly checked "N" (no) in the summary report (Y/N, reporting yes/no) field for 694 summary reports (11%) and erroneously listed "n=1" under the number of events field for 423 summary reports (7%), causing an undercount of 11 902 adverse events. The majority (55%) of summary reports failed to comply with the FDA reporting deadline of 30 days after the manufacturer became aware of the adverse event.

Conclusions

Adverse event summary reports in MAUDE are frequently incomplete, inaccurate, and delayed. Improvements are needed to ensure timely identification of device safety signals and uphold FDA transparency standards.
title: Evaluation of the accuracy, completeness, and compliance of current summary reporting of adverse events to the Food and Drug Administration using the manufacturer and user facility device experience (MAUDE) database: cross sectional study.

summary: Medicare Program; Implementation of Sections 6219, 6220, and 6224 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CMS-4214-P) Background On Oct. 16, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a proposed rule to implement key sections of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026 including section 6220 (Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act) and section 6224 (Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability). This rule also proposes a conforming change mandated by section 6219 of the CAA (Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals) that would reduce the generic drug copayment from $1 to $0 for full-benefit dual eligible individuals. Implementing Certain Provisions of Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 On February 3, 2026, the CAA of 2026, which included several changes to the MA and Part D programs, was signed into law. In this rule, we are proposing to implement the following sections: Adjustments to Medicare Part D Cost-Sharing Reductions for Low-Income Individuals (Section 6219): This proposed rule implements Section 6219 of the CAA that would reduce the generic drug copayment from $1 to $0 for full-benefit dual eligible individuals at or below 100% of the Federal Poverty Level, effective for plan years starting Jan. 1, 2028. Requiring Enhanced and Accurate Lists of (REAL) Health Providers Act (Section 6220): CMS proposes to codify regulations to implement the REAL Health Providers Act, which establishes new provider directory verification and accuracy requirements for MA organizations beginning in contract year 2028. Specifically, CMS proposes requirements to implement this new law related to provider directory verification and maintenance standards, annual accuracy analysis and reporting, public reporting of accuracy scores, and cost-sharing protections for enrollees who rely on inaccurate provider directory information. CMS also proposes to codify the statutory requirements for contract year 2029, including that CMS must publicly display provider directory accuracy scores in a machine-readable format, and MA organizations must prominently display those scores in their provider directories. Through these proposed codifications implementing the REAL Health Providers Act, CMS seeks to promote provider directory accuracy and accountability among MA organizations to ensure that beneficiaries are provided with clear, accurate information on the network of providers available to meet their healthcare needs. Modernizing and Ensuring Pharmacy Benefit Manager Accountability (Section 6224): CMS has several proposals to implement section 6224 of the CAA, which established requirements related to pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and their affiliates specific to the Medicare Part D program. These proposals include new requirements governing the remuneration that PBMs and their affiliates may receive for services in connection with the utilization of Part D drugs, data reporting by PBMs to Part D prescription drug plan (PDP) sponsors and CMS, transparency in PBM price guarantee arrangements, disclosure by PBMs to PDP sponsors of the terms of certain agreements between PBMs or their affiliates and pharmaceutical manufacturers, and other requirements added by the CAA. CMS also proposes to define key terms related to such requirements and establish compliance and enforcement mechanisms, including disgorgement of funds to CMS for violations of the remuneration requirements. The proposed rule will be open for public comment for 60 days following publication in the Federal Register. View this regulation on the Federal Register . The proposed rule will be open for public comment for 60 days following publication in the Federal Register. ### CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145

summary:
Background

Medicare Advantage insurers conduct in-home health risk assessments (HRAs) to identify high-risk patients and facilitate appropriate care. Critics argue this practice increases risk-adjusted payments without improving quality. Comprehensive data on use of in-home HRAs and downstream treatment are lacking.

Objective

To examine trends in cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs, characteristics associated with HRA-based diagnoses, and treatment rates after diagnoses.

Design

Cohort study.

Setting

Population-based.

Participants

Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.

Measurements

Using 100% Medicare claims, trends in the proportion of cardiovascular conditions diagnosed during in-home HRAs (vs. facility-based visits) were examined. Multivariable logistic regression models were fit to estimate the association between beneficiary- and plan-level characteristics and HRA-based diagnoses and compare treatment rates across settings.

Results

Among 21 496 506 Medicare Advantage beneficiaries diagnosed with a cardiovascular risk factor or disease, the proportion diagnosed during in-home HRAs increased between 2018 and 2022 for hypertension (45.9% to 47.7%), hyperlipidemia (57.8% to 66.7%), diabetes (47.8% to 51.6%), atrial fibrillation (30.0% to 36.0%), ischemic heart disease (37.2% to 41.6%), peripheral vascular disease (64.5% to 73.9%), and heart failure (34.7% to 42.6%). Racial and ethnic minority beneficiaries and those enrolled in lower-rated plans were more likely to receive HRA-based diagnoses. Treatment rates were substantially lower after HRA-based diagnoses across all conditions.

Limitations

Differences in the severity of conditions between groups could not be assessed. Prescription fills were used as a proxy for management. Observed differences in the diagnosis and treatment of conditions across encounter settings may be susceptible to unmeasured confounding.

Conclusion

Among Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, an increasingly large share of cardiovascular conditions are being diagnosed through in-home HRAs, but treatment rates after these diagnoses are consistently lower than after facility-based encounters.

Primary funding source

National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.
title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiovascular Conditions in Medicare Advantage In-Home Health Risk Assessments.

summary:
Objective

To evaluate whether providing authors with a manuscript template structured according to the Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials (SPIRIT) 2025 reporting guideline for use during revision improves the completeness of reporting in randomised trial protocols.

Design

Randomised controlled trial.

Setting

BMJ Open.

Population

70 of 74 manuscripts screened between 29 April and 27 May 2025 that reported randomised controlled trial protocols with a decision of minor or major revision after the first round of peer review were randomly allocated (1:1) using an R generated sequence. Authors were not informed of the study.

Interventions

Handling editors asked the intervention group authors to use a SPIRIT based manuscript template when preparing their first revision. The template included structured subheadings corresponding to SPIRIT 2025 items, along with guidance on reporting. Editorial decisions were not conditional on use of the template. Control group manuscripts underwent standard peer review.

Main outcome measures

The primary outcome was completeness of reporting score in the revised manuscript (adjusted for baseline), calculated as the mean of 11 SPIRIT items that are frequently inadequately reported (each scored 0, 0.5, or 1) and linearly rescaled to a 0-10 score. After submission of their first revision, authors in the intervention group completed an online survey. The survey included both fixed response and open ended questions designed to capture the authors' perceptions of ease of use, helpfulness, and any challenges encountered when using the template. Secondary outcomes included mean completeness of reporting scores for each item, median time to submission of the revised manuscript, and authors' experiences of using the template. Outcome assessors, but not editors or investigators, were masked.

Results

Of the 70 manuscripts randomised (35 in each group), all were analysed, with no loss to follow-up. In the intervention group, completeness of reporting in randomised trial protocols improved by 0.61 points (95% confidence interval 0.20 to 1.01) compared with the control group, with mean (standard deviation) scores increasing from 5.42 (1.07) to 6.70 (1.23) and 5.77 (1.19) to 6.32 (0.94), respectively. The largest improvements were observed for recruitment, data collection methods, and access to data. Median time to submission of the first revision was similar between the intervention and control groups (27.10 v 29.86 days, respectively). Data on harms were not systematically collected. Among 14 of 35 survey respondents (40%), many (8/13, 62%) reported the template as time consuming and some (5/13, 39%) as burdensome. Most respondents, however, found it easy to use (10/13, 77%), helpful for improving the manuscript (9/13, 69%), and reassuring for adherence to SPIRIT (13/13, 100%).

Conclusions

Providing authors of randomised controlled trials with a SPIRIT based template during manuscript revision modestly improved the completeness of reporting in the trial protocols without extending revision times.

Trial registration

Open Science Framework 10.17605/OSF.IO/C4YQZ.
title: Effectiveness of a structured template to improve completeness of reporting randomised trial protocols: randomised controlled trial.

summary:
Background

The Choosing Wisely initiative made recommendations where screening, testing, or treatment may be overused, with caveats around appropriate use. Clinicians are increasingly using large language models (LLMs).

Objective

To evaluate whether commercial LLMs appropriately call for restraint or action from scenarios based on Choosing Wisely recommendations.

Design

Benchmark evaluation. Fifteen Choosing Wisely recommendations were used to develop 225 scenarios (per recommendation, 10 in which restraint was appropriate and 5 in which action was appropriate). Six commercial LLMs (3 runs each) generated 4050 responses to the 225 scenarios, using a prompt from the clinician perspective.

Setting

Production application programming interfaces of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google from February to March 2026.

Participants

No human participants were involved.

Measurements

Co-primary outcomes were the overuse rate (endorsing action when restraint was appropriate) and the false restraint rate (withholding an appropriate action).

Results

The rate of LLM-recommended overuse was 5.4% (95% CI, 0.6% to 12.2%); LLMs did not recommend overuse in 8 of 15 recommendations. Two recommendations accounted for most LLM-recommended overuse: thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimeter nodule (overuse recommended in 42.8% of LLM responses) and routine electrocardiography in low-risk adults (overuse recommended in 28.3% of LLM responses). The LLMs recommended overuse in 0.6% to 3.3% of responses for the remaining 5 recommendations. False restraint was rare (0.6% [CI, 0.1% to 1.2%]), was absent for 11 of 15 recommendations, and was highest for prostate-specific antigen screening (3.3%).

Limitations

Single prompts without follow-up; a benchmark rather than real-world use; responses classified by LLM judge with physician adjudication. Findings may not extend to consumer-facing use.

Conclusion

The LLMs rarely withheld recommendations for treatment when it was appropriate. Overuse was concentrated in 2 recommendations.

Primary funding source

None.
title: Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.

summary:
Background

The United States recently proposed changes to the recommendations for childhood hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination.

Objective

To project the effect of vaccine policy changes, if fully implemented, on chronic HBV infections.

Design

Markov cohort state transition model of perinatal and childhood HBV infection.

Data sources

Published data on maternal HBV prevalence (0.4%) and hepatitis B surface antigen testing (99.5% sensitivity), childhood vaccine completion (universal birth-dose strategy: 91.1%; deferred strategy: 87.1%; shared decision-making strategy: 50.0%), and age-stratified risk for chronic HBV infection.

Target population

One-year birth cohort of U.S.-born infants (n = 3.6 million).

Time horizon

20 years.

Intervention

Universal birth-dose vaccination, deferred (2-month) vaccination, and vaccination through shared decision making.

Outcome measures

Numbers with chronic HBV infection and susceptibility to HBV, with 95% uncertainty intervals (UIs) derived from probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

Results of base-case analysis

Compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (255 childhood infections [95% UI, 130 to 530]), the deferred and shared decision-making strategies would increase chronic HBV infections in the 2026 birth cohort by 19% to 303 (95% UI, 155 to 610) and by 83% to 467 (95% UI, 209 to 1032), respectively. These strategies would also increase the number of HBV-susceptible people at year 20 (474 000 and 1 806 000) compared with the universal birth-dose strategy (232 000).

Results of sensitivity analysis

In a scenario with lower vaccine coverage (84.5%) and higher HBV prevalence (maternal prevalence of 0.72% and higher risk for horizontal infection), chronic HBV infections would increase to 1700 and 2192, respectively, with the deferred and shared decision-making strategies.

Limitation

Uncertainty in horizontal HBV infection risk.

Conclusion

Proposed policy changes for vaccination through shared decision making are projected to result in an 83% increase in childhood HBV infections, and between 50% and 70% of children entering adulthood annually would be susceptible to HBV infection. Policymakers should reimplement recommendations for universal birth-dose vaccination.

Primary funding source

National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.
title: Projected Effect of 2026 Federal Changes to the Childhood Immunization Schedule on Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infections in the United States.

summary:
Objective

To assess the added value of acetic acid chromoendoscopy (AAC) for the detection of dysplasia and oesophageal adenocarcinoma during Barrett's oesophagus surveillance endoscopies.

Design

Prospective, open label, stepped wedge cluster, randomised trial.

Setting

18 Dutch community hospitals.

Participants

Patients undergoing surveillance for Barrett's oesophagus were eligible, excluding those with known or previously treated dysplasia.

Interventions

Hospitals randomly shifted from surveillance without AAC (control) to AAC (intervention), with endoscopists trained before implementation. Targeted biopsies were obtained if lesions were present; random four quadrant biopsies were conducted.

Main outcome measures

The primary endpoint was the neoplasia detection rate, defined as the percentage of participants with low grade dysplasia, high grade dysplasia, and oesophageal adenocarcinoma in any biopsy, confirmed by an experienced gastrointestinal pathologist. The secondary endpoint was the neoplasia detection rate in targeted biopsies.

Results

2267 participants were included, of whom 1438 (63%) were allocated to surveillance without AAC and 829 (37%) to surveillance with AAC; AAC was applied in 679 (82%) allocated participants. Overall, neoplasia was diagnosed in 163 (7.2%) participants (111 (4.9%) low grade dysplasia, 30 (1.3%) high grade dysplasia, and 22 (1.0%) oesophageal adenocarcinoma). AAC use did not increase the neoplasia detection rate (7.4% (50/679) with AAC versus 7.1% (113/1588) without AAC; odds ratio 0.97, 95% confidence interval 0.65 to 1.44; adjusted for calendar time and Barrett's oesophagus length). Suspected lesions were detected in 95 (14.0%) participants receiving AAC versus 101 (6.4%) without AAC (P<0.001), but the targeted neoplasia detection rate was not higher (2.1% (14/679) versus 1.8% (29/1588); odds ratio 1.05, 0.49 to 2.24).

Conclusions

Use of AAC did not improve detection of neoplasia in patients with Barrett's oesophagus undergoing endoscopic surveillance in routine clinical practice.

Trial registration

www.onderzoekmetmensen.nl; NL-OMON25059 (prospective registration; 4 Dec 2019).
title: Acetic acid chromoendoscopy for detection of neoplastic Barrett's oesophagus: stepped wedge cluster randomised controlled trial (ACID-trial).

summary:
Background

Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint blockade induces high pathological response rates in patients with locally advanced mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) colon cancer, yet long-term survival outcomes have not been established. Previously, we reported safety (a primary endpoint) and pathological response (a secondary endpoint) data from the NICHE-2 trial. Here, we report the primary efficacy endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival and the exploratory endpoint of 5-year overall survival.

Methods

In this single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial, patients with previously untreated, clinical stage 2 or 3, resectable dMMR colon cancer received a single dose of intravenous ipilimumab (1 mg per kg) on day 1, and two doses of intravenous nivolumab (3 mg per kg) on days 1 and 15, followed by surgery in one of the six participating hospitals in the Netherlands. Here, we report the independent primary efficacy endpoint of 3-year disease-free survival (time from surgery until disease recurrence or death from any cause) and the secondary endpoint of circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) analysis. Overall survival (time from study enrolment until death from any cause) is reported as an exploratory post-hoc analysis. All endpoints were assessed in the per-protocol population (patients who met the eligibility criteria and received at least one cycle of therapy). The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03026140, and has completed accrual.

Findings

From July 4, 2017, to July 18, 2022, 123 patients were screened, of whom 115 were treated and 111 were included in the per-protocol population. At the data cutoff (June 19, 2026), the postoperative median follow-up was 58·7 months (IQR 49·0-72·9). The 3-year disease-free survival was 100% (97·5% CI 100-100). After a median follow-up of 60·4 months (IQR 50·6-74·1), calculated from time of study enrolment, the 5-year overall survival was 100% (95% CI 100-100). In patients with available plasma samples, ctDNA was detected in 99 (92%) of 108 patients at baseline, and ctDNA clearance was observed in 44 (45%) of 98 patients after the first cycle in week 2 and in 80 (82%) of 97 patients after the second cycle before surgery. In patients with a pathological near-complete response and complete response, presurgery ctDNA clearance was observed in 19 (70%) of 27 patients and 60 (92%) of 65 patients, respectively. Assessment for minimal residual disease after surgery revealed that all patients were ctDNA negative.

Interpretation

In patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer, treatment with ipilimumab and nivolumab before surgery resulted in a 3-year disease-free survival and 5-year overall survival of 100%. These findings support neoadjuvant nivolumab plus ipilimumab as a potential standard of care for patients with locally advanced dMMR colon cancer.

Funding

Bristol Myers Squibb.
title: Disease-free survival and overall survival after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in mismatch repair-deficient colon cancer in the Netherlands: results of the single-arm, multicentre, phase 2, NICHE-2 trial.

summary:
Background

Endometrial ablation is an established and effective treatment for women with heavy menstrual bleeding, but many patients require further treatment, with approximately 10% ultimately undergoing a hysterectomy within 2 years. The insertion of a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) immediately after endometrial ablation might inactivate residual untreated endometrium or prevent its regeneration, thereby preventing recurrent symptoms necessitating a hysterectomy. The aim of the study was to assess whether LNG-IUS insertion immediately after endometrial ablation in women with heavy menstrual bleeding reduced the need for subsequent hysterectomy within 2 years compared with endometrial ablation alone.

Methods

This multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial was conducted in 34 hospitals in the Netherlands. Women younger than 60 years with heavy menstrual bleeding who were eligible for endometrial ablation were included and randomly assigned (1:1) to combined treatment comprising endometrial ablation plus LNG-IUS or to standard care comprising endometrial ablation alone (stratified by dysmenorrhoea and age). Masking was not applied. Endometrial ablation was done using electrical radiofrequency ablation or by transcervical resection of the endometrium. In participants allocated to combined treatment, intrauterine insertion of an LNG-IUS containing a total of 52 mg of levonorgestrel (releasing 20 μg per day in the first year) was done immediately after the ablative procedure. The primary outcome was the incidence of hysterectomy within 2 years, analysed on a modified intention-to-treat basis in all participants with available data. Serious adverse events were systematically assessed at 6 weeks, 12 months, and 24 months after the intervention. This study was registered on the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (NL-OMON54839) and is complete.

Findings

Between Nov 19, 2019, and April 5, 2023, 715 participants were randomly assigned to combined treatment (n=359) or endometrial ablation alone (n=356). The median age of all participants was 45 years (IQR 40-48). 42 (6%) participants had missing data for the primary outcome at 2 years of follow-up. A hysterectomy was done in 15 (4%) of 342 participants in the combined treatment group versus 34 (10%) of 331 participants in the endometrial ablation group, corresponding to a relative risk (RR) of 0·43 (95% CI 0·24 to 0·77; p=0·0050), with a risk difference of -0·06 (95% CI -0·10 to -0·02; p=0·0040). Serious adverse events were reported in 27 (8%) of 346 participants in the combined treatment group and 26 (8%) of 327 participants in the endometrial ablation alone group (RR 0·98, 95% CI 0·59-1·65; p=0·94), and there were no treatment-related deaths.

Interpretation

The combination of endometrial ablation and LNG-IUS significantly reduced the incidence of hysterectomy compared with endometrial ablation alone. The combined treatment appears to be a safe adjunctive strategy for heavy menstrual bleeding that does not increase the risk of complications.

Funding

The Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development.
title: Endometrial ablation plus levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system versus endometrial ablation alone in women with heavy menstrual bleeding in The Netherlands (MIRA2): a multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial.
