summary: Plan Year 2027 Marketplace Plans and Prices Fact Sheet The Open Enrollment Period to choose Healthcare.gov coverage for 2027 begins on November 1, 2026, and runs through January 15, 2027. In the upcoming year, Americans using HealthCare.gov will have robust access to low-cost plans. President Trump has delivered the largest decrease in Americans’ prescription drug prices in nearly 70 years; made historic investments to expand healthcare access in rural communities; and maximized price transparency. The Trump Administration continues to fight to lower insurance premiums and send money directly to the American people—not big insurance companies. Robust Access to Low-Cost Plans: More than 75% of Americans who purchase coverage through HealthCare.gov will continue to have access to premiums at or below $50 in 2027. The millions of Americans eligible for tax credits will have access to a plan with nearly 90% of the lowest-cost premium paid for by the federal government, compared to 85% in 2020—the last year not impacted by temporary COVID-19 policies. Building off the Historic Health Savings Account (HSA) Eligibility Expansion: Thanks to President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts, every American purchasing healthcare through HealthCare.gov has access to HSA-eligible plans. HSAs allow American families to put more money back into their pockets by cutting taxes on healthcare while giving people, not insurance companies, greater control over their health spending. In 2027, eligible enrollees will have access to 35 different health plans on average that are HSA-eligible, a more than 1,000% increase over the status quo prior to President Trump’s historic Working Families Tax Cuts. Robust Choice: In 2027, families using HealthCare.gov will have access to a broad selection of plans to choose from. On average, Americans have access to 100 different plans and five to six different insurance companies. Low-Cost Catastrophic Plans: Catastrophic plans offer access to co-pay-free preventive care and protections for individuals with pre-existing conditions at lower costs. The average premium of the lowest-cost catastrophic plan is nearly 10% cheaper than the next lowest-cost plan at other coverage levels. The Trump Administration will continue to fight to lower drug prices and insurance premiums, hold big insurance companies accountable, and maximize price transparency. To learn more, visit whitehouse.gov/greathealthcare . CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145
title: Plan Year 2027 Marketplace Plans and Prices Fact Sheet

summary: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a common cause of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure in patients with pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration of gastric contents, severe trauma, or other inciting triggers. Although the definition of the syndrome has evolved over the past several decades, the core elements (acute onset, hypoxemia, and bilateral radiographic opacities) remain consistent. Critical components of management include identification and treatment of the underlying cause of ARDS as well as avoidance of ventilator-induced lung injury and volume overload. Ongoing areas of controversy include the best strategy for supporting nonintubated patients, personalization of positive end-expiratory pressure, the role of innovative ventilatory strategies, and the use of glucocorticoids. New research suggests that precision medicine approaches to ARDS management that focus on discrete biologic, radiographic, or physiological subphenotypes may improve outcomes, and prospective trials of these approaches are ongoing.
title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome.

summary:
Importance

Cesarean delivery is the most common surgery in the US and the most significant risk factor for postpartum infection. Although trial evidence demonstrated that adjunctive azithromycin use at the time of birth reduces postpartum infection in pregnant persons who undergo an unscheduled cesarean delivery, use of azithromycin outside that trial has not been reported.

Objective

To determine the adoption of trial evidence in clinical practice and describe postpartum infection trends among US pregnant persons undergoing unscheduled cesarean delivery.

Design, setting, and participants

Data from Epic Cosmos were used to conduct a difference-in-differences analysis including pregnant individuals who received prenatal care, labored, and gave birth to a liveborn singleton infant at 24 to 43 weeks' gestation from 2013 to 2024. Cesarean birth was considered the treatment group and vaginal birth was considered the control group. The analysis was conducted from July 2025 to June 2026.

Exposure

Relative to the publication of trial evidence in 2016, births that occurred from January 1, 2013, to September 28, 2016, were compared with births that occurred from January 1, 2017, to December 31, 2024.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcomes were perioperative administration of azithromycin and postpartum infection within 6 weeks of delivery. Patient-level linear regression was used to obtain the difference-in-differences estimate.

Results

Of the 1 663 441 infant deliveries included in the analysis, there were 202 234 cesarean births and 1 461 207 vaginal births (mean age of pregnant individuals, 29.3 [SD, 5.7] years; median body mass index at time of delivery, 31.8 [IQR, 28.2-36.5]). From January 1, 2013, to September 28, 2016, azithromycin was administered during 2.2% of cesarean births (721/32 970) vs 0.01% of vaginal births (15/261 624) compared with 39.6% (67 094/169 264) vs 0.04% (421/1 199 583), respectively, from January 1, 2017, to December 31, 2024 (adjusted difference-in-differences estimate, 37.6 percentage points [95% CI, 33.1 to 42.2]). From January 1, 2013, to September 28, 2016, postpartum infection occurred after 9.2% of cesarean births (3048/32 970) vs 2.0% of vaginal births (5311/261 624) compared with 8.0% (13 555/169 264) vs 2.7% (32 581/1 199 583), respectively, from January 1, 2017, to December 31, 2024 (adjusted difference-in-differences estimate, -2.0 percentage points [95% CI, -2.6 to -1.4]).

Conclusions and relevance

After publication of the trial evidence in 2016, azithromycin use for pregnant persons undergoing unscheduled cesarean delivery increased and postpartum infection rates decreased in the US.
title: Adoption of Adjunctive Azithromycin for Unscheduled Cesarean Delivery and Postpartum Infections.

authors: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance–Guided Management of Mild to Moderate Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction Trial Investigators.
summary:
Importance

Current guidelines do not recommend primary prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) unless a patient's left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is 35% or less. Many sudden cardiac deaths (SCD) occur when LVEF is 36% to 50%. Myocardial scar (a key arrhythmic substrate) can be assessed by late gadolinium enhancement on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR), but robust evidence is lacking regarding a scar-based approach to ICD insertion.

Objective

To determine whether implantation of ICDs reduces SCD or hemodynamically significant ventricular arrhythmia (HSVA) in patients with an LVEF of 36% to 50% and myocardial scar.

Design, setting, and participants

An open-label randomized clinical trial enrolled adults between 2015 and 2022 who had ischemic or nonischemic cardiomyopathy, an LVEF of 36% to 50%, CMR-defined myocardial scar, and were receiving guideline-directed medical therapy at 18 sites in Australia, Germany, and the UK. Follow-up assessments were completed in 2026.

Interventions

A primary prevention ICD (n = 180) vs an implantable loop recorder (ILR) (n = 173).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary composite outcome was SCD or HSVA. Five secondary outcomes were evaluated: SCD, HSVA, heart failure-related hospitalization, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality.

Results

Of 353 patients randomized (median age, 65 years [IQR, 57-61 years]; 18% female; and 72% had an ischemic etiology), 70% had an LVEF of 40% or greater. The median follow-up was 6.3 years (IQR, 4.8-7.6 years). The primary composite outcome occurred in 14 patients (7.8%) in the ICD group compared with 16 patients (9.2%) in the ILR group (hazard ratio [HR], 0.76 [95% CI, 0.37-1.58]). For the individual components of the primary composite outcome, SCD occurred in 3 patients (1.7%) vs 10 patients (5.8%) in the ILR group (HR, 0.26 [95% CI, 0.07-0.95]) and HSVA occurred in 12 patients (6.7%) vs 6 patients (3.5%), respectively (HR, 1.77 [95% CI, 0.65-4.81]). The rates for all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and heart failure-related hospitalization were similar between groups. In a prespecified analysis of 6 subgroups, the primary outcome occurred less often in patients younger than 70 years in the ICD group (3.3%) vs patients in the ILR group (10.0%) (HR, 0.28 [95% CI, 0.09-0.89]) but not in those aged 70 years or older (16.9% vs 7.5%, respectively) (HR, 2.33 [95% CI, 0.75-7.26]; P = .01 for interaction).

Conclusions and relevance

Implantation of an ICD did not reduce the composite outcome of SCD or HSVA in patients with an LVEF of 36% to 50% and myocardial scar.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT01918215.
title: Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance to Guide Defibrillator Implantation for LVEF of 36% to 50%: The CMR GUIDE Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Background

Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-guided percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) improves clinical outcomes. Coronary computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) provides anatomical and physiological information before cardiac catheterization that may enable PCI planning. Data regarding the use of CCTA-guided PCI as compared with IVUS-guided PCI with respect to clinical outcomes are lacking.

Methods

In this investigator-initiated, international, open-label, randomized, noninferiority trial with blinded end-point adjudication, we randomly assigned patients with a clinical indication for revascularization, at least one epicardial lesion with a diameter stenosis of more than 70%, and a fractional flow reserve derived from CCTA of 0.80 or less in a 1:1 ratio to a CCTA-guided or IVUS-guided PCI strategy. The primary end point was target-vessel failure, defined as a composite of death from cardiac causes, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or ischemia-driven target-vessel revascularization, at 12 months. The noninferiority margin for the absolute risk difference was 4.5 percentage points, with a prespecified hierarchical testing strategy for superiority.

Results

A total of 1105 patients underwent randomization: 556 to the CCTA-guided PCI group and 549 to the IVUS-guided PCI group. The median age of the patients was 65 years, and 21.7% were women. At 12 months, target-vessel failure had occurred in 23 patients (4.1%) in the CCTA-guided PCI group and in 25 patients (4.6%) in the IVUS-guided PCI group (risk difference, -0.42 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -2.82 to 1.99; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.73 for superiority). A total of 6 patients in the CCTA-guided PCI group and 9 patients in the IVUS-guided PCI group had clinical procedural complications.

Conclusions

A CCTA-guided PCI strategy was noninferior to IVUS-guided PCI with respect to target-vessel failure at 12 months. (Funded by GE HealthCare and Heartflow; P4 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05253677.).
title: Coronary CT Angiography versus Intravascular Ultrasound Guidance for PCI.

summary:
Importance

One in 5 heart transplant candidates in the US die or are delisted without transplant. Donor hearts are currently allocated by a 6-status therapy-based system criticized for limited risk stratification and susceptibility to gaming.

Objective

To develop a new heart allocation policy based on an objective medical urgency score that ranks candidates based on the interaction between physiology and mechanical circulatory support.

Design, setting, and participants

Registry-based observational study using data from the US organ transplant system. All adult (aged ≥18 years) heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025 were included, split into training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024), and test (2024-2025) datasets.

Main outcomes and measures

A marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant was estimated (the US Candidate Risk Score [US-CRS]). Eight models were compared in held-out data by weighted time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and calibration by status. Finally, US-CRS was converted into an allocation policy and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering was performed compared with the current 6-status system.

Results

Adult heart transplant candidates were partitioned into consecutive training (n = 21 859), validation (n = 7897), and test (n = 8256) datasets (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). The chosen US-CRS model included 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support). In test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the current 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693, respectively) and acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception. In match-run analysis (n = 45 530 donor hearts), a US-CRS-based system led to 67% of transplant recipients moving down in rank order and increased observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under the US-CRS-based system.

Conclusions and relevance

In this registry-based study of US heart transplant candidates, a US-CRS-based allocation system prioritized sicker candidates with higher mortality without transplant compared with the current medical urgency statuses.
title: Development and Validation of an Adult Medical Urgency Score for US Donor Heart Allocation.

summary:
Importance

Statin nonadherence is a leading, addressable driver of preventable cardiovascular events. Although health systems routinely use outreach to promote preventive care, most strategies are static and lack evidence from randomized clinical trials.

Objective

To determine whether an adaptive, sequential digital outreach strategy improves short-term statin refill vs usual communication among adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or high ASCVD risk and recent nonadherence within a rapidly implemented, health system-embedded randomized clinical trial.

Design, setting, and participants

Pragmatic, health system-embedded, prospective randomized open blinded end point (PROBE) clinical trial using a 2-stage sequential, multiple assignment, randomized trial (SMART) design. The trial was conducted via Kaiser Permanente Northern California, an integrated health care delivery system serving more than 4.6 million members. Eligible participants were adults 18 years or older with established ASCVD or high ASCVD risk, recent statin nonadherence, and eligibility for all study communication modalities.

Interventions

Participants were randomized 1:1:1:1 to receive secure portal messaging, SMS/text messaging, nonsecure email, or usual communication. Initial nonresponders within 14 days underwent prespecified second-stage randomization to repeat the same outreach, switch communication modality, or receive usual communication.

Main outcomes and measures

Rates of 14-day statin refill following each randomization, with 28-day follow-up.

Results

Among 20 604 participants (mean [SD] age, 54.8 [9.0] years; 40.9% female; 27.8% Asian, 10.9% Black, 33.6% Hispanic; 15.3% with established ASCVD), initial digital outreach increased 14-day statin refill vs usual communication (14.4% vs 12.0%; adjusted risk difference, 2.3 percentage points [95% CI, 1.3-3.4]; adjusted risk ratio, 1.20 [95% CI, 1.10-1.30]). Among initial nonresponders, second-stage outreach further increased refill (13.0% vs 10.4%; adjusted risk difference, 2.5 percentage points [95% CI, 1.3-3.7]; adjusted risk ratio, 1.25 [95% CI, 1.11-1.39]). Switching communication modalities did not improve refill vs repeating the same modality (13.2% vs 12.5%; adjusted risk ratio, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.94-1.17]). Cumulative statin refill through 28 days was higher in those receiving any digital outreach vs usual communication (24.9% vs 21.2%; adjusted hazard ratio, 1.21 [95% CI, 1.13-1.30]). Results were consistent across prespecified subgroups.

Conclusions and relevance

Among adults with a statin indication and recent statin nonadherence, adaptive outreach improved short-term refill vs usual communication. A second outreach produced additional gains among initial nonresponders, although switching communication modalities provided no additional benefit. These findings support adaptive, sequential health system outreach strategies to improve cardiovascular prevention when integrated into population health programs.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07522645.
title: Digital Outreach to Improve Statin Refills in Patients With Low Statin Adherence: The ADHERE-ASCVD Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Background

Mortality among infants with severe HIV-associated pneumonia remains high globally. The EMPIRICAL trial evaluated whether empirical tuberculosis treatment (eTB-T) improves survival compared with the currently recommended microbiologically and clinically guided strategy.

Methods

This multicentre, open-label, group-sequential designed, 2×2 factorial, randomised, controlled, superiority trial was conducted in 19 hospitals across Côte d'Ivoire, Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Infants aged 28-365 days admitted with severe HIV-associated pneumonia, without a current tuberculosis diagnosis or contact, were centrally and individually randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) using a secure web-based system stratified by site and severity. A computer-generated block randomisation schedule was used, with fixed blocks of eight allocations (two allocations to each factorial treatment group) within each stratum. Participants received standard of care (SoC) comprising treatment for bacterial (WHO-recommended antibiotics) and Pneumocystis jirovecii (cotrimoxazole and steroids) pneumonia, SoC plus 15 days of oral valganciclovir (16 mg/kg per 12 h), or SoC plus 6 months of tuberculosis treatment (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, plus isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 subsequent months), or both interventions combined. Here, we report the comparison between the eTB-T (ie, SoC plus tuberculosis treatment and SoC plus oral valganciclovir plus tuberculosis treatment) and non-eTB-T (ie, SoC or SoC plus 15 days of oral valganciclovir) groups. Nasopharyngeal aspirates, stools for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing, and urine for tuberculosis lipoarabinomannan assay were collected at recruitment. In the non-eTB-T groups, tuberculosis treatment was initiated if microbiological results collected at recruitment yielded positive results or if, during follow-up, the treating clinician suspected tuberculosis on clinical grounds, including radiological findings, in accordance with routine clinical practice and guidelines. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality (at 15 days and 360 days). Survival was estimated using flexible parametric models with covariate-adjusted conditional estimates; missing data were imputed by chained equations. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03915366) and is now complete.

Findings

Between March 15, 2020, and Jan 31, 2024, 563 participants were enrolled; 558 were analysed after excluding five patients who did not meet eligibility criteria. 276 participants were allocated to the eTB-T groups (n=140 eTB-T and n=136 valganciclovir plus eTB-T) and 282 to the non-eTB-T groups (n=142 SoC and n=140 valganciclovir). 17 (6%) of 276 in the eTB-T groups and 20 (7%) of 282 in the non-eTB-T groups were lost to follow-up. Median age was 4·4 months (IQR 3·2-7·4) and 274 (49%) of participants were female and 284 (51%) were male. In the non-eTB-T groups, 130 (46%) of 282 participants eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment at a median of 4·0 days (IQR 3·0-15·0) after recruitment due to positive microbiological findings in 55 (20%) cases (53 confirmed by tuberculosis lipoarabinomannan assay and two by nasopharyngeal aspirates Xpert MTB/RIF) or clinical decision in 75 (27%) cases. There was no evidence of interaction between valganciclovir and eTB-T (adjusted hazard ratio 1·19, 95% CI 0·73-1·95; pheterogeneity=0·4836). At 12 months, 132 (48%) of 276 participants in eTB-T groups and 121 (43%) of 282 participants in non-eTB-T groups died. In the eTB-T groups, the adjusted hazard ratio for death was 1·12 (95% CI 0·87-1·43; p=0·3868). At 15 days, the odds ratio was 1·24 (95% CI 0·83-1·84; p=0·2950). Serious adverse events did not differ between groups (1·19, 0·82-1·73; p=0·3523). There were no treatment-related deaths. The most common adverse events were elevation of transaminases (72 [26%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 74 [26%] in the non-eTB-T group), anaemia (163 [59%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 169 [60%] in the non-eTB-T groups), and infectious disease requiring antimicrobial treatment (161 [58%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 176 [62%] in the non-eTB-T groups).

Interpretation

In contrast to empirical treatment with valganciclovir, there was no evidence that eTB-T was superior to a clinically and microbiologically guided strategy in reducing all-cause mortality among infants with HIV-associated pneumonia. However, the high proportion of infants who eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment during follow-up in the non-eTB-T groups might have reduced the contrast between strategies and attenuated the ability to detect differences in outcomes.

Funding

European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership.
title: Empirical tuberculosis treatment in infants living with HIV hospitalised with severe pneumonia in Africa (EMPIRICAL): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, 2 × 2 factorial, controlled superiority trial.

summary:
Importance

Heart failure affects more than 6 million US adults; approximately 4% to 5% progress to advanced disease despite optimal therapy. Heart transplant is a class I guideline-recommended therapy for select individuals with advanced heart failure.

Observations

Early referral for heart transplant is guided by the "I NEED HELP" mnemonic, a tool that identifies patients with advanced heart failure based on criteria such as use of inotropes, persistent symptoms (New York Heart Association class III or IV), end-organ dysfunction, left ventricular ejection fraction, defibrillator shocks, hospitalizations for heart failure, persistent edema or escalating use of diuretics, and low blood pressure. Each criterion is associated with higher risk of death or first heart failure hospitalization over a median follow-up of 260 days (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.19 [95% CI, 1.11-1.27] for each additional criterion). Typical absolute contraindications to heart transplant include active systemic infection, malignancy with limited life expectancy, severe and irreversible end-organ dysfunction (eg, cirrhosis, severe pulmonary hypertension), active substance use, major untreated psychiatric illness, inadequate social support, and severe frailty. Approximately 4600 heart transplants are performed annually in the US. The mortality rate was 8.5 deaths/100 patient-years for adults on the transplant waiting list in 2023. Leading causes of early death after transplant include primary graft dysfunction (39.5%), multiorgan failure (18.5%), and infection (13.9%). Among adults, contemporary survival rates after heart transplant are 91.5% at 1 year and 80.3% at 5 years. Lifelong maintenance immunosuppression typically combines a calcineurin inhibitor, antiproliferative agents (typically mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine) and corticosteroids, with selective use of induction therapy (intensive immunosuppression immediately after transplant). Acute rejection requiring treatment occurs in 20% to 25% of recipients within a year, and may be treated with high-dose corticosteroids, antithymocyte globulin, and B-cell-targeted therapies (such as rituximab or bortezomib). Rejection surveillance with endomyocardial biopsies of the right ventricular septum is performed 5 to 10 times within the first year after transplant. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (chronic rejection that causes diffuse coronary narrowing) affects 29% of heart transplant recipients within 5 years and 46.8% by 10 years and is the leading cause of late mortality. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is treated with statins, mechanistic target of rapamycin inhibitors (such as sirolimus or everolimus), and retransplant for severe cases. Infections (62.5% are bacterial, 30.0% are viral, 6.7% are fungal, and 0.8% are parasitic) and malignancy (10.7% within 5 years after heart transplant) are other leading causes of late mortality.

Conclusions and relevance

Heart transplant is the definitive therapy for carefully selected patients with advanced heart failure despite receiving optimal, guideline-directed therapy. After heart transplant, lifelong multidisciplinary care is necessary to manage immunosuppression, prevent and treat rejection and cardiac allograft vasculopathy, and monitor for infection and malignancy.
title: Heart Transplant for Advanced Heart Failure: A Review.

summary:
Importance

Although metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is traditionally associated with obesity, it is increasingly recognized in individuals with normal weight (ie, lean MASLD).

Objective

To characterize the clinical, histologic, and prognostic features of lean MASLD, and evaluate the performance of noninvasive tests for advanced fibrosis.

Design, setting, and participants

Multinational, retrospective observational study of adults with biopsy-confirmed MASLD from 41 countries from the Global MASLD project.

Exposures

Lean vs overweight/obese MASLD, defined by body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference.

Main outcomes and measures

Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and clinical events (hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatic decompensation, liver transplant, death), intermediate outcomes included histologic fibrosis severity, and tests included the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score and liver stiffness measurement (LSM) by transient elastography.

Results

Among 18 326 patients (mean [SD] age, 50.9 [13.1] years; 8714 [47.6%] male), 6.7% were lean by BMI. Among 12 202 patients with waist circumference available, 6.0% were lean by waist circumference (κ = 0.41). Lean MASLD was most prevalent in Asia (11.3% by BMI, 11.7% by waist circumference). Compared with overweight/obese MASLD, lean MASLD had lower prevalence of type 2 diabetes (38.2% vs 48.3%; difference, -10.2% [95% CI, -13.0% to -7.4%]), advanced fibrosis (29.3% vs 37.2%; difference, -7.8% [95% CI, -10.5% to -5.2%]), and Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease Activity Scores (mean [SD], 3.96 [1.81] vs 4.41 [1.68]; difference, -0.44 [95% CI, -0.56 to -0.33]). The FIB-4 demonstrated lower accuracy for predicting advanced fibrosis (F3-F4) in lean vs overweight/obese MASLD (area under the curve, 0.76 [95% CI, 0.73-0.79] vs 0.79 [95% CI, 0.78-0.80]; difference, -0.03 [95% CI, -0.06 to 0.00]), while LSM had higher accuracy (area under the curve, 0.87 [95% CI, 0.84-0.90] vs 0.83 [95% CI, 0.82-0.84]; difference, 0.04 [95% CI, 0.01-0.07]). Unadjusted rates per 100 person-years in lean vs overweight/obese MASLD were 1.08 vs 0.91 for all-cause mortality and 1.51 vs 1.43 for clinical events, respectively; lean status was not independently associated with all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 0.90 [95% CI, 0.69-1.16]) or clinical events (aHR, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.76-1.17]). Advanced fibrosis (F3-F4) was associated with all-cause mortality (1.46 vs 0.77 per 100 person-years; aHR, 2.10 [95% CI, 1.71-2.57]) and clinical events (3.21 vs 0.89 per 100 person-years; aHR, 3.41 [95% CI, 2.90-4.03]).

Conclusions and relevance

Lean MASLD represents a distinct phenotype with milder histologic disease but similar clinical outcomes compared with overweight/obese MASLD. Fibrosis severity, rather than body composition, was associated with prognosis and LSM was reliable in lean individuals.
title: Histologic Features and Clinical Outcomes of Lean Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease.

summary: In the past 5 years, substantial changes have been made in the use of intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) in patients with acute ischemic stroke. Integrating IVT with endovascular thrombectomy, which improves outcomes in patients with stroke due to large cerebral vessel occlusion, has been a particular challenge. This review discusses the underlying vascular targets for IVT and thrombectomy, the increasing use of tenecteplase instead of alteplase, broadening indications for the use of IVT, and ancillary drugs and dosing methods that may augment the success of IVT.
title: Intravenous Thrombolysis for Acute Ischemic Stroke - New Directions.

summary:
Importance

Effective neuroprotective and neuroreparative therapies for acute ischemic stroke remain limited. Loberamisal is a small-molecule compound that dually targets the postsynaptic density 95 (PSD-95) pathway and α2 γ-aminobutyric acid type α (α2-GABAA) receptor.

Objective

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of intravenous loberamisal for improving functional outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke.

Design, setting, and participants

The Loberamisal for Acute Ischemic Stroke (LAIS) trial was a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 clinical trial conducted at 32 hospitals in China. Adults aged 18 to 80 years with acute ischemic stroke, a baseline National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score of 7 to 20, and no prestroke disability (modified Rankin Scale score, ≤1) who presented within 48 hours of symptom onset were enrolled between July 24, 2024, and December 7, 2024, with final follow-up on April 8, 2025.

Interventions

Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive intravenous loberamisal (40 mg) or matching placebo once daily for 10 consecutive days, in addition to standard stroke care.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was achieving a full functional outcome at 90 days, defined as a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0 to 1. Safety outcomes included adverse events, serious adverse events, and mortality.

Results

Among 998 randomized participants, 997 received at least 1 dose of the study drug and were included in the primary analysis (502 in the loberamisal group and 495 in the placebo group). The median age was 64 years (IQR, 57-71), 336 participants (33.7%) were women, and the median baseline NIHSS score was 8 (IQR, 7-9). At 90 days, 350 participants (69.7%) in the loberamisal group achieved an mRS score of 0 to 1 compared with 279 (56.3%) in the placebo group (relative risk, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.12-1.36; risk difference, 13.28%; 95% CI, 7.24%-19.32%). Adverse events occurred in 441 participants (87.8%) in the loberamisal group and 439 (88.7%) in the placebo group. Serious adverse events occurred in 43 participants (8.6%) in the loberamisal group and 53 (10.7%) in the placebo group. All-cause mortality occurred in 6 participants (1.2%) in the loberamisal group and 10 (2.0%) in the placebo group.

Conclusions and relevance

Among patients with acute ischemic stroke treated within 48 hours of symptom onset, intravenous loberamisal, compared with placebo, resulted in a higher proportion of patients achieving full functional outcomes at 90 days. Further studies are needed to validate these findings and establish whether the benefits could extend to a broader patient population.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06517173.
title: Loberamisal for Acute Ischemic Stroke: The LAIS Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Importance

Nicotinamide riboside, a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide precursor, has been proposed as a potential disease-modifying therapy for Parkinson disease based on preclinical and early studies. Whether prolonged oral nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in Parkinson disease is unknown.

Objective

To determine whether nicotinamide riboside improves clinical outcomes in Parkinson disease compared with placebo.

Design, setting, and participants

Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 clinical trial conducted at 11 centers in Norway. Eligible participants were patients aged 35 years or older with Parkinson disease diagnosed within 2 years before enrollment, Hoehn and Yahr disease stage less than 3, abnormal dopamine transporter scintigraphy findings confirming dopaminergic nigrostriatal denervation, and stable dopaminergic treatment before enrollment. Of 537 screened individuals, 410 were randomized from May 6, 2020, to June 20, 2024, and 393 were included in the primary analysis. Final follow-up was completed on June 19, 2025.

Interventions

Patients were randomized to receive oral nicotinamide riboside, 500 mg twice daily (n = 206), or matching placebo (n = 204) for 52 weeks.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was change from baseline to week 52 in the Movement Disorder Society Unified Parkinson Disease Rating Scale total score (MDS-UPDRS parts I-III; range, 0-236, with higher scores indicating more severe disease; clinically important differences for improvement and worsening, 6.7 and 5.2 points, respectively), analyzed using a mixed model for repeated measures. The 5 key secondary outcomes were the individual parts I, II, and III of the MDS-UPDRS; dopamine transporter single-photon emission computed tomography brain imaging findings; and the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale score (NMSS; range, 0-360, with higher scores indicating greater nonmotor symptom burden).

Results

Among the 393 participants in the primary analysis, the mean age was 65.6 (SD, 9.4) years and 133 (34%) were female. At week 52, the total MDS-UPDRS score increased by 2.45 (95% CI, 0.80-4.10) points with nicotinamide riboside and decreased by 0.27 (95% CI, -1.95 to 1.40) points with placebo, yielding an adjusted mean difference of 2.72 points (95% CI, 0.47-4.98 points; P = .02), favoring placebo. Of the 5 prespecified key secondary outcomes, 4 showed no significant difference, but nonmotor symptom burden worsened more with nicotinamide riboside (NMSS score adjusted mean difference, 4.22 [95% CI, 1.07-7.37] points; P = .009). Serious adverse events occurred in 17 (8.3%) of 205 participants receiving nicotinamide riboside and 29 (14.1%) of 205 receiving placebo in the safety population.

Conclusions and relevance

Among patients with early Parkinson disease, nicotinamide riboside treatment for 52 weeks did not improve clinical outcomes and was associated with worse clinical outcomes than placebo. These findings do not support nicotinamide riboside as a disease-modifying treatment for Parkinson disease.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03568968.
title: Nicotinamide Riboside for Patients With Early-Stage Parkinson Disease: The NOPARK Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Importance

Obesity affects 15% of children aged 2 to 5 years and 22% of children aged 6 to 11 years in the US. Obesity in children is associated with dyslipidemia, hypertension, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and obstructive sleep apnea. Compared with normal-weight peers, children with obesity have lower quality of life and are 5 times more likely to have obesity in adulthood.

Observations

Body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) is used to identify children at risk for excess adiposity, and guidelines recommend that clinicians screen for obesity using BMI starting at age 2 years. Among children, obesity is defined using standardized age- and sex-specific growth charts, with obesity defined as BMI in the 95th or higher percentile and severe obesity as BMI of 120% or greater of the 95th percentile. Obesity treatment in children includes intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, consisting of at least 26 contact hours of face-to-face group or family-based activities that incorporate nutrition, physical activity, and behavior change education delivered to the child and caregivers over a 3- to 12-month period. Intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment reduces BMI by 0.7 compared with children who do not participate in intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment. The only obesity pharmacotherapy currently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for children younger than 12 years is setmelanotide, a melanocortin-4 receptor agonist, which is indicated for 3 forms of rare monogenic obesity (LEPR, POMC, and PCSK1 genetic variants), Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and acquired hypothalamic obesity. Liraglutide is currently only FDA approved for youth aged 12 years or older; however, a randomized clinical trial among children aged 6 to younger than 12 years demonstrated that, compared with placebo, liraglutide reduced BMI by 7.4%. Metabolic and bariatric surgery is rarely used in children younger than age 12 years and evidence supporting its use in children is limited. Early identification and treatment of obesity during childhood may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and mortality in adulthood.

Conclusions and relevance

Obesity in children is associated with chronic disease, such as hypertension, and with poor quality of life. Evidence-based treatment for obesity in children includes intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, and pharmacotherapy may provide additional benefit, although short- and long-term safety and efficacy data are limited. Early identification and treatment of obesity during childhood may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and mortality in adulthood.
title: Obesity in Children Aged 2 to 12 Years: A Review.

summary:
Importance

Patent protection allows pharmaceutical companies to charge high prices for prescription drugs during periods of market exclusivity, and their expiration usually defines when generic competitors can enter the US market. Patents on drug active ingredients are classified as primary patents, while patents on formulations, methods of use, and delivery devices are nonprimary.

Objective

To evaluate how pharmaceutical patent portfolios for US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drugs have evolved over time.

Evidence review

Patents on small-molecule drugs approved by the FDA from 1990 to 2019 were examined and assessed for changes in the number and types of patents per product. The additional duration of total patent exclusivity associated with each patent type was quantified, and how often patents of each type were enforced against generic manufacturers in litigation was determined.

Findings

The FDA approved 1981 small-molecule drugs during the study period, and manufacturers listed 10 940 patents on these drugs. The mean number of patents per drug increased from 2.1 in 1990 to 6.9 in 2019, driven primarily by nonprimary patents. The mean number of nonprimary patents per drug rose from 1.2 in 1990 to 5.6 in 2019. Nonprimary patents represented majorities of FDA-listed patents (84% [9236/10 940]) and litigated patents (87% [4586/5253]). Nearly all patents listed after drug approval were nonprimary (96% [4874/5064]), and these patents extended market exclusivity by a mean of 6.1 years (SD, 5.8 years) and a median of 4.7 years (IQR, 0.2-10.1 years).

Conclusions and relevance

Pharmaceutical patent portfolios have grown over the last 2 decades. These portfolios have largely been built on nonprimary patents, which are then enforced against generic firms at higher rates than primary patents. Large patent portfolios can complicate routine generic competition and prolong periods of high drug prices.
title: Patents on Small-Molecule Drugs Approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, 1990-2019.

summary:
Background

Severe hypertriglyceridemia is associated with an increased risk of acute pancreatitis. Plozasiran, a small interfering RNA targeting APOC3 messenger RNA, lowers triglyceride levels and potentially mitigates the risk of acute pancreatitis.

Methods

In two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, 757 adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive plozasiran (25 mg) or placebo at baseline and at months 3, 6, and 9. These trials had identical designs, end points, and analytic plans. The primary end point was the percent change in the fasting plasma triglyceride level from baseline to month 12. Key secondary end points were the percent change in the fasting triglyceride level from baseline to month 10, a fasting triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter (5.6 mmol per liter) and less than 150 mg per deciliter (1.7 mmol per liter), the percent change in the fasting serum triglyceride level at month 12 for patients with a baseline triglyceride level of 880 mg per deciliter or greater, and changes in remnant cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol. A pooled analysis addressed adjudicated acute pancreatitis, incidence, and first-event timing.

Results

At month 12, patients in the plozasiran groups had a median triglyceride level that was lower than the baseline level by 79% and 81% in the two trials. These reductions corresponded to a median difference in the plozasiran groups as compared with the placebo groups (placebo-adjusted change) of -45 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], -51 to -38) and -47 percentage points (95% CI, -54 to -39). A triglyceride level of less than 500 mg per deciliter at 12 months was reported in 91% and 93% of the patients in the plozasiran groups and in 51% and 50% of those in the placebo groups (P<0.001). The rates of acute pancreatitis were 1 per 100 patient-years with plozasiran and 5 per 100 patient-years with placebo (rate ratio, 0.22; P = 0.008). Adverse events during treatment occurred in 73% of the patients in both the pooled plozasiran and placebo groups.

Conclusions

Among patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia, the use of plozasiran resulted in lower triglyceride levels and a lower risk of acute pancreatitis than placebo at 12 months. (Funded by Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals; SHASTA-3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06347003; SHASTA-4, NCT06347016.).
title: Plozasiran for Severe Hypertriglyceridemia and Risk of Pancreatitis.

summary: Malaria continues to be a major health challenge worldwide, causing an estimated 282 million cases of illness and 610,000 deaths in 2024, predominantly among African children. Despite recent stagnation in the progress of malaria prevention, the landscape is undergoing rapid transformation. This review examines current and emerging approaches to preventing malaria infection and supporting malaria elimination, including vector control, transmission-blocking interventions, chemoprevention, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines. Next-generation insecticide-treated nets, expanded use of seasonal malaria chemoprevention, and the introduction of RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M vaccines are already reshaping control strategies. Looking ahead, long-acting injectable chemoprevention, transmission-blocking medicines and vaccines, and improved surveillance-driven deployment may further accelerate progress. As funding becomes constrained and decision making shifts increasingly to countries where malaria is endemic, effective malaria prevention will depend on locally tailored, integrated combinations of interventions supported by strong surveillance, regulatory capacity, and national leadership.
title: Preventing Malaria Infections and Moving toward Malaria Elimination.

summary:
Background

Studies comparing aspirin with anticoagulants for venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty have had conflicting results.

Methods

In a comparative-effectiveness noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned patients undergoing elective hip or knee arthroplasty to receive aspirin (81 mg twice daily), warfarin (to a target international normalized ratio of 2.0), or rivaroxaban (10 mg daily) for 30 days. The composite primary effectiveness outcome (death from any cause or symptomatic VTE) and primary safety outcome (bleeding, reoperation for wound problems, or myocardial infarction) were evaluated through 6 months in a blinded fashion. The noninferiority margin for the risk difference was 0.69 percentage points.

Results

Among 18,883 participants who had undergone randomization, 15,317 (7214 with hip arthroplasty and 8103 with knee arthroplasty) were included in the primary per-protocol analysis. A primary effectiveness outcome event occurred in 77 of 6090 participants (1.26%) in the aspirin group, in 52 of 4231 (1.23%) in the warfarin group, and in 47 of 4996 (0.94%) in the rivaroxaban group; a primary safety outcome event occurred in 177 (2.91%), 142 (3.36%), and 174 (3.48%), respectively. In pairwise comparisons, 6-month risks of a primary effectiveness outcome event were 1.24% and 0.94% for aspirin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.30 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.20 to 0.81); 1.24% and 1.01% for aspirin versus warfarin (difference, 0.23 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.34 to 0.81); and 1.13% and 1.10% for warfarin versus rivaroxaban (difference, 0.03 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.57 to 0.63). Risks of a primary safety outcome event were 3.70% and 3.02% for rivaroxaban versus aspirin (difference, 0.68 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.41); 3.65% and 2.88% for warfarin versus aspirin (difference, 0.77 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.04 to 1.58); and 3.59% and 3.61% for rivaroxaban versus warfarin (difference, -0.02 percentage points; 95% CI, -0.89 to 0.85). Intention-to-treat analyses yielded similar results.

Conclusions

Aspirin prophylaxis after total hip or knee arthroplasty was not noninferior to rivaroxaban or warfarin with respect to death or symptomatic VTE. Warfarin and rivaroxaban were not noninferior to aspirin for safety. (Funded by the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute; PEPPER ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02810704.).
title: Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism after Total Hip or Knee Replacement.

summary:
Importance

Whether intravenous tenecteplase before endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) improves outcomes in patients with basilar artery occlusion presenting 4.5 to 24 hours after stroke onset remains uncertain.

Objective

To evaluate the efficacy and safety of intravenous tenecteplase before EVT vs EVT alone in patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion admitted within 4.5 to 24 hours from stroke onset.

Design, setting, and participants

This multicenter, open-label, blinded end point, randomized clinical trial was conducted at 40 stroke centers in China. Between March 16, 2023, and February 4, 2025, a total of 330 patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score ≥10) presenting within 4.5 to 24 hours from stroke onset to EVT-capable centers were enrolled. Final follow-up was completed on May 4, 2025.

Interventions

Patients were randomized 1:1 via a centralized web server using a minimization method to receive either intravenous tenecteplase (bolus injection, 0.25 mg/kg; maximum, 25 mg) followed by EVT (n = 166) or EVT alone (n = 164).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was functional independence (modified Rankin Scale score, 0-2) at 90 days. Safety outcomes included symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and 90-day mortality.

Results

Among 332 patients randomized, 2 withdrew consent. Of the remaining 330 patients (mean [SD] age, 66 [11] years; 241 males [73%]; 89 females [27%]), 329 completed 90-day follow-up. Of whom, 50 of 165 (30%) in the tenecteplase plus EVT group and 50 of 164 (30%) in the EVT alone group achieved functional independence (adjusted rate ratio, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.67 to 1.25]; risk difference, -0.18% [95% CI, -10.13% to 9.76%]). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 8 patients (5%) in the tenecteplase plus EVT group and 6 (4%) in the EVT alone group. Mortality at 90 days was similar between the groups (66 [40%] vs 70 [43%], respectively).

Conclusions and relevance

Among patients with moderate to severe basilar artery occlusion admitted directly to EVT-capable centers who presented 4.5 to 24 hours after stroke onset, the addition of intravenous tenecteplase before EVT did not result in improved functional outcomes compared with EVT alone.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05701956.
title: Tenecteplase Before Thrombectomy at 4.5 to 24 Hours for Basilar Artery Occlusion: The ATTENTION LATE Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Importance

Following a left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) procedure, antithrombotic therapy is administered to safely allow time for device endothelialization. However, the optimal postimplant antithrombotic regimen is unknown.

Objective

To determine if either reduced-dose non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs) or aspirin alone are noninferior to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) for the composite clinical end point of death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding through 6 months post LAAC.

Design, setting, and participants

This open-label, 3-group, multicenter clinical trial randomized 1857 patients between October 2024 and December 2025 at 87 US investigational sites, with the final 6-month follow-up in July 2026. Enrolled patients had nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, underwent successful LAAC, and were eligible for all 3 regimens.

Interventions

Patients were randomly allocated 1:1:1 to DAPT for 6 months followed by aspirin (n = 624), a reduced-dose NOAC for 3 months followed by aspirin (n = 620), or aspirin alone for 12 months (n = 613).

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was the 6-month composite of all-cause death, stroke, systemic embolism, or major bleeding. Noninferiority was tested in the primary analysis population with a 1-sided Farrington-Manning test (α = .025). Bleeding and 45-day device-related thrombus rates were exploratory without multiplicity adjustment.

Results

The cohort had a mean age of 76 (SD, 8) years, 42.9% were female, the mean CHA2DS2-VASc score was 4.2 (SD, 1.3), and 68.0% had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. The primary outcome occurred in 41 patients (6.9%) with DAPT vs 31 (5.1%) with a reduced-dose NOAC (risk ratio, 0.75 [95% CI, 0.48-1.18]; risk difference, -1.7 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, 1.2) and 20 (3.3%) with aspirin alone (risk ratio, 0.49 [95% CI, 0.29-0.82]; risk difference, -3.5 percentage points; 97.5% upper bound, -0.8). Both monotherapy strategies met noninferiority criteria (P < .001 for noninferiority for both). Major bleeding was 4.5% with DAPT, 2.7% with reduced-dose NOACs, and 1.7% with aspirin alone; clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was 8.7%, 4.8%, and 3.8%, respectively. Device-related thrombus was observed in 3.4%, 0.9%, and 2.7%, respectively.

Conclusions and relevance

Both reduced-dose NOACs and aspirin alone were noninferior to DAPT for 6-month outcomes after uncomplicated LAAC.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06521463.
title: Antithrombotic Therapy After Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: The SIMPLAAFY Randomized Clinical Trial.

summary:
Background

For patients with moderate aortic stenosis, current guidelines recommend clinical surveillance with echocardiographic assessment every 1 or 2 years. Whether transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) will improve outcomes in these patients remains unknown.

Methods

We conducted an international, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate whether TAVR will result in better outcomes than clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature (i.e., a symptom or structural or functional abnormality that has been shown to be associated with faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes). The patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance. The primary effectiveness end point was a composite of death from any cause or a heart-failure event with or without hospitalization at 2 years. Superiority testing was performed in the intention-to-treat population.

Results

A total of 744 patients underwent randomization: 373 patients were assigned to the TAVR group and 371 to the clinical-surveillance group. The mean age of patients was 78 years, 39.1% were women, and 45.6% were at low surgical risk. The mean aortic-valve area was 1.2 cm2, and the mean aortic-valve peak velocity was 3.3 m per second. At 2 years, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients with a primary effectiveness end-point event was 16.7% in the TAVR group and 23.9% in the clinical-surveillance group (risk difference, -7.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -13.1 to -1.3; P = 0.02 for superiority). The Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients who died from any cause was 8.4% in the TAVR group and 7.3% in the clinical-surveillance group; the estimates for a heart-failure event were 10.8% and 19.0%, respectively. The incidence of procedure-related adverse events did not differ meaningfully between the patients in the TAVR group and those in the clinical-surveillance group who underwent aortic-valve replacement.

Conclusions

Among patients with moderate aortic stenosis and at-risk features, a strategy of TAVR was superior to clinical surveillance in lowering the incidence of death or a heart-failure event at 2 years. (Funded by Edwards Lifesciences; PROGRESS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04889872.).
title: TAVR in Patients with Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features.

summary:
Background

Randomized trials have shown limited benefits and increased risks of adding spinal fusion surgery to decompression for degenerative spondylolisthesis. Decompression with fusion has increasingly been used in the United States.

Objective

To examine the comparative effectiveness of decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for patient subgroups.

Design

Cohort study using the target trial framework.

Setting

Norwegian Registry for Spine Surgery and nested NORDSTEN-DS (Norwegian degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis) randomized trial.

Patients

Adults aged 18 to 80 years with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least 3 months.

Intervention

Lumbar spinal decompression surgery with fusion versus lumbar spinal decompression surgery alone.

Measurements

The primary outcomes were Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) score and reoperation at 12 months. Linear regression models with inverse probability weighting to control for baseline confounding were used to obtain effect estimates with 95% CIs for decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for prespecified subgroups, including sex, age, smoking, body mass index (BMI), back pain intensity, and American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade.

Results

Of 2252 patients, 236 were in the NORDSTEN-DS randomized trial. The mean age was 66 years, and 1576 (70%) women were included. A total of 1446 patients had decompression alone, and 806 had decompression with fusion; respective unadjusted baseline ODI scores were 38.9 (SD, 14.9) and 41.4 (SD, 14.7). At 12 months, the ODI score was 22.3 (95% CI, 15.5 to 29.1) for decompression alone and 20.0 (CI, 13.9 to 26.2) for decompression with fusion; the mean difference was 2.2 (CI, -1.6 to 6.1). In exploratory analyses, the ODI score was worse for decompression with fusion for men with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher. Reoperation risk at 12 months did not differ.

Limitation

Possible residual confounding.

Conclusion

Patient subgroups did not have differential effects from the addition of fusion to decompression at 12 months.

Primary funding source

Research Council of Norway.
title: Decompression With or Without Fusion Across Subgroups With Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis : A Target Trial Emulation.

summary:
Background

Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents has been widely used to treat patients with left main coronary artery disease; however, long-term comparative outcomes versus coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in real-world populations remain poorly characterised. We aimed to compare long-term all-cause mortality after PCI or CABG in Asian patients with unprotected left main coronary artery disease.

Methods

We analysed prospectively collected data from the multicentre IRIS-MAIN registry, conducted at 46 hospitals in South Korea, India, Japan, Indonesia, and Malaysia. The registry enrolled adults aged 18 years or older with unprotected left main coronary artery disease (defined as a stenosis diameter of ≥50% as visually estimated on angiography), who had been treated with PCI, CABG, or medical therapy alone. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. We used a target trial emulation framework to compare the long-term risk of all-cause mortality between PCI with drug-eluting stents and isolated CABG. We used propensity-score overlap weighting to adjust for measured baseline covariates. The IRIS-MAIN Registry study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01341327).

Findings

Between Jan 1, 2003, and Dec 31, 2024, 6900 patients were enrolled in the IRIS-MAIN registry, of whom 5379 (78·0%) underwent coronary revascularisation through either PCI with drug-eluting stents (3836 [71·3%]) or CABG (1543 [28·7%]) and were included in the analysis. The median duration of follow-up for all patients was 10·0 years (IQR 5·0-16·7). In the overlap-weighted population, no statistically detectable difference in 10-year weighted Kaplan-Meier rates of all-cause mortality was observed between PCI and CABG (24·0% vs 22·9%; overlap-weighted hazard ratio 1·00 [95% CI 0·87-1·14]; p=0·99). The confidence interval does not exclude a mortality benefit or harm with either strategy.

Interpretation

In this non-randomised registry analysis of patients with left main coronary artery disease, there was no statistically detectable difference in all-cause mortality between PCI and CABG. For patients considered suitable for either strategy, multidisciplinary Heart Team discussion might help patients and clinicians weigh potential trade-offs in the choice between PCI and CABG. These findings are observational and cannot establish causal treatment effects or equivalence in survival.

Funding

The CardioVascular Research Foundation (South Korea).
title: Long-term outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents versus coronary artery bypass grafting for left main coronary artery disease: a prospective analysis of the multicentre IRIS-MAIN registry.

summary:
Background

Long COVID (LC) is widespread; however, limited information has been reported on the likelihood that symptoms remit over time.

Objective

To evaluate the likelihood of improvement among persons with likely LC.

Design

Prospective, multisite cohort study (RECOVER-Adult [Researching COVID to Enhance Recovery]).

Setting

83 U.S.-based sites across 33 states; Washington, DC; and Puerto Rico.

Participants

1019 persons in RECOVER-Adult with likely LC (LC Research Index [LCRI] ≥11) 12 months after first SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Measurements

The primary outcome was time until 2 consecutive study visits with LCRI less than 11. Secondary outcomes were time until LCRI measure reduced 50% or more and quality of life was good or better, and LCRI decreased to 0. Unadjusted estimates of cumulative incidence and adjusted marginal cumulative incidence by age, sex, SARS-CoV-2 wave, and LC subtype were reported across all follow-up time points.

Results

An estimated 36.2% (95% CI, 33.0% to 39.5%) met the primary outcome by 24 months after infection, and 50.1% (CI, 46.1% to 54.0%) met the primary outcome by 36 months. An estimated 56.4% (CI, 52.2% to 60.4%) and 26.9% (CI, 23.3% to 30.5%), respectively, met the 2 secondary outcomes by 36 months. Among persons who still reported likely LC at 18 months and 24 months after first infection, relative timing of subsequent symptom improvement was similar.

Limitation

Findings in this observational cohort are interpretable in a population with prevalent likely LC and do not address causal relationships between individual characteristics and symptom improvement.

Conclusion

Among persons with likely LC 12 months after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, one half experience meaningful reductions in symptoms by 36 months, whereas a quarter experience complete remission of symptoms. These findings underscore both the potential for natural recovery and the urgent need for placebo-controlled therapeutic intervention trials.

Primary funding source

National Institutes of Health.
title: Timing of Long COVID Improvement in Prospectively Followed RECOVER-Adult Participants.

summary: Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Home Health Prospective Payment System Final Rule Fact Sheet (CMS-1844-P) On November 4, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule that announces policy changes under the Home Health (HH) Prospective Payment System (PPS), consistent with the legal requirements to update Medicare payment policies for home health agencies (HHAs) annually. This fact sheet discusses the final rule’s major provisions. Medicare Provider Enrollment In its ongoing efforts to crush fraud, waste, and abuse, CMS is finalizing several provider enrollment provisions. Most of the provisions will apply to all provider types enrolled in the Medicare program. T hese changes will help reduce improper Medicare payments and protect beneficiaries. The provisions include, but are not limited to, the following: Retroactive Revocations — Under current regulations, certain Medicare enrollment revocations become effective prospectively — specifically, 30 days after the date that CMS or the CMS contractor mails notice of the revocation to the affected provider or supplier (hereafter “provider”). However, other revocations take effect retroactively to the date the provider’s noncompliance began. CMS is finalizing a policy to make all revocation grounds retroactive. This action will help CMS recover monies paid to non-compliant providers and help ensure taxpayer money is paid only to legitimate, compliant providers. Adding or Expanding Bases for Revocation or Denial — CMS is adding several new grounds for revocation or denial of enrollment and expanding some of its existing grounds. Among these provisions are the following: Change in Majority Ownership — Hospices; HHAs; and suppliers of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) must reenroll in Medicare as a new provider and undergo a survey/accreditation if they experience certain changes in majority ownership. CMS will have the authority to deny or revoke enrollment if the provider does not comply with this requirement. Program or License Suspension/Termination — CMS currently may deny or revoke enrollment if a provider: (1) has a suspended/revoked license in another state; or (2) is suspended/revoked from Medicaid or another federal healthcare program. We are expanding this to include similar suspensions/revocations involving the provider’s owners or managing employees/organizations. The final revocation/denial authorities address situations noted by CMS as involving provider noncompliance and actual and potential fraud, waste, and abuse. They also would allow the agency to target improper activity by those who own or operate Medicare providers. CY 2027 Final Payment and Policy Updates for Home Health Agencies The provisions in this final rule will help improve patient care and protect the Medicare program’s sustainability for future generations. This rule finalizes routine, statutorily required updates to the home health payment rates for CY 2027. The CY 2027 updated rates include the final CY 2027 home health payment update of 2.1% ($365 million increase) and an estimated 0.3% increase that reflects the updated fixed dollar loss (FDL) amount ($50 million increase). CMS estimates that Medicare payments to HHAs in CY 2027 would increase in the aggregate by 2.4%, or $415 million, compared to CY 2026, based on the finalized policies. In this final rule, CMS is also continuing its implementation of a 30-day unit of payment and of the Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM) case-mix adjustment methodology within the HH PPS per the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018. Specifically, it includes an analysis of the difference between assumed versus actual behavior change on estimated aggregate expenditures for home health payments linked to these changes. This rule also discusses the permanent adjustments to HH PPS payment rates applied in previous years and finalizes a temporary adjustment to the CY 2027 home health base payment rate of -3.0%. CMS did not propose an additional permanent adjustment to the CY 2027 30-day base payment rate; however we continue to annually analyze the data through CY 2026 claims, as required by section 1895(b)(3)(D)(ii) of the Social Security Act (the Act), to determine any additional permanent adjustments to account for the impact of implementing the PDGM. In addition, CMS finalizes the recalibrated PDGM case-mix weights; updates the FDL for outlier payments; and updates the low utilization payment adjustment (LUPA) thresholds, functional impairment levels, and comorbidity adjustment subgroups for CY 2027. This final rule also responds to comments received on the provision of palliative care services under the Medicare home health benefit and the request for information (RFI) regarding the construction of a home health specific wage index included in the proposed rule. PDGM and Behavior Assumptions On January 1, 2020, CMS implemented the home health PDGM and a 30-day unit of payment (previously 60 days), as required by section 1895(b) of the Social Security Act, as amended by the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018. The PDGM better aligns payments with patient care needs, especially for clinically complex individuals. The law required CMS to make assumptions about behavior changes that could occur because of the 30-day unit of payment and the PDGM. CMS finalized three behavior assumptions in the CY 2019 HH PPS final rule: clinical group coding, comorbidity coding, and LUPA threshold. The law also requires CMS to annually determine the impact of differences between assumed behavior changes and actual behavior changes on estimated aggregate expenditures, beginning with 2020 and ending with 2026, and to make temporary and permanent increases or decreases, as needed, to the 30-day payment amount to offset such increases or decreases. In the CY 2023 HH PPS final rule (87 FR 66790), CMS finalized a methodology for analyzing the differences between assumed and actual behavior changes on estimated aggregate expenditures and calculated levels of actual and estimated aggregate expenditures. Based on analyses of CYs 2020 and 2021 claims data, CMS determined a permanent adjustment was needed and finalized implementing half (-3.925%) of the permanent adjustment estimated at the time (-7.85%). For CYs 2024 (88 FR 77676) and 2025 (88 FR 88373), using CY 2022 and 2023 claims, respectively, CMS similarly implemented half of the permanent adjustments estimated at those times (-2.890% out of -5.779% total for 2024 and -1.975% out of -3.95% total for 2025). In the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule (90 FR 55342), CMS finalized a policy applying the remaining permanent adjustment for claims years 2020-2022, as our analysis indicated that behavior changes after 2022 could be related to other policy factors beyond the PDGM implementation. As such, we exercised the authority expressly delegated under the statute to apply permanent adjustments “at a time and in a manner appropriate” to the remaining permanent adjustment of -1.023% to account for behavior changes associated with the PDGM implementation in CYs 2020 through 2022. We also exercised our authority to begin recouping retrospective overpayments (i.e., the temporary adjustment) for CYs 2020 through 2024 and finalized a temporary adjustment with a 3.0% reduction in CY 2026. In the CY 2027 HH PPS final rule, similar to the policies finalized in the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule (90 FR 55364 through 55365), we state that behavior changes reflected in preliminary CY 2025 claims for this CY 2027 final rule may not be directly attributable to the PDGM. Other confounding factors began in CY 2023 (i.e., continued recalibration of case-mix weights, a change to the OASIS-E, and previous reductions to the home health payment rate). While we did not propose an additional permanent adjustment to the CY 2027 30-day base payment rate, this final rule continues to satisfy the statutory requirements at section 1895(b)(3)(D)(ii) of the Act as it includes our annual analysis of the data, as required by law, to determine if any additional permanent adjustments would be needed based on the impact of assumed versus actual behavior change on estimated aggregate expenditures from implementing the PDGM and the 30-day unit of payment. In accordance with the statutory requirement to ensure that the permanent adjustments are implemented in a budget-neutral manner, we finalized our proposal to implement a temporary adjustment of -3.0% to the CY 2027 national, standardized payment rate. This finalized proposal continues recoupment of the retrospective overpayments made for CYs 2020 through 2025 through “one or more” temporary adjustments. We believe that continuing to incrementally adjust the base payment rate to account for the calculated temporary dollar amount to date may help reduce the need for a large reduction in future years. Update to the Fixed-Dollar Loss Amount The HH PPS allows outlier payments to be made to providers for periods of care with unusually large costs due to patient home healthcare needs. Outlier payments are made for periods of care when the estimated costs exceed a threshold amount. To determine the threshold, the 30-day period of care payment rate is multiplied by a fixed-dollar loss (FDL) ratio and then wage-adjusted to derive the FDL amount. The FDL ratio is determined so outlier payments do not exceed 2.5% of total payments (as required by section 1895(b)(5)(A) of the Act) and are annually recalibrated as part of the routine payment update. The final FDL for CY 2027 is 0.29%. Recalibration of PDGM Case-Mix Weights Each of the 432 payment groups under the PDGM has an associated case-mix weight and LUPA threshold. CMS’ policy is to annually recalibrate the case-mix weights and LUPA thresholds with the most complete utilization data available at the time of rulemaking. In this final rule, CMS is finalizing the recalibrated case-mix weights — including the functional levels and comorbidity adjustment subgroups — and LUPA thresholds with CY 2025 data to more accurately pay for the types of patients HHAs are serving. Provision of Palliative Care Services Under the Home Health Benefit CMS is interested in encouraging beneficiary access to community-based palliative care under the Medicare home health benefit and believes the Medicare home health benefit can be an important step in the care continuum when a patient needs palliative care, either during episodes of serious or progressive illness. In this rule, we respond to comments received on how to best promote access to community-based palliative care services through the Medicare home health benefit. This final rule acknowledges the role of home health in palliative care services and confirms that CMS will provide examples of such services through future sub-regulatory guidance. Request for Information (RFI) on a Home Health-Specific Wage Index This final rule also summarizes and responds to comments received on an RFI on the potential development of a home health-specific wage index from an alternate data source (e.g., Bureau of Labor Statistics) consistent with CMS’s statutory authority and regulatory requirements. Durable Medical Equipment Benefit Expansion for Infusion Pumps and Drugs CMS is amending the Medicare Part B definition of durable medical equipment (DME) at 42 CFR 414.202 to implement Section 6222(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA, 2026), which expands coverage under the DME benefit to certain external infusion pumps and associated home infusion drugs that would be considered appropriate for home use if certain criteria are met, such as the requirement for the drug to be administered by or under the supervision of a healthcare professional. The effective date of this provision is April 1, 2027.
