title: Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Home Health Prospective Payment System Final Rule - CMS-1844-F

summary: Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule On 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule that finalizes policy changes for Medicare payments under the Physician Fee Schedule (PFS), and other Medicare Part B issues, effective on or after Jan. 1, 2027. The calendar year (CY) 2027 PFS final rule is one of several that reflect a broader Administration-wide strategy to create a healthcare system that results in better quality, efficiency, empowerment, and innovation for all Medicare beneficiaries. Background on the Physician Fee Schedule Since 1992, Medicare payment has been made under the PFS for the services of physicians and other billing professionals in a variety of settings. For most services furnished in a physician’s office, Medicare pays physicians and other professionals at a single rate based on the full range of resources involved in furnishing the service. In contrast, PFS rates paid to physicians and other billing practitioners in facility settings, such as a hospital outpatient department (HOPD) or an ambulatory surgical center (ASC), reflect only the portion of the resources typically incurred by the practitioner while furnishing the service. For many diagnostic tests and a limited number of other services under the PFS, separate payment may be made for the professional and technical components of services. The technical component is frequently billed by suppliers for which no institutional payment is made, like independent diagnostic testing facilities and radiation treatment centers, while the professional component is billed by the physician or practitioner. Payments are based on the relative resources typically used to furnish the service. Relative value units (RVUs) are applied to each service for work, practice expense, and malpractice expense. These RVUs become payment rates through the application of a conversion factor. Geographic adjusters (geographic practice cost indices) are also applied to the total RVUs to account for variation in costs by geographic area. Payment rates are calculated to include an overall payment update specified by statute. CY 2027 PFS Rate Setting and Conversion Factor As required by statute, beginning in CY 2026, there are two separate conversion factors: one for qualifying alternative payment model (APM) participants (QPs) and one for physicians and practitioners who are not QPs. By statute, QPs are those that meet certain thresholds for participation in an Advanced APM, which means generally that the payment model has features to ensure accountability for quality and cost of care. The update to the qualifying APM conversion factor for CY 2027 is +0.75% while the update to the non-qualifying APM conversion factor for CY 2027 is +0.25%. The changes to the PFS conversion factors for CY 2027 include these updates as required by statute and an estimated -0.12% adjustment necessary to account for proposed changes in work RVUs for some services. However, Public Law 119-21, which CMS refers to as the Working Families Tax Cut (WFTC) legislation, provided a one-year PFS conversion factor increase of 2.50% for CY 2026, which will no longer be in effect for CY 2027. This effectively means that current law requires -2.50% reduction in Medicare payment under the PFS compared to CY 2026. The CY 2027 qualifying APM conversion factor of $32.95 represents a projected decrease of $0.62 (-1.83%) from the current conversion factor of $33.57. Similarly, the CY 2027 nonqualifying APM conversion factor of $32.63 represents a projected decrease of $0.77 (-2.31%) from the current conversion factor of $33.40. Accounting for Overlap Between Stand-Alone E/M Visits and Global Periods For CY 2027, we proposed to reduce payment when a separately identifiable office/outpatient evaluation and management (E/M) visit is furnished by the same physician (or a physician in the same practice) on the same day as a 0-, 10-, or 90-day global procedure. The most expensive service (either surgical or E/M visit) would be paid at 100% and all other surgical procedure(s) or E/M visit(s) furnished on the same day would be paid at 50%. A similar policy was first proposed in the CY 2019 PFS proposed rule, made in the context of a broader proposal that would have modified the payment structure of E/M visits. While we did not finalize the proposal at that time, we noted in the CY 2019 PFS final rule that we continued to believe that there are efficiencies when the same physician (or a physician in the same group practice) provides an E/M service for the same patient in conjunction with a procedure with a global period and that we are likely duplicating payment under the current payment methodology. After considering the comments we received from the public, we made two significant modifications to our proposed policy. We are finalizing payment reduction when a separately identifiable office/outpatient (O/O) evaluation and management (E/M) visit is furnished on the same day as a 0-day global procedure, rather than also including the 10- or 90-day global procedures as proposed. Additionally, when O/O E/M visits are billed separately with procedures on the same day, the most expensive service (either surgical or E/M visit) will be paid at 100% and the other surgical procedure(s) or O/O E/M visit(s) furnished on the same day will be paid at 80%, rather than 50% as proposed. E/M Visit Complexity Add-On (HCPCS code G2211) In the CY 2021 PFS final rule, we finalized separate payment for the office/outpatient evaluation and management (O/O E/M) visit complexity add-on code, HCPCS code G2211. Policy implementation was temporarily delayed by statute but implemented for CY 2025. For CY 2027, we are finalizing two changes, as proposed. We will transition HCPCS code G2211 to a modifier that can be appended to the associated E/M base code. (This was placeholder modifier MOD1 in the proposed rule. We are finalizing this as modifier B1.) This modifier will increase the payment of the associated E/M code by 16%, instead of a flat rate, maintaining an equal percentage increase across all levels of E/M codes. We believe this will result in more streamlined billing that will be easier for beneficiaries to understand. We also propose to recognize additional resource costs incurred by practitioners in Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) when providing longitudinal care, such as maintaining total cost of care accountability and reporting quality measures that can align with providing longitudinal care and care coordination. This modifier (placeholder modifier MOD2, now being finalized as modifier B2) will be available only for practitioners participating in a Shared Savings Program ACO or Participant Providers in a Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model ACO and would increase payment of the associated E/M visit by 32%. Under the Shared Savings Program, use of the B2 modifier is voluntary and available to be billed for all beneficiaries to whom an ACO participant or provider furnishes services, not limited only to Shared Savings Program-assigned beneficiaries. The B2 modifier would also be voluntary for the LEAD Model and will be available to be billed for all beneficiaries to whom the Participant Provider furnishes services, not limited only to LEAD-aligned beneficiaries. Claims submitted with B2 will be included in beneficiary assignment calculations, historical benchmark expenditures, and performance year expenditures for both the Shared Savings Program and the LEAD Model. Remote Monitoring Recently, we have established payment for two code families that describe certain remote monitoring services: remote physiologic monitoring (RPM) and remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM). For CY 2027, we proposed: (1) RTM services be furnished only to established patients; (2) practitioners reporting RPM or RTM services must furnish a separately reportable initiating visit in association with the onset of RPM or RTM services; (3) updates to how these services are valued under the PFS; and (4) only allowing payment for RPM or RTM services when performed by clinical staff employed by the practice and not when those services are delivered by contractors. We are finalizing the first three of these policies as proposed for CY 2027. After consideration of the public comments, we are delaying for two years, to Jan. 1, 2029, the requirement to only allow payment for RPM or RTM services when performed by clinical staff employed by the practice to provide additional time for practices to adapt to this aspect of the policy. This policy will be effective for RPM and RTM services beginning with CY 2029. We also sought comment in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule on bundling the RPM and RTM CPT codes and creating four new HCPCS G-codes to describe remote monitoring services. We received public comments on this proposal and may consider these comments for future rulemaking. Practice Expense CMS has historically relied on the American Medical Association (AMA) surveys to estimate physician work, direct practice expense (PE) inputs, and overall PE for calculating payment rates. These recommendations have been limited by several factors, especially from a reliance on resource-intensive but ultimately unreliable surveys with low response rates asking for expert estimates that present significant discrepancies with alternative empirical data sources, in the cases where empirical data exists. These dynamics are particularly problematic for specialty-level practice expense data. In these cases, data collection is particularly burdensome and subject to volatility based on low response rates and significant incongruities in collection methodologies between physician groups and other entities paid under the PFS. We are engaged in a multi-year effort to transition the PE methodology away from reliance on the AMA’s data and toward an approach that relies on more objective, routinely updated and auditable cost data. We believe this change will lead to PFS payments being more sensitive to market pressures, open broader possibilities for right-sizing payments across outpatient care settings and make payments more transparent for practitioners and beneficiaries. As part of reforming the way PE RVUs are assigned to specific services, we are finalizing our proposal to reduce reliance on outdated specialty-specific practice expense per hour (PE/HR) data. Specifically, we are finalizing the phase-out of the indirect practice cost index (IPCI), which ensures the overall number of PE RVUs by specialty is consistent with the old PE/HR data from 2007 or earlier. Under the methodology, the final PE RVUs would still be derived from the input data (including both work RVUs and direct PE inputs, as well as specialty-specific indirect allocators). However, the IPCI will be phased out over two years and replaced with a PE stabilizer that mitigates short term volatility without anchoring overall values to a specific point in time. We are finalizing our proposal to allocate indirect PE on both the work RVU and clinical labor PE RVU, rather than just the maximum of the two, for all codes except 10- and 90-day global period codes. We are also finalizing our proposal to adjust the indirect PE allocation for visits furnished to beneficiaries in a Part A stay in a skilled nursing facility consistent with our site of service payment differential policy finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule. We also received feedback in response to our comment solicitation on whether the site of service payment differential between Facility and Non-facility is still appropriate, or whether we should consider an alternative approach to improve assumptions about indirect practice costs, particularly for physicians employed by a hospital, health system, or other entity. We will consider these comments for future rulemaking. Comment Solicitation on Redesigning Primary Care to Make America Healthy Again For CY 2027, we sou

summary: Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1848-F) — Medicare Shared Savings Program On November 4, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued the calendar year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule (CMS-1848-F), which includes changes to the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program). These policies aim to accelerate accountable care service delivery, further CMS’ goal of aligning spending and value in Original Medicare, and support achieving other related strategic objectives. This fact sheet summarizes the major changes to the Shared Savings Program included in the CY 2027 PFS final rule. We are finalizing changes to the Shared Savings Program’s benchmarking and financial methodology to strengthen financial incentives for ACOs to participate in the program while mitigating selection issues and benchmark rebasing concerns. The changes are projected to grow the program by adding up to 1 million assigned beneficiaries in an average year during the 10-year projection period, increase net federal savings by $5.5 billion over 10 years (range of uncertainty +/- $3.3 billion), and generate an overall increase in shared savings net of losses to ACOs by $1.1 billion over 10 years (+/- $3.6 billion). Modifications to the Shared Savings Program Financial Methodology Strengthen Financial Incentives to Participate and Encourage Additional Savings in Two-Sided Risk We are finalizing the following changes to the Shared Savings Program’s financial methodology which, in combination, would balance incentives between Level E of the BASIC track and the ENHANCED track, mitigate selection issues and benchmark rebasing concerns, and encourage participation by ACOs with higher risk and higher cost populations. Given the timing of CY 2027 PFS rulemaking and the Shared Savings Program application cycle for the Jan. 1, 2027 start date (occurring in CY 2026), we are providing additional flexibility to ACO applicants in making their final selection of track/level of participation. Accordingly, following the issuance of the CY 2027 PFS final rule, ACOs applying for an agreement period start date of Jan.1, 2027, will be able to change their final selection during Phase 2 RFI (Nov. 6-12, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. (noon) ET). (1) Increase the shared savings rate (“sharing rate”) for Level E of the BASIC track from 50% to 60%. The Shared Savings Program is structured into risk tracks that financially reward ACOs that transform their care delivery practices by taking on higher levels of financial risk and reward on behalf of taxpayers. Currently, evidence suggests that ACOs in BASIC track Level E generate higher savings to the Trust Funds than ACOs in the ENHANCED track, and there are fewer ACOs participating in Level E of the BASIC track than the ENHANCED track. Increasing the sharing rate for BASIC track Level E could more properly balance this participation option relative to the ENHANCED track (with a 75% sharing rate). By reducing the savings percentage gap between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track, we may increase the participation and long-term success of ACOs, particularly those with less experience with the Shared Savings Program, with unique patient and/or provider populations, and low revenue ACOs (which tend to be small, rural, and physician-only ACOs). (2) Reduce the maximum weight used in calculating the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs participating under the ENHANCED track from 50% to 35%. Our analysis indicates that ENHANCED track ACOs on average, achieve higher gross savings than BASIC track Level E ACOs and have substantially larger positive regional adjustments. Moreover, the average size of the positive regional adjustment has gone up while the share of ACOs receiving such an adjustment has remained stable over the same period. This pattern suggests that, while the prevalence of regional adjustments has remained broadly unchanged, the financial impact of those adjustments has increased over time, amplifying the influence of regional cost variation adjustments on ACO benchmark calculations. In the current structure, ENHANCED track ACOs with lower spending than their region are receiving both a higher shared savings rate and larger positive regional adjustment on average. Together, these advantages may incentivize selection into the ENHANCED track independent of an ACO’s capacity to achieve genuine cost savings to Medicare. The reduction in the positive regional adjustment weight for these ACOs, paired with an increase in the shared savings rate for BASIC track Level E, is designed to rebalance financial incentives across tracks and encourage ACOs to select their tracks based on their actual capacity to reduce costs rather than differences in financial advantages embedded in track design, thereby potentially improving Trust Funds net savings. (3) Increase the prior savings adjustment’s scaling factor from 50% to 75%. Increased prior savings adjustment amounts could provide additional relief from the rebasing “ratchet effect,” in which the savings an ACO achieves in one agreement period can reduce its rebased benchmark for the subsequent period by lowering the historical spending that forms the basis for that benchmark. This change could incentivize ACOs to generate more savings in their initial agreement period and encourage long-term participation in the Shared Savings Program. (4) Risk adjust the 5% cap on upward adjustments to the historical benchmark. ACOs with higher risk populations have expressed concern that the current 5% cap that applies to the three upward adjustments to the historical benchmark (regional adjustment, prior savings adjustment, and population adjustment) is too restrictive. Under the approach we are finalizing, we will account for the severity and case mix of the ACO’s assigned population in calculating the 5% cap, which is based on national per capita FFS expenditures for the assignable beneficiary population. This approach will result in potentially higher upward adjustments to the benchmark for ACOs whose assigned beneficiary populations have higher risk, and potentially higher costs, and thereby encourage such ACOs to enter and remain in the Shared Savings Program. Growth Adjustment to the Historical Benchmark to Incentivize New Participation We are finalizing a growth adjustment to the historical benchmark to reward ACOs for recruiting ACO professionals who are inexperienced with value-based care arrangements and serving beneficiaries new to value-based care. This growth adjustment will be applied on top of the highest existing benchmark adjustments for which an ACO is eligible, either a positive regional adjustment, prior savings adjustment, or population adjustment, and will not exceed the finalized risk adjusted 5% cap. Additionally, the growth incentive will be included in a subsequent agreement period’s prior savings adjustment (if applicable), if the ACO continued to maintain or increase the growth it achieved in the previous agreement period. Reform ACPT Component of the Benchmark Update Factor The Accountable Care Prospective Trend (ACPT) is part of a three-way blended benchmark update factor that projects an administrative growth target to partially insulate ACOs from a downward “ratchet effect” in benchmarks from both individual and collective success in lowering programmatic costs. However, the ACPT depends on cost growth projections that could be subject to potential projection errors. For agreement periods beginning on Jan. 1, 2027, and in subsequent years, we are finalizing an ACPT guardrail policy that limits the effect of under-projection or over-projection as compared to observed growth in expenditures for the national assignable FFS population such that the ACPT is no more than 1 percentage point below (or no more than 1.5 percentage points above) national growth. For ACOs within existing agreement periods with 2024, 2025, and 2026 start dates, we are retroactively applying the lower guardrail, which will limit the ACPT to no more than 1 percentage point below the national growth rate in determining financial reconciliation for PY 2025 and any subsequent performance year of the ACO’s agreement period. We are delaying PY 2025 financial reconciliation until November 2026, after the final rule is issued, so that we can implement this policy for PY 2025 reconciliation. We also are finalizing the policy to calculate annualized growth rates used in determining the ACPT for each performance year for all ACOs in agreement periods beginning on or after Jan. 1, 2027, rather than calculating the annualized growth rates on an agreement period basis (under the existing policy). This approach will improve consistency in the calculations across agreement periods. Changes to the Shared Savings Program Beneficiary Assignment Methodology We are finalizing several changes to the Shared Savings Program’s beneficiary assignment methodology, applicable for the performance year starting on Jan. 1, 2028, and subsequent performance years, with the goal of increasing the number of Medicare beneficiaries involved in accountable care relationships. First, we are excluding from assignment calculations allowed charges for primary care services billed through a non-ACO Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) by an ACO professional used in assignment. We would apply this approach in determining whether a beneficiary received the plurality of primary care services under the stepwise claims-based assignment methodology. This policy will be a tailored approach reducing the potential for ACO professionals’ billing patterns, inside and outside the ACO, for the care of the same beneficiaries, to result in differences in assignment outcomes that advantage the ACO’s financial performance. Second, we are finalizing modifications to assignment eligibility criteria and prospective assignment exclusion criteria based on Medicare enrollment status. Currently, to be eligible for assignment to an ACO for a performance year or benchmark year, a beneficiary must meet criteria including having at least one month of Part A and Part B enrollment without any month of Part A only or Part B only enrollment, or Medicare group health plan enrollment (including Medicare Advantage (MA)), during the assignment window. For an ACO participating under prospective assignment, a beneficiary may be excluded later from the ACO’s prospective assignment list if they no longer meet these eligibility criteria. We are finalizing modifications to the assignment criteria based on Medicare enrollment status to align with our current operational approach to identifying the assignable beneficiary population. Under our new approach, we will consider as eligible for assignment beneficiaries who have at least one month of Part A and Part B enrollment and no Medicare group health plan enrollment (including MA) during that same month during the 12-month assignment window for the relevant performance year or benchmark year. Third, we are finalizing updates to the definition of primary care services used for beneficiary assignment under the Shared Savings Program to align with payment policy proposals under the Medicare PFS. We are finalizing to include, among other services for determining beneficiary assignment for the performance year starting on Jan. 1, 2027, and subsequent performance years, new codes for Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment, Vaccine Adverse Effects Management, and Advance Care Planning. Shared Savings Program ACOs and ACO participants may also be impacted by the replacement of HCPCS code G2211 (E/M Visit Complexity Add-On) with a modifier and should review the CY 2027 PFS Final Rule Fact Sheet for additional information. summary: Calendar Year 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Final Rule (CMS-1850-F) On November 4, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule that updates Medicare payment policies and rates for hospital outpatient and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) services under the Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and ASC Payment System for calendar year (CY) 2027. CMS is publishing this final rule consistent with statutory requirements to review and update Medicare payment rates for hospital outpatient departments and ASCs annually. This fact sheet discusses the final rule’s major provisions. These payment updates affect approximately 3,500 hospitals and approximately 6,400 ASCs. In addition to finalizing the payment rates, this year’s rule includes updates to the methodology used to calculate the Overall Hospital Quality Star Rating to emphasize the Safety of Care measure group in hospitals’ star ratings. CMS is also finalizing changes to the Hospital Outpatient Quality Reporting (OQR) and ASC Quality Reporting (ASCQR) programs to further meaningful measurement and reporting for outpatient quality of care. Updates to OPPS and ASC Payment Rates In accordance with statutory requirements, CMS is finalizing an update to the OPPS payment rates for hospitals that meet applicable quality reporting requirements by 2.3%. This update is based on the projected hospital market basket percentage increase of 3.2%, reduced by a 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment. For CY 2027, using the hospital market basket update, CMS is finalizing an update factor to the ASC rates of 2.3%. The update applies to ASCs meeting relevant quality reporting requirements. This update is based on the IPPS market basket percentage increase of 3.2%, reduced by 0.9 percentage point for the productivity adjustment. Expanding the Method to Control Unnecessary Increases in the Volume of Outpatient Services In the CY 2019 OPPS/ASC final rule, CMS adopted a method to control unnecessary increases in the volume of clinic visit services furnished in excepted off-campus provider-based departments (PBDs). This method prevents Medicare and beneficiaries from paying significantly more in the excepted off-campus PBD setting than in the physician office setting for some services. In the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule, CMS finalized a policy expansion to include drug administration services furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. For CY 2027, CMS is finalizing a policy to apply this volume control method to imaging without contrast services, which include certain bone density scans, x-rays, ultrasounds, CT scans and MRIs, furnished in excepted off-campus PBDs. Specifically, CMS is using the agency’s authority under section 1833(t)(2)(F) of the Social Security Act to apply the Physician Fee Schedule equivalent payment rate for any HCPCS codes assigned to the imaging without contrast ambulatory payment classifications (APCs) when provided at an off-campus PBD excepted from section 603 of the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015. As with the existing volume control method for off-campus clinic visits and drug administration services, CMS is exempting rural Sole Community Hospitals from this policy. For CY 2027, we estimate this provision would reduce Medicare Part B expenditures by approximately $260 million in the first year, including approximately $190 million in Part B savings and approximately $70 million in reduced beneficiary premiums. In addition, beneficiary cost-sharing obligations are estimated to decrease by approximately $70 million in the first year. This policy helps ensure that beneficiaries are not subject to higher premiums and cost sharing based solely on the site at which care is furnished. Reduced Payments for 340B-Acquired Drugs Based on the Medicare OPPS Drugs Acquisition Cost Survey Section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Social Security Act requires the Secretary to periodically conduct hospital drug acquisition cost surveys for specified covered outpatient drugs and use this information to help set the payment rates for such drugs. Additionally, on April 18, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order (E.O.) 14273, “Lowering Drug Prices by Once Again Putting Americans First.” Section 5 of the E.O., “Appropriately Accounting for Acquisition Costs of Drugs in Medicare” directs the Secretary of HHS to publish in the Federal Register a plan to conduct a survey under section 1833(t)(14)(D)(ii) of the Social Security Act to determine the hospital acquisition cost for covered outpatient drugs at hospital outpatient departments. Accordingly, from Jan. 1, 2026, through April 7, 2026, we conducted a survey of the acquisition costs for each separately payable drug acquired by all hospitals paid under the OPPS. The survey revealed significant disparities between hospital acquisition costs for drugs acquired through the 340B program and those drugs acquired outside of the 340B program. In some instances, the survey revealed that the beneficiary cost-sharing amount, typically 20% of the total payment amount, was greater than the total price that the hospital paid for the drug. Taking the survey’s results into account to more accurately align Medicare payments with hospital drug acquisition costs, we are finalizing for CY 2027 to pay for 340B-acquired drugs at the drug’s Average Sales Price (ASP) minus 28%. This payment policy is estimated to reduce Original Medicare drug payment by $4.35 billion and beneficiary drug payments by $1.1 billion in the first year. Statute requires that this policy be implemented in a budget neutral manner, so this policy will increase OPPS payments for non-drug services by an equivalent amount. The individual beneficiary who receives a qualifying drug in the hospital outpatient department is expected to save an average of $900 in drug costs in CY 2027. CY 2027 Prospective Adjustment to Payments for Non-Drug Items and Services to Offset the Increased Payments for Non-Drug Items and Services Made in CY 2018 Through CY 2022 as a Result of the Prior 340B Payment Policy The November 2023 340B Remedy final rule (88 FR 77150) finalized changes to the calculation of the OPPS conversion factor applicable to non-drug items and services beginning in CY 2026. Specifically, effective Jan. 1, 2026, the rule codified a 0.5% reduction in the OPPS conversion factor applicable to non-drug items and services, excluding hospitals that enrolled in Medicare after Jan. 1, 2018. This reduction would remain in effect until the estimated aggregate payment reduction reached the $7.8 billion of increased non-drug items and services payments made from CY 2018 through CY 2022. This prospective offset aimed to balance the goal of restoring hospitals to their financial position had the original 340B policy never existed with avoiding burdening them with an immediate single year recovery. After subsequent reconsideration of balancing these two goals, CMS has determined a shorter timeframe to be more appropriate, consistent with our discussion in the CY 2026 OPPS/ASC final rule with comment period. During CY 2026 rulemaking, we proposed, but did not finalize, a 2% reduction in the OPPS conversion factor for CY 2026. Although we did not finalize an increase to the 0.5% reduction for CY 2026, we indicated in the CY 2026 final rule that we anticipated delaying an increase for only a single year and that commenters should expect an increase greater than 0.5% in CY 2027. Consequently, after consideration of the public comments received on the proposed rule, CMS is finalizing a revision to the annual offset percentage for non-drug items and services from 0.5% to 2% effective CY 2027, excluding hospitals that enrolled in Medicare after Jan. 1, 2018. This 2% reduction will remain in effect until the estimated payment reduction reaches $7.8 billion, which CMS estimates will occur in CY 2031. Eliminating the Inpatient Only (IPO) List To give beneficiaries more choices on where to obtain care with the potential for lower out-of-pocket expenses, CMS is continuing to phase out the IPO list over a three-year period. For this second year of the phase out, CMS is finalizing its proposal to remove 637 services from the following clinical families: auditory, digestive, endocrine, female genital, hemic and lymphatic systems, integumentary, male genital, maternity care and delivery, mediastinum and diaphragm, respiratory, and urinary. CMS believes that the evolving nature of medical practice allows more procedures to be performed on an outpatient basis with a shorter recovery time. This will allow for these services to be paid by Medicare in the hospital outpatient setting when determined to be clinically appropriate, giving physicians greater flexibility in determining the most appropriate site of service. Adjustment to Cost-of-Living in Alaska and Hawaii Hospitals located in Alaska and Hawaii face unique geographical circumstances, including dependency on outside goods and components, remote locations and transportation challenges, and other factors inherent to providing healthcare in these noncontiguous states. While higher labor-related costs for these two states are considered under the OPPS through the IPPS hospital wage index, the nonlabor portion of OPPS payment does not currently address higher nonlabor costs in these states as in the IPPS through a Cost-of-Living-Adjustment (COLA) policy. To resolve this inconsistency between the IPPS and OPPS, we are applying a COLA to the nonlabor share of outpatient hospital service payments provided in Alaska and Hawaii for CY 2027 and future years based on the IPPS COLA. The finalized policy is budget neutral across the OPPS and is projected to increase payments to hospitals in these states by $66 million in CY 2027. Intensive Outpatient and Partial Hospitalization Programs Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) and Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) Rate Setting The CY 2027 OPPS/ASC final rule updates Medicare payment rates for IOP and PHP services furnished in hospital outpatient departments and Community Mental Health Centers (CMHCs). The IOP is a distinct and organized outpatient program of psychiatric services provided for individuals who have an acute mental illness or substance use disorder, consisting of a specified group of behavioral health services paid on a per diem basis for a minimum of nine hours of IOP services per week under the OPPS, or other applicable payment system, when furnished in hospital outpatient departments, CMHCs, Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), and Rural Health Clinics (RHCs). IOP services may also be furnished in Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) for opioid use disorder (OUD). The PHP is an intensive, structured outpatient program provided as an alternative to psychiatric hospitalization, consisting of a specified group of mental health services paid on a per diem basis for a minimum of 20 hours of PHP services per week under the OPPS, based on PHP per diem costs. Update to IOP and PHP Payment Rates in Hospital Outpatient Departments and CMHCs CMS is finalizing its proposal to maintain the existing rate structure, with two IOP APCs for each provider type and two PHP APCs for each provider type. For CY 2027, CMS is calculating hospital-based PHP payment rates for three services per day and four or more services per day based on cost per day using OPPS data that includes IOP or PHP and non-IOP or PHP days. CMS believes continuing to use the OPPS data set will allow CMS to capture data from hospital claims that are not identified as IOP or PHP but that include the service codes and intensity required for an IOP or PHP day. CMS calculates CMHC costs based on 40% of the hospital-based PHP and IOP costs. summary:
Objective

To compare the benefits and harms of therapeutic interventions for adhesive capsulitis.

Design

Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

Data sources

Medline, Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to 1 May 2025, with an update in November 2025.

Eligibility criteria for selecting studies

Randomised controlled trials enrolling adults with adhesive capsulitis, comparing active treatment with another intervention, placebo, or usual care.

Main outcome measures

Pain, function, range of motion, and adverse events.

Results

A total of 189 randomised controlled trials involving 12 988 participants and 59 interventions were included. Most trials contributing to principal outcomes were at high risk of bias (71% for pain, 72% for function, and 71% for range of motion). At short term follow-up, moderate certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy probably reduced pain compared with usual care (mean difference -1.97 on a 0-10 scale, 95% confidence interval (CI) -2.97 to -0.97). Low certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy may improve function (mean difference -11.42 on a 0-100 scale, 95% CI -16.68 to -6.15), although direct and indirect estimates were limited by important incoherence. For short term range of motion, moderate certainty evidence suggested that manipulation under anaesthesia combined with intra-articular steroid injections probably improved flexion (mean difference 33.29°, 95% CI 11.19° to 55.39°), as did manipulation under anaesthesia alone (26.16°, 8.19° to 44.13°). Low certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy may improve flexion (22.42°, 12.99° to 31.84°) and abduction (18.62°, 8.09° to 29.14°), but both comparisons were limited by important incoherence. At mid-term follow-up, evidence for possible improvements in function with extracorporeal shockwave therapy and flexion with passive mobilisation was of low certainty, while evidence for pain reduction with extracorporeal shockwave therapy was of very low certainty. Most other comparative estimates were supported by low or very low certainty evidence. Comparative safety remained highly uncertain because adverse events were incompletely and inconsistently reported; the absence of reported adverse events should not be interpreted as evidence of absence of harm.

Conclusion

Moderate certainty evidence suggests short term pain reduction with extracorporeal shockwave therapy and improved short term flexion with manipulation under anaesthesia, with or without intra-articular steroid injections. Most other treatment effects remain uncertain because of low certainty and incoherence, and comparative safety and mid-term effects are poorly established. The available evidence is mainly short term and outcome specific. Longer term comparative effectiveness, overall benefits and harms, and applicability beyond predominantly primary adhesive capsulitis remain uncertain.

Systematic review registration

PROSPERO CRD420251070468.
title: Interventions for adhesive capsulitis: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.

summary:
Objective

To assess the effect of ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) compared with endotracheal tube (ETT) on perioperative respiratory adverse events (PRAEs) in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy.

Design

Multicentre, randomised, parallel group trial.

Setting

Four tertiary hospitals in China, 2023-24.

Participants

400 children aged ≥2 years and <7 years who were scheduled for adenotonsillectomy under general anaesthesia.

Interventions

Participants were randomised 1:1 to receive ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway (n=200) or an endotracheal tube (n=200) during adenotonsillectomy.

Main outcome measure

The primary outcome was the proportion of participants who developed any perioperative respiratory adverse event (PRAE): laryngospasm, bronchospasm, desaturation, airway obstruction, severe cough, or stridor in the intention-to-treat population.

Results

400 children (mean age 4.7 (standard deviation 1.0) years; 155 (38.7%) girls) were enrolled between 24 May 2023 and 4 April 2024, with last follow-up on 4 May 2024. LMA was converted to ETT in three participants. Overall, 22.5% (45/200) participants in the LMA group experienced PRAEs versus 57.5% (115/200) in the ETT group (absolute risk difference -35.0 percentage points, 95% confidence interval -43.5 to -25.7; P<0.001). The LMA group had fewer PRAEs in both the intraoperative (9.0% (18/200) v 17.5% (35/200); -8.5, -15.2 to -1.8; P=0.01) and the postoperative period (16.5% (33/200) v 49.5% (99/200); -33.0, -41.2 to -24.0; P<0.001). The LMA group also had a lower proportion of participants with laryngospasm (0.0% v 3.0%; P=0.03), desaturation (15.0% v 28.0%; P=0.002), airway obstruction (3.5% v 12.5%; P<0.001), and severe cough (10.5% v 42.0%; P<0.001). Neither group experienced serious adverse events.

Conclusion

Ventilation with an LMA by experienced anaesthesiologists resulted in fewer perioperative respiratory adverse events than ventilation with an ETT in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy.

Trial registration

Chictr.org.cn ChiCTR2300071399.
title: Perioperative respiratory adverse events in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy with laryngeal mask airway versus endotracheal tube ventilation: multicentre, randomised controlled trial.

summary:
Background

The comparative effectiveness of conservative kidney management and dialysis in older people (aged ≥80 years regardless of frailty and comorbidity or aged 65-79 years if frailty or multimorbidity are present) living with kidney failure is unknown. We aimed to assess the relative effectiveness of preparing for responsive management-a protocolised version of conservative kidney management-and preparing for renal dialysis.

Methods

Prepare for Kidney Care was a two-arm, superiority, parallel-group, open-label, pragmatic, phase 3, individually randomised controlled trial conducted in 31 kidney centres in England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Eligible patients had an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 15 mL/min per 1·73 m2, confirmed by at least one additional reading in the 12 months preceding consent that was not due to acute kidney injury, and were either aged 80 years or older, or aged 65-79 years with a WHO performance status of at least 3 or a Davies comorbidity score of at least 2. Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to prepare for responsive management-a patient-centred approach focused on slowing disease progression, active symptom management, and preserving quality of life without the use of dialysis or kidney transplantation-or to prepare for renal dialysis. Randomisation was stratified by centre and minimised by age; a centralised system ensured allocation concealment until randomisation had taken place. The primary outcome was the mean difference in quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), combining length and health-related quality of life from the patient-reported EQ-5D-5L scale, including all follow-up from randomisation to Aug 31, 2025. The primary outcome was analysed by intention to treat in the full analysis set, which included all randomly assigned participants, with missing EQ-5D-5L values for living participants imputed. Harms (hospital admissions and dialysis access complications) and adverse events (deaths and hospital admissions, by cause) were assessed in the full analysis set. The trial was registered with ISRCTN, 17133653 (completed).

Findings

From July 1, 2017, to Aug 31, 2024, 6120 patients were screened across 31 kidney centres in the UK, 445 (7%) of whom were eligible and agreed to be randomly assigned. 228 (51%) of 445 participants were randomly assigned to prepare for responsive management and 217 (49%) of 445 participants were randomly assigned to prepare for renal dialysis. Median age was 82 years (IQR 80 to 86) and 137 (31%) of 445 participants were female. After a mean follow-up duration of 4·5 years (SD 2·1), mean QALYs were 1·354 (95% CI 1·201 to 1·508) in the prepare for responsive management group and 1·472 (1·288 to 1·655) in the prepare for renal dialysis group (adjusted mean difference -0·147 [95% CI -0·350 to 0·056] p=0·16). Specific harms outcomes were not prespecified, but hospital admission rates were similar in the two groups and dialysis access complications were significantly lower in the prepare for responsive management group (adjusted incident rate ratio 0·41 [95% CI 0·19 to 0·88]), based on 74 events in 36 participants across both groups. There were 667 serious adverse events in the prepare for responsive management group (157 [69%] of 228 participants died, with 510 hospital admissions) and 578 in the prepare for renal dialysis group (136 [63%] of 217 participants died, with 442 hospital admissions). None of these serious adverse events met the criteria for expedited reporting.

Interpretation

Among older people living with kidney failure and frailty or multimorbidity, we found no evidence that either preparing for responsive management or preparing for renal dialysis was superior in terms of QALYs over a mean follow-up duration of 4·5 years. This trial provides novel comparative information for clinical decision making.

Funding

National Institute for Health Research Health Technology Assessment programme.
title: Preparing for responsive management versus renal dialysis in older people living with kidney failure and frailty or multimorbidity in the UK (Prepare for Kidney Care): a two-arm, superiority, parallel-group, open-label, pragmatic, phase 3, individually randomised controlled trial.

summary: Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, represents a substantial global health equity concern, exemplifying profound disparities in global burden and outcome despite being a largely curable cancer. Retinoblastoma is thought to arise from cone photoreceptor precursor cells of the developing retina, mainly driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene. Fewer than 2% of cases have no detectable RB1 pathogenic variant; approximately half of these cases instead show high-level amplification of the MYCN oncogene. Diagnosis and monitoring currently rely on clinical examination and multimodal imaging. Emerging molecular diagnostic approaches such as aqueous humour liquid biopsy hold promise for minimally invasive tumour characterisation and real-time disease monitoring. Management has shifted towards eye-preserving strategies, with intra-arterial, intravitreal, and intracameral chemotherapy showing efficacy and safety. The global burden and mortality of retinoblastoma remains highest in regions with a low sociodemographic index, highlighting the need for continued interdisciplinary, equity-focused efforts to ensure timely diagnosis and accessible, high-quality care worldwide. This Seminar reviews the advances in retinoblastoma biology, diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, and global efforts to reduce inequities.
title: Retinoblastoma.

summary: The eating and feeding disorders are serious psychiatric disorders at the mind-body interface, often with an exceptionally high burden for affected individuals, their families and supporters, and wider society. In anorexia nervosa, high acute medical risk and patients' ambivalence about treatment can make a challenging combination that can impede engagement. First-line treatments for eating disorders are mainly psychological, with medications playing an adjunctive role. Novel biological and technology-based interventions are only slowly emerging. Compared with other psychiatric disorders, research into these disorders is seriously underfunded. Many uncertainties regarding their aetiology, maintenance, and treatment remain. Controversies mainly concern the treatment and care of those with the most severe and longstanding forms of illness. Advances in knowledge are most likely to arise from longitudinal studies combining multimodal assessments, using big data to develop better mechanistic understanding, and greater use of flexible trial designs to allow development of more personalised and precise interventions.
title: Eating disorders.

summary: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) (CMS-3484-P) Overview On Nov. 5, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued the Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) proposed rule. This rule proposes regulatory revisions to the Conditions of Participation (CoPs), Conditions for Coverage (CfCs), and Requirements for Participation for Medicare- and Medicaid-participating providers and suppliers (collectively referred to as CoPs). These revisions would reduce costs, increase transparency, enhance flexibility for providers to deliver innovative patient care, and streamline existing regulations. It also proposes to rescind certain Medicaid institutional payment transparency reporting requirements to reduce burden for states and institutional providers. Background CMS conducted a comprehensive review of the CoPs for all 21 provider and supplier types, as well as some payment policies, to identify opportunities to reduce administrative burden while maintaining patient safety and quality care. The agency identified obsolete, outdated, and excessively burdensome regulations that CMS proposes to eliminate or reform to enhance the effectiveness of facility operations and reduce unnecessary burden or other costs, with a particular focus on freeing up resources that healthcare providers could otherwise use to improve patient health and safety. Collectively, CMS estimates the proposals would save $320 million, returning more than 3.26 million hours of staff time to providers. This proposed rule would alleviate unnecessary regulatory burden through deregulation in the following ways: Hospitals Remove the staff training requirements for transfer protocols and emergency services readiness (both currently effective), and obstetric (OB) care (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027). Remove the OB care-specific Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) requirements (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027). Propose to establish new requirements regarding patients’ rights related to birth tissue collection by hospitals that provide OB care services, including standards for informed consent and policies and procedures to support families requesting their birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons. Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) Remove the staff training requirements related to emergency services readiness (currently effective) and OB care (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027). Remove the OB care-specific Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) requirements (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027). Propose to establish new requirements regarding patients’ rights related to birth tissue collection by CAHs that provide OB care services, including standards for informed consent and policies and procedures to support families requesting their birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons. Revise regulations to clarify current CMS policy that CAH distance eligibility determinations are based on proximity to hospitals that provide acute care inpatient services or another CAH. Implement new statutory requirements to allow CAHs that meet certain qualifying criteria, as defined by the statute, to be exempt from the distance eligibility requirements. Long-Term Care (LTC) Facilities Remove the COVID-19 vaccine requirements related to educating staff about the benefits and risks, offering the vaccine, and documenting these actions. Streamline the remaining COVID-19 vaccine requirements for residents. Remove the continuing respiratory illness data reporting requirement while retaining the requirement for specific reporting during a future Secretary-declared public health emergency (PHE). Modify the requirement for LTC facilities to provide a state ombudsman with notice of resident transfers related to emergent care. Revise the requirements for the active involvement of representatives of direct care staff in conducting the LTC facility assessment. Revise the physical environment requirements to exempt existing facilities from the room occupancy and bathroom facility standards. Intermediate Care Facilities for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ICFs/IID) Remove the requirements related to educating staff about the COVID-19 vaccine and its benefits and risks, offering it to them, and documenting these actions. Streamline the remaining COVID-19 vaccine requirements for clients. Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs) Remove expired COVID-19 and seasonal influenza reporting requirements related to ongoing data reporting and staff vaccination. Remove REH data reporting requirements during a PHE. Physical Environment Life Safety Code (LSC) and Health Care Facilities Code (HCFC) Updates and Emergency and Standby Powers Systems (ESPS) Codes Adopt the 2024 editions of National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) LSC and HCFC and the 2022 edition of the ESPS Codes. Outside Window or Door Requirement Remove the requirement that patient care areas have access to natural light and ventilation through exterior windows and doors for hospitals, CAHs, and other providers with similar regulations (Religious Nonmedical Health Care Institutions, LTC facilities, ICFs/IID and hospice inpatient care facilities). Waiver Authority Codify in the regulations CMS’ authority to permit facilities to comply with specific provisions of a newer edition of the LSC or HCFC. Medicaid Payment Transparency for Nursing Facilities and ICFs/IID Rescind the following Medicaid institutional payment transparency reporting requirements to reduce burden for states and institutional providers: The percentage of Medicaid payments for nursing facility services spent on compensation for direct care workers, The percentage of Medicaid payments for nursing facility services spent on compensation for support staff, and The percentage of Medicaid payments for ICFs/IID services spent on compensation for support staff. Comment Solicitations CMS is including comment solicitations in this proposed rule to obtain input from interested parties related to the following topics: Allowing LTC facility residents to opt-out of having a discharge notice sent to the state ombudsman office; Strategies to minimize burden for hospitals and CAHs to comply with ongoing respiratory illness and PHE infectious illness data reporting requirements; Approaches to allow flexibility for providers regarding the requirement for physician supervision of certified registered nurse anesthetists (CRNAs); Expanding the scope of practice of physician assistants and nurse practitioners providing care in LTC facilities, especially as it pertains to performing visits currently required by a physician; Revising criteria for transplant program initial certification to reduce barriers to entry for new transplant programs while maintaining patient safety and ensuring the transplant program’s competence; and Future policies to address Medicaid institutional workforce shortages and strengthen the institutional workforce. View the final rule on the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/2026-22812/medicare-and-medicaid-programs-cutting-administrative-requirements-for-excellence-in-patient-care . CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145
title: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) (CMS-3484-P)

summary: Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program Final Rule (CMS-4215-F) On Nov. 5, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule that codifies policies established in guidance documents for the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (“Negotiation Program”) for initial price applicability year 2029 and beyond (CMS-4215-F). For initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028 of the Negotiation Program, statute directed CMS to implement the Negotiation Program through program instruction and other forms of program guidance. With this authority expiring, CMS is codifying the Negotiation Program for 2029 and beyond. In addition to codifying these policies, we are establishing new policies to continue implementation of statutory provisions under the Negotiation Program as well as finalizing revisions or clarifications to certain policies previously established to incorporate lessons learned from ongoing experience. 1 The Negotiation Program final rule is one of several activities that reflect a broader CMS-wide strategy to lower prescription drug costs for people with Medicare. CMS is approaching codification of the Negotiation Program consistent with the goals of achieving greater value for beneficiaries and taxpayers and continuing to foster innovation. The final rule is effective Dec. 5, 2026. Background on the Negotiation Program Sections 11001 and 11002 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (P.L. 117-169) establish the Negotiation Program to negotiate maximum fair prices (MFPs) for certain high expenditure, single source drugs and biological products. Specifically, in accordance with section 1191(c)(3) of the Social Security Act (the Act), MFP means, with respect to a year during a price applicability period and with respect to a selected drug (as defined in section 1192(c) of the Act) with respect to such period, the MFP negotiated in accordance with section 1194 of the Act, and updated to account for inflation in accordance with section 1195(b) of the Act, as applicable, for such drug and year. Under the IRA, with respect to each initial price applicability year, CMS will: (1) publish a list of selected drugs for negotiation and renegotiation, if any; (2) enter into agreements with manufacturers of selected drugs that choose to participate; (3) negotiate (or renegotiate) MFPs for such selected drugs; (4) publish any agreed-upon MFPs for selected drugs; (5) carry out administrative and compliance duties; and (6) impose civil monetary penalties (CMPs), when applicable. CMS will select up to 20 drugs covered under Part D and/or payable under Part B for initial price applicability year 2029 and for each subsequent initial price applicability year. In addition to the drugs selected for negotiation, CMS may also select drugs for renegotiation if selected drugs with an agreed-upon MFP meet certain eligibility and selection criteria. Codification of the Negotiation Program In codifying the requirements for the Negotiation Program, CMS builds upon policies established for the first three cycles of negotiations and establishes new requirements for the fourth and future cycles of negotiations with a particular focus on continuing to increase transparency in the Negotiation Program. The final regulations include, but are not limited to: Identification of Selected Drugs. Section 1192 of the Act establishes the requirements governing the publication of the selected drug list for an initial price applicability year, the identification of selected drugs, ranking of negotiation-eligible drugs, and the identification of qualifying single source drugs. CMS codifies these policies consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, with a new policy to clarify how CMS will identify qualifying single source drugs to address potential program integrity concerns posed by specific new formulations. Additionally, CMS clarifies the treatment of withdrawn approvals for indications when identifying whether a drug that formerly qualified for the orphan drug exclusion meets eligibility criteria to be a qualifying single source drug, in accordance with amendments made by the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation (Pub. L. 119-21). Requirements for Manufacturers of Selected Drugs. Section 1193(a) of the Act establishes the Negotiation Program Agreement and the requirements for a willing primary manufacturer to enter into and sign the Negotiation Program Agreement no later than Feb. 28 following the selected drug publication date. The Negotiation Program Agreement will remain in effect, including through renegotiation, as applicable, until the selected drug is no longer considered a selected drug under section 1192(c) of the Act (due to a determination that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that the generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing) unless it is terminated sooner by the primary manufacturer under specified conditions. CMS finalizes additional details related to the primary manufacturer transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to another entity. In addition, CMS codifies the timing and process for executing and terminating a Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS and the requirements a willing primary manufacturer is subject to upon executing the Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS, including mandatory submission of data to CMS, consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. Negotiation Factors. After entering into an Agreement with CMS and in accordance with section 1193(a)(4) of the Act, the primary manufacturer of each selected drug must submit the following information with respect to the selected drug: information on the non-Federal Average Manufacturer Price (non-FAMP) and any information that CMS requires to carry out the Negotiation Program, including but not limited to, information related to the manufacturer-specific factors listed in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act. Additionally, primary manufacturers and any interested party may voluntarily submit evidence about the selected drugs and potential therapeutic alternatives as described in section 1194(e)(2) of the Act. In accordance with section 1194(e) of the Act, CMS uses manufacturer-specific data and available evidence about the selected drugs and their therapeutic alternatives as the basis for determining offers and considering counteroffers in the negotiation process. CMS codifies these policies, including submission requirements for primary manufacturers, requirements for primary manufacturers to update submitted data, and how CMS will consider evidence from comparative effectiveness studies. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. Negotiation Process. CMS develops and uses a consistent methodology and process for negotiation with the aim of achieving agreement on “the lowest [MFP] for each selected drug” in accordance with section 1194(b)(1) of the Act. The negotiation process includes engagement with primary manufacturers and interested parties, including patients; the development and delivery of the written initial offer, including a concise justification, to the primary manufacturer of a selected drug; the ability for the primary manufacturer to accept an offer or provide a statutory written counteroffer; optional negotiation meetings between CMS and the primary manufacturer; additional price exchange opportunities; the conclusion of negotiation, including a final offer sent by CMS to the primary manufacturer, where applicable; and the publication of agreed-upon MFPs and explanations of such MFPs. CMS codifies these policies for the negotiation process, including engagement with primary manufacturers and interested parties, the offer and counteroffer process, and the publication and explanation of the MFP. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. Ineligibility for Selection, or Deselection of a Selected Drug Before or During Negotiation, or Following the Negotiation Period . In accordance with sections 1192(c) and 1192(e) of the Act, a potential qualifying single source drug is not eligible for selection, a selected drug will no longer be subject to the negotiation process, and a selected drug will cease to be a selected drug, subject to certain timing and situations, if CMS determines: (1) the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a generic drug under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act that identifies as its reference-listed drug a product that is included in the potential qualifying single source drug or selected drug (as applicable), or FDA has licensed a biosimilar under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act that identifies as its reference product a product that is included in the potential qualifying single source drug or selected drug (as applicable); and (2) the generic drug or biosimilar, as applicable, is marketed pursuant to such approval or licensure. CMS codifies provisions regarding its identification of when such generic drug or biosimilar is marketed within the meaning of these statutory requirements (“Bona Fide Marketing”). Further, CMS codifies the criteria, process, and timing related to the determination of ineligibility of a potential qualifying single source drug that would otherwise be eligible for selection and to the determination of the deselection of a selected drug, with additional information provided on the points in time CMS reviews the information to determine if a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that the generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. CMS also codifies the criteria, process, and timing related to monitoring that the approved generic drug(s) or licensed biosimilar(s) continue to be subject to Bona Fide Marketing for any potential qualifying single source drug(s) that were previously considered ineligible for selection or for any selected drug(s) deselected because CMS determined that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. These policies are consistent with statute and build on CMS guidance regarding the timing of review of the information to evaluate whether a generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. Renegotiation of an MFP. Section 1194(f) of the Act establishes the requirements governing the identification of renegotiation-eligible drugs, the selection of drugs for renegotiation, and the renegotiation process. CMS codifies the criteria CMS will use to determine renegotiation eligibility and selection, the types of information CMS will consider when determining renegotiation eligibility and selection, opportunities and requirements for data submission, and the process for renegotiation, which will remain consistent, to the extent practicable, with the process and methodology used for negotiation. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. For renegotiation with respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and beyond, CMS finalizes its policy to consider the agreed-upon MFP for a drug selected for renegotiation as part of the consideration of section 1194(e)(1) factors. Strengthening Program Integrity to Address Fixed Combination Drug Loophole Under policy established for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, if a drug is a fixed combination drug with two or more active moieties, active ingredients, or, for a vaccine for infectious disease(s), antigen components, a potential qualifying single source drug is identified using the same distinct combination of active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components. Under this policy, CMS is aware of a program integrity risk

summary:
Importance

Refusal of newborn prophylactic vitamin K has been increasing in the US, placing more infants at risk for vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

Objective

To describe US trends in nonreceipt of newborn vitamin K and infant bleeding, and to compare risks of bleeding and mortality with concurrent bleeding among infants who did and did not receive newborn intramuscular (IM) vitamin K.

Design, setting, and participants

This retrospective cohort study included infants born at 35 to 43 weeks' gestation between January 1, 2017, and December 31, 2025, at hospitals and health systems from 50 states contributing to the Epic Cosmos dataset.

Exposure

Nonreceipt of newborn IM vitamin K.

Main outcomes and measures

The primary outcome was bleeding within the first 6 months of life based on International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision codes. Secondary outcomes were bleeding during the birth hospitalization and after discharge, intracranial bleeding, and mortality with concurrent bleeding during the birth hospitalization. Robust Poisson regression was used to estimate relative risks while adjusting for covariates.

Results

Among 5 240 780 infants, the rate of vitamin K nonreceipt increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225.3 to 394.0 per 10 000 births in infants who did not receive newborn IM vitamin K, compared with 136.6 to 221.8 per 10 000 in infants who received vitamin K. Infants who did not receive vitamin K had significantly higher risk of bleeding by 6 months than infants who did receive vitamin K (288.0 vs 185.9 per 10 000; adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 1.47; 95% CI, 1.43-1.51). They also had higher risk of intracranial bleeding (33.0 vs 13.2 per 10 000; ARR, 2.43; 95% CI, 2.26-2.62) and mortality with concurrent bleeding during the birth hospitalization (2.9 vs 1.1 per 10 000; ARR, 2.69; 95% CI, 2.09-3.47).

Conclusions and relevance

Nonreceipt of vitamin K and infant bleeding incidence have increased in the US, and newborns who did not receive vitamin K were at significantly higher risk of bleeding during their first 6 months.
title: Nonreceipt of Newborn Vitamin K and Risk of Bleeding.

summary:
Objectives

To evaluate the effectiveness of paravertebral blockade versus thoracic epidural during the perioperative period in reducing chronic post-thoracotomy pain.

Design

Open label, parallel group, superiority, multicentre, randomised controlled trial.

Setting

15 thoracic centres in the UK.

Participants

Adult patients undergoing thoracotomy randomised (1:1) to either paravertebral blockade or thoracic epidural using a web based service between January 2019 and September 2023.

Interventions

Participants in the paravertebral group received three single-shot paravertebral injections of local anaesthetic before incision followed by placement of a paravertebral catheter. Participants in the epidural group had a thoracic epidural catheter placed and loaded with local anaesthetic before incision.

Main outcome measure

The primary outcome was incidence of chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six months after randomisation, defined as a 100 mm visual analogue score greater than or equal to 40 mm (indicating moderate pain) when considering worst chest pain over the past week. Secondary outcomes included acute pain (visual analogue score of 100 mm) and complications.

Results

770 patients were enrolled, of which 428 (56%) were male (mean (standard deviation, SD) age 66.6 (11.0) years). After 33 exclusions of patients after randomisation who did not proceed to thoracotomy, 737 remained in the modified intention-to-treat population (364 in the paravertebral group, 373 in the epidural group). Six months after randomisation, 59 (22%) of 272 participants in the paravertebral group and 47 (16%) of 292 participants in the epidural group developed chronic post-thoracotomy pain (adjusted risk ratio 1.32 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.93 to 1.86), adjusted risk difference 0.05 (95% CI -0.01 to 0.11), P=0.12). During the acute phase, worst and average pain was greater on day 1 with paravertebral blockade (adjusted mean difference 7.7 mm (95% CI 2.8 to 12.5 mm) and 7.0 mm (95% CI 2.7 to 11.2 mm), respectively), but no different on days 2-3. Hypotension was less common in the paravertebral group than the epidural group (12% v 18%, respectively, adjusted risk ratio 0.66 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.94), adjusted risk difference -0.06 (95% CI -0.11 to -0.01)), as was pruritis (4% v 12%, adjusted risk ratio 0.37 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.64), adjusted risk difference -0.07 (95% CI -0.11 to -0.03)), although more participants in this group experienced urinary retention (12% v 6%, adjusted risk ratio 2.21 (95% CI 1.35 to 3.61), adjusted risk difference 0.05 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.09)), complications were similar otherwise.

Conclusions

Paravertebral blockade did not reduce chronic post-thoracotomy pain at six month follow-up compared to thoracic epidural. Thoracic epidural provided marginally better acute pain relief one day after the operation, but showed no difference thereafter. Postoperative complications were comparable between groups. The findings support the ongoing use of both techniques.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03677856.
title: Thoracic epidural versus paravertebral blockade for reducing chronic post-thoracotomy pain (TOPIC-2): open label, parallel group, superiority, multicentre, randomised controlled trial.
