summary: Background: Few studies have investigated automated case finding in hospital-based cancer registries despite their crucial role in supporting population-based surveillance. In these settings, data completeness is often compromised by referral patterns, yet the influence of weakly supervised learning strategies on model performance remains underexplored. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different supervision approaches (inaccurate, inexact, and report-level labeling) on deep learning model performance for cancer case finding in a hospital-based registry setting and assess model generalizability across patient-level and report-level classification tasks. Methods: Hospital-based cancer registry and pathology report data from Songklanagarind Hospital (2005-2023) were used for model development and evaluation. Three labeling approaches were implemented: inaccurate (all reports from patients with cancer labeled positive), inexact (concatenated reports from patients with cancer labeled positive), and report-level (only registrar-annotated tumor-related reports labeled positive). Model performance was evaluated on max-pooled, concatenated, and individual report classification tasks using a simple word embedding model, multilayer perceptron, recurrent neural network, convolutional neural network (CNN), and hierarchical self-attention network architectures. Results: Models trained using weakly supervised labeling achieved the highest performance across patient-level evaluation tasks, and CNN models consistently showed superior performance. While report-level labeling yielded superior accuracy for individual reports, it suffered substantial degradation in patient-level evaluations. This suggests that models trained on curated data overfitted to primary tumor patterns, failing to recognize secondary evidence (eg, metastatic or surveillance findings). Conversely, weakly supervised approaches enabled the detection of patients with cancer via diverse report types. Error analysis revealed that false negatives were primarily driven by insufficient institutional data—specifically, referred patients lacking primary diagnostic reports—rather than algorithmic failure. Conclusions: In this single tertiary referral hospital setting, weakly supervised labeling outperformed report-level human annotation for patient-level case finding, whereas report-level labeling performed best for individual report classification. The CNN architecture achieved the highest or near-highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve in most configurations.
title: Development and Application of Deep Learning Models for Case Finding From Pathology Reports in a Hospital-Based Cancer Registry: Algorithm Development and Validation

reviews.support: A metadata-driven rule repository integrated with a daily screening data mart and RPA can operationalize payer review criteria as versioned data rather than hard-coded logic, enabling proactive coding

summary: Background: Under the new diagnosis-related group (NDRG) payment system in Korea, the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA) applies disease-specific diagnosis coding approval criteria that differ from the coding guidelines of the Korean Classification of Diseases (KCD), frequently leading to claim denials for conditions such as acute kidney injury, pleural effusion, and malnutrition. Repeated denials also induce conservative down-coding among coders. Because denial notifications are issued 9 to 18 months after discharge, reactive, denial-triggered quality management is insufficient. Objective: We implemented a metadata-driven rule repository that operationalizes HIRA’s review criteria as data, coupled with a daily-refreshed screening data mart (encompassing 6 clinical data domains and 14 data sources) and a robotic process automation (RPA) notification pipeline, to enable proactive, preclaim coding quality management. Methods: This Implementation Report describes the design, deployment, and 12-month operational experience of the system at an 820-bed NDRG pilot hospital. HIRA’s criteria were externalized into a 4-layer rule repository—criteria definitions, clinical concepts, disease-specific attributes, and decision rules. A nightly extract, transform, and load pipeline populates a patient-by-attribute screening data mart within the clinical data warehouse; each morning, Python-based RPA compiles and emails review candidate lists to coders. Descriptive statistics summarized coverage and detection outcomes; precision (equivalent to positive predictive value) was calculated with Wilson score 95% CIs. Implementation (Results): At the end of the evaluation period, the rule repository comprised 11 review criteria, 271 clinical concepts, 77 attributes, and 96 decision rules. Over the 12-month evaluation period (July 2025 to June 2026), the system evaluated 17,138 diagnosis- or episode-level targets across 15,388 distinct episodes—67% of the hospital’s 22,970 NDRG episodes—and flagged 576 (3.4%) review candidates, of which 50 (8.7%, 95% CI 6.6%-11.3%) were confirmed by coders as actual coding errors. The proportion of confirmed coding errors among review candidates differed significantly across the 3 monitored categories (=39.9; <.001): present-on-admission (POA) coding items showed the highest precision (20/82, 24%), followed by the NDRG cost-outlier category (17/134, 12.7%) and frequently denied diagnoses (13/360, 3.6%). The system was designed, built, and operated by existing departmental staff without additional budget or dedicated IT support, required an estimated 1 to 1.5 hours of coder review time per week, and has continued to operate daily on weekdays since launch. Conclusions: A metadata-driven rule repository integrated with a daily screening data mart and RPA can operationalize payer review criteria as versioned data rather than hard-coded logic, enabling proactive coding surveillance before claim submission. The approach was implemented without additional budget or dedicated IT staff, but its performance may vary across institutions. Further validation against formal HIRA review outcomes and multi-institutional evaluation are needed to establish its performance and transferability across NDRG hospitals.
title: Development and Evaluation of a Metadata-Driven Rule Repository and Daily Screening System for Diagnosis Coding Compliance Under the Korean New Diagnosis-Related Group Payment System: Implementation Report

summary: IDR Gateway Now Available The new Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) Gateway improves functionality, security, and efficiency of the Federal IDR process On November 13, 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Labor, and the Department of the Treasury (the Departments) launched the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) Gateway, a new platform for group health plans, health insurance issuers, providers, facilities, and providers of air ambulance services (collectively referred to as “parties”) and their representatives to manage disputes under the Federal IDR process. The IDR Gateway provides a secure, centralized system that streamlines the dispute lifecycle, allowing users to submit, track, and manage payment disputes from start to finish. Managing Disputes Throughout the IDR Lifecycle The IDR Gateway is a single platform for managing payment disputes from start to finish. In the IDR Gateway, parties and their representatives can start a dispute using the “Notice of IDR Initiation” feature, respond to certified IDR entity selections by completing the “IDR Entity Selection Response” and “IDR Entity Reselection Response” feature, and submit payment offers by completing the “Notice of Offer” feature. IDR Gateway users can also view reports and access dispute records for all open and some closed disputes associated with their organization. Moreover, the IDR Gateway allows parties and their representatives to track disputes by phase and identify critical upcoming dispute deadlines. Tools available to IDR Gateway users include: IDR Gateway Dashboard: The IDR Gateway Dashboard is available to users who have joined an organization. It provides a visual snapshot of disputes associated with an organization by displaying color-coded information on dispute phases for open disputes. Phases can help organizations determine the current status or next actions on a dispute. Each color-coded section displays the total number of disputes in the IDR Entity Selection, IDR Entity Eligibility Review, Offer Submission, and IDR Entity Offer Review phases of the Federal IDR process. Search: The search function allows IDR Gateway users who have joined an organization to find disputes using dispute numbers or keywords. This function also provides filters to narrow search results by date range, dispute status or phase, or disputes with selection or offers due. Reports: Users who have joined an organization can view and filter a wide range of data associated with the organization’s disputes by generating specific reports to better monitor and analyze IDR processes and outcomes. Specifically, users can generate detailed reports of: open and closed disputes; open dispute line items; closed dispute line items; resubmission requested line items; disputes with selection due; and disputes with offers due. Notifications: System notifications provide important updates or actions related to a user’s account or disputes. Users can view a summary of recent system notifications, as well as manage, archive, filter, and review notifications by specific notification types (active, by dispute, by user, by organization, and archived). New tools and features that further enhance disputing party access and experience – such as the IDR Registry – will be added in the future on a rolling basis. Enhanced Security The IDR Gateway provides important new security features to protect the integrity of the Federal IDR process. Specifically, the IDR Gateway includes new identity verification processes and protocols that permit only U.S.-based users to access the Federal IDR process. All IDR Gateway users must verify their identity with an approved credential service provider during the account creation process. Individuals who do not verify their identity cannot access the IDR Gateway, helping to prevent fraud and unauthorized access. In addition to identity verification, the IDR Gateway will require users to agree to terms and conditions for responsible and secure usage of the IDR Gateway. The agreements signed by users include notice that unauthorized users may be subject to criminal prosecution, administrative actions or other adverse actions as needed. The Future of Web Forms Outside the IDR Gateway The IDR Gateway is replacing the single-use web forms that parties currently use to manage disputes. For a limited period, parties may continue to submit web forms without signing in to the IDR Gateway. The web forms will no longer be available outside the IDR Gateway after January 15, 2027 (with the exception of the “Notice of IDR Initiation – Resubmission” web form, which will remain available until that functionality is ended as finalized in the Federal IDR Operations final rule.) ### CMS News and Media Group Catherine Howden, Director Media Inquiries Form 202-690-6145
title: IDR Gateway Now Available

summary: Background: Digital nursing technologies (DNTs) have the potential to improve the quality and continuity of home care by supporting nurses, care recipients, and informal caregivers. Despite growing research on DNTs, the home care setting remains underrepresented, particularly regarding implementation strategies using an established implementation science framework. Therefore, this scoping review systematically maps implementation strategies for DNTs in home care using the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) framework. Objective: We aimed to identify and map ERIC implementation strategies proposed or used for DNTs in home care. Additionally, we aimed to derive operationalized practical recommendations for decision-makers and implementation practitioners in nursing services. Methods: We conducted a scoping review with a systematic literature search in MEDLINE via PubMed, CINAHL via EBSCO, and Scopus via Elsevier in March 2025, with an updated search in July 2026. Guided by the PCC (Population, Concept, and Context) framework, we included primary studies and study protocols that addressed the implementation of a DNT in home care and were published between 2015 and 2026. We excluded studies from other health care settings, technologies not related to nursing, concept papers, and reviews. Data charting was conducted in MAXQDA 24 (VERBI Software) using deductive content analysis. We applied and operationalized the 73 ERIC implementation strategies to define our deductive category system. Results: A total of 22 articles with 18 distinct DNTs were included in this review. Most of them are implementation studies conducted in Europe and published in 2022. Most DNTs focused on home care using sensor-based monitoring and telehealth solutions for people with dementia, chronic conditions, or palliative care needs. Additional DNTs included mobile apps for symptom monitoring, decision-support systems, communication platforms, and a robotic medication management system. Deductive analysis based on the ERIC framework identified 48 of 73 implementation strategies across the included DNTs. The most frequently reported ERIC strategies were: conduct educational meetings (n=14), promote adaptability (n=14), conduct ongoing training (n=9), and train-the-trainer (n=9). The identified ERIC implementation strategies showed high heterogeneity across the included DNTs. Conclusions: These frequently reported ERIC implementation strategies may function as a multifaceted implementation strategy. However, they need to be empirically evaluated regarding their feasibility, appropriateness, and effectiveness for the implementation of DNTs in home care. In addition, researchers should ensure transparent reporting of implementation strategies by explicitly operationalizing them and applying established frameworks, such as the ERIC framework, to facilitate comparability across studies. Finally, practical guidance derived from ERIC implementation strategies should be specified in greater detail, including information on how, when, and for what duration individual implementation strategies should be applied. Trial Registration: OSF Registries osf.io/dsrh8; https://osf.io/dsrh8/overview
title: Implementation Strategies for Digital Nursing Technologies in Home Care: Scoping Review

summary: Background: Serum urate testing requires venipuncture; urine dipstick testing is inexpensive and routine. Whether dipstick results add information on hyperuricemia beyond age, sex, and BMI is unknown. Objective: This study aims to develop and externally validate machine learning models estimating the probability of hyperuricemia from 9 dipstick fields, age, sex, and BMI, and to quantify what the dipstick adds. Methods: The development dataset included 129,535 adults with first urine tests and same-day serum urate and BMI measurements at a Korean tertiary hospital (2010-2025); 21,124 had urate levels ≥7.0 mg/dL, and 81.6% (n=105,704) had a same-day health checkup. Calibrated 12-input ensembles of Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Categorical Boosting (CatBoost) were trained on a person-level 80% split (103,628 persons) for serum urate ≥7.0 mg/dL (primary) and ≥9.0 mg/dL (secondary). They were tested in the remaining 25,907 persons (4225 events at ≥7.0 mg/dL) and in 49,987 adults in the KNHANES (Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey; 2016-2024; 5068 events). Inputs, KNHANES coding, split, and training procedure were fixed before fitting. We assessed discrimination, calibration, operating points by sex, decision curves, and increments over age-sex-BMI models. Results: At ≥7.0 mg/dL, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.825 (95% CI 0.820-0.831) internally and 0.845 (95% CI 0.840-0.849) externally, but 0.710 in men and 0.795 in women. Across 4 model classes, the dipstick added 0.017 to 0.024 to the external AUROC of age-sex-BMI models (0.814-0.823), or 3.1 cases per 1000 screened with top-10% referral. Externally, the models overpredicted (observed-to-expected ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.71-0.75); an intercept update fitted in half of KNHANES restored it to 1.00 in the other half. The internally derived 80%-sensitivity threshold flagged 29.8% (14,916/49,987) of adults, 97.4% (14,533/14,916) of them men; sensitivity was 77.1% (3907/5068) overall but 10.1% (53/527) in women, and positive predictive value (PPV) was 26.2% (3907/14,916). Flagging all men gave 89.6% (4541/5068) sensitivity and slightly less net benefit than the model at threshold probabilities up to 10%. At ≥9.0 mg/dL, external results were AUROC 0.860, increment 0.052 to 0.074 (1.6 cases per 1000), observed-to-expected ratio 0.48, scaled Brier score 0.002 (no better than predicting the prevalence), and PPV 2.6% at 82% sensitivity. Conclusions: Routine dipstick results add a small increment to age, sex, and BMI for identifying serum urate ≥7.0 mg/dL. Ranking transferred from the hospital to a national survey sample, but absolute risk did not, and at the tested thresholds the models mainly selected men. Both cohorts comprised people who had blood drawn, so triage of serum urate testing in urine-only encounters, in which BMI is usually missing, remains an untested hypothesis. Before any use, the models would need local recalibration and evaluation in the intended setting.
title: Machine Learning Models Combining Routine Urine Dipstick Results With Age, Sex, and BMI to Triage Serum Urate Testing: Development and External Validation Study

summary: Background: Head circumference (HC) is a routine clinical parameter in pediatric patients indicating brain growth and neurodevelopment. Although usually obtained with a tape measure, this method is operator-dependent and prone to variability. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides a retrospective alternative, but existing imaging-based approaches can be limited by predefined measurement planes, restricted clinician review, and cranial surface artifacts. Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate a clinician-guided software tool for measuring pediatric HC from routinely acquired 3D MRI examinations. Methods: We developed a desktop application in Python using PySide6, the Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit, and the Visualization Toolkit for MRI-based HC measurement. The workflow included outer skin surface reconstruction, placement of 3 landmarks to define a freely orientable measurement plane, contour extraction, and circumference calculation. Optional Delaunay-based interpolation was implemented to reduce the influence of local cranial surface irregularities. In this retrospective evaluation, the tool was applied to 23 pediatric MRI examinations, including 18 without and 5 with clinically identified cranial surface irregularities. Two clinicians independently performed 3 repeated software measurements per examination. Median software measurements were compared with a single tape-based HC measurement obtained on the date of MRI. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis, mean absolute error (MAE), proportional bias analysis, and a linear mixed-effects model. Interrater differences and preliminary usability feedback were also evaluated. Results: Software-based HC measurement was feasible in all 23 examinations. In cases without cranial surface irregularities, the raw and interpolated contours showed similar agreement with tape-based measurements (bias 0.415 cm and 0.410 cm; MAE 0.429 cm and 0.423 cm, respectively). In the 5 examinations with irregularities, the intersection contour showed a greater bias of 1.420 cm and wider limits of agreement (LoA; −0.182 to 3.021 cm), whereas the interpolated contour showed a lower bias of 0.448 cm and narrower LoA (−0.119 to 1.014 cm). The estimated coefficient for the contour-by-subgroup interaction was −0.967 cm (SE 0.195 cm, 95% CI −1.349 to −0.584 cm; <.001). No statistically significant proportional trend was detected, although the analysis had limited power to exclude proportional bias. Interrater differences were small. The 2 clinicians reported System Usability Scale scores of 92.5 and 95.0, representing preliminary descriptive feedback. Conclusions: The clinician-guided workflow enabled MRI-based HC measurement in all examined cases and showed small interrater differences. Delaunay-based interpolation was associated with closer agreement with tape-based measurements in the small subgroup with cranial surface irregularities, while both contour variants performed similarly in examinations without irregularities. These findings are preliminary because of the small cohort, the single tape-based reference measurement per patient, and the 5-case irregularity subgroup. Larger studies using repeated reference measurements and broader cranial morphologies are needed to validate the workflow.
title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging–Based Measurement of Pediatric Head Circumference by a Clinician-in-the-Loop 3D Surface Tool: Development and Validation Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> High-risk alcohol use and alcohol use disorder (AUD) are significant contributors to surgical risk and complications yet remain underidentified in surgical populations. While electronic health records (EHRs) contain relevant information about patients’ alcohol use in clinical notes, manual chart review is time-intensive and impractical at scale. Natural language processing (NLP) offers a path to automated identification, but alcohol-related risk classes are highly imbalanced in clinical populations, making multiclass classification particularly challenging. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aims to develop an automated NLP pipeline for 4-class alcohol risk classification using clinical notes in a surgical population, addressing class imbalance by leveraging intermediate annotation evidence generated during the human labeling process. <strong>Methods:</strong> We manually labeled 1000 surgical patients drawn from a large academic health system into ordinal alcohol risk classes (no-alcohol, low-risk, high-risk, and probable-dependence) and a fifth class indicating no mention of alcohol use. We used a structured annotation process with 6 trained annotators and expert-developed guidelines. We developed a multistage NLP pipeline operating on 3 years of clinical notes per patient. First, a rules-based preprocessing stage filtered notes to clinically relevant sections containing alcohol-related content. No-mention cases were excluded from further modeling. Second, a BioClinicalBERT-based multilabel classifier (“auto-annotator”) was fine-tuned to reproduce the annotations created by human labelers at the section level, producing a structured 26-dimensional probability vector for each section. Finally, a bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network classified patients into the 4 risk categories by processing each patient’s ordered sequence of auto-annotation vectors, allowing the model to capture temporally accumulating evidence across clinical encounters. <strong>Results:</strong> Human annotators achieved 93.7% first-pass agreement overall (Fleiss κ=0.8891), but agreement was as low as 67.5% for probable-dependence cases. The 4-class LSTM classifier achieved a weighted-average <i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 0.86 and a macroaverage <i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 0.77 on a held-out validation set of 195 patients. One-vs-rest area under the curve (AUC) scores were 0.97 for no-alcohol, 0.88 for low-risk, 0.90 for probable-dependence, and 0.71 for high-risk. Collapsed to a binary high/low risk classification, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.92 and a macro-<i>F</i><sub>1</sub>-score of 0.80. Performance was comparable across biological sex without explicit sex-specific training. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> We used a 2-stage NLP pipeline to identify 4 ordinal classes of alcohol use risk in surgical patients. Four-class alcohol-use classification presents a highly imbalanced problem that constrains the availability of high-importance but rare labels in the dataset. We addressed this data scarcity by using intermediate annotation evidence as well as final labels to enrich the feature space for the classification task. The pipeline was able to separate patient records into 4 strata of alcohol-use risk, with “high-risk” patients being most likely to be misclassified into an adjacent class.
title: Natural Language Processing Supported by Annotation Process Artifacts to Detect Risky Alcohol Use in Electronic Health Records: Algorithm Development and Validation Study

summary: High-fidelity computational models of cardiac mechanics provide mechanistic insight into the heart function but are computationally prohibitive for routine clinical use. Surrogate models can accelerate simulations, but generalization across diverse anatomies is challenging, particularly in data-scarce settings. We propose a two-step framework that decouples geometric representation from learning the physics response, to enable shape-informed surrogate modeling under data-scarce conditions. First, a shape model learns a compact latent representation of left ventricular geometries. The learned latent space effectively encodes anatomies and enables synthetic geometries generation for data augmentation. Second, a neural field-based surrogate model, conditioned on this geometric encoding, is trained to predict ventricular displacement under external loading. The proposed architecture performs positional encoding by using universal ventricular coordinates, which improves generalization across diverse anatomies. Geometric variability is encoded using two alternative strategies, which are systematically compared: a PCA-based approach suitable for working with point cloud representations of geometries, and a DeepSDF-based implicit neural representation learned directly from point clouds. Overall, our results, obtained on idealized and patient-specific datasets, show that the proposed approaches allow for accurate predictions and generalization to unseen geometries, and robustness to noisy or sparsely sampled inputs.
title: Shape-informed cardiac mechanics surrogates in data-scarce regimes via geometric encoding and generative augmentation

summary: Computed tomography (CT) is central to craniomaxillofacial (CMF) deformity care, yet dependence on in-hospital imaging constrains remote preoperative assessment and outcome visualization, and repeated imaging can increase radiation and access burdens, particularly for children. We developed Tele-Cranio, a telemedicine-oriented artificial intelligence framework that uses mobile-acquired 2D facial photographs to reconstruct 3D facial morphology, estimate corresponding skeletal morphology and support postoperative facial simulation conditioned on surgeon-defined skeletal plans. Tele-Cranio was developed using 539 paired multimodal samples comprising 2D facial photographs, 3D facial scans and CT-derived skeletal models from individuals aged 3–60 years, including 334 patients with CMF deformities across malocclusion, cleft lip with/without palate, hemifacial microsomia and rare anomalies. Its core model, the Bidirectional Craniomaxillofacial Model-Deformity, learns a shared anatomical representation linking facial soft tissue and skeletal structures across normal and pathological morphology. For remote assessment, Tele-Cranio converts facial photographs into 3D facial surfaces and then infers 3D patient-specific skeletal geometry. For simulation, it generates individualized 3D postoperative facial previews after clinicians complete skeletal planning using standard clinical tools. Validated across heterogeneous CMF subgroups, Tele-Cranio provides an interpretable CT-free layer for remote triage, pre-CT consultation, radiation-free follow-up and surgeon–patient communication, while complementing rather than replacing CT-based definitive diagnosis and operative planning.
title: Tele-Cranio: a CT-free AI solution for remote diagnosis and planning of craniomaxillofacial deformities

summary: AI-powered cardiac screening could evolve sports medicine by boosting accuracy, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness, with automated ECG interpretation based on foundation models becoming key for large-scale athlete screening. Before deployment, it is crucial to verify whether these clinically developed models are applicable to this population. We evaluated whether ECG foundation models trained on general clinical populations can diagnose athlete-specific ECG findings. We fine-tuned three models (ECG-FM, HuBERT-ECG, ECGFounder) on PhysioNet/CinC 2021, 87,662 samples, and tested them on 43 expert-annotated ECGs from highly trained/national-level athletes. Performance was strong on PhysioNet/CinC 2021 (AUROC 0.97, AUPRC 0.57, Sensitivity 0.89) but dropped on athletes’ data, confirming domain shift. ECGFounder performed best (AUROC 0.84, AUPRC 0.72, Sensitivity 0.57) and detected the most frequent findings, Sinus Bradycardia (AUROC 0.87) and Sinus Arrhythmia (AUROC 0.95), well. Per-label estimates for rare classes must be interpreted cautiously, given the small cohort. This work contributes to developing athlete-focused AI frameworks for reliable ECG-based screening.
title: ECG foundation models for cardiovascular screening in a cohort of young competitive athletes

summary: Asthma affects over 260 million people worldwide, yet diagnosis remains dependent on spirometry and specialist assessment, limiting accessibility in primary care and low-resource settings. Vocal biomarkers offer a promising non-invasive alternative, but prior studies have largely focused on acoustic features without integrating clinical context. We present a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts framework for asthma identification that adaptively combines acoustic embeddings from sustained vowel phonation and reading passage tasks with structured clinical and demographic data. The model was evaluated on a matched cohort of 1218 self-reported asthma cases and healthy controls from the Colive Voice study. The multimodal model achieved an AUROC of 0.83 and Brier score of 0.18, outperforming unimodal approaches. Exploratory analysis of the gating mechanism in asthma cases showed that greater respiratory symptom burden was associated with increased weighting of reading-passage modality and reduced weighting of sustained-vowel phonation modality. These findings support the feasibility of voice-based identification of self-reported asthma; however, independent prospective validation remains necessary before clinical use.
title: Multimodal digital biomarker for asthma: complementary roles of vocal, clinical and demographic factors

summary: The tumour microenvironment (TME) is a multidimensional dynamic and complex system of cells and non-cellular components that not only drives tumour progression but also substantially influences response to therapy. Understanding TME biology for basic research and identifying biomarkers in the TME to stratify patients for therapy is crucial for optimizing therapeutic outcomes. Current standards for investigating TME dynamics, if even considered beyond preclinical work, rely predominantly on samples for tissue staining and sequencing and require invasive procedures to obtain tissue via surgery or biopsies. This leads to limited assessment of spatial heterogeneity and minimal temporal information as this depends on the timing of tissue sampling, which results in undefined clinical utility. Molecular imaging provides promising solutions by enabling non-invasive, real-time multidimensional spatiotemporal probing of the TME that can complement current ex vivo practices. This Review highlights the relevance of molecular imaging agents and methods that can effectively capture spatiotemporal TME characteristics in situ, offering critical insights into tumour behaviour and treatment response. We provide an overview of current preclinical imaging strategies and their applications in identifying cellular and non-cellular components of the TME, along with monitoring progression-associated processes and treatment response. We showcase new developments and avenues being explored in preclinical imaging, as well as offer perspectives into existing and emerging clinical imaging of the TME to enhance patient care and highlight opportunities for improvement. Overall, integrating TME imaging into clinical practice holds the potential to bridge critical gaps in spatiotemporal resolution, ultimately enabling more precise diagnosis, patient stratification and personalized therapeutic interventions. This Review discusses molecular imaging probes and modalities for studying the complexity and dynamics of the tumour microenvironment in preclinical research and further highlights emerging clinical applications in diagnostics and intervention.
title: Advances in molecular imaging of the tumour microenvironment

summary: Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological–environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure–function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic–exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions. The generation of individual biophysical digital twins at massive scale from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging enables individualized insights into regional signatures and excitatory/inhibitory balance, with features that can be linked to key phenotypes and expotypes.
title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype–expotype architecture of ageing and dementia

summary: Background: Tobacco use remains a major global public health challenge, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries. China, with the largest smoking population worldwide, faces additional challenges in smoking cessation due to sociocultural factors such as limited depth of risk awareness and strong social norms supporting smoking. Mobile health (mHealth) interventions, particularly smoking cessation apps, offer scalable and accessible support for behavior change. Limited qualitative research explores how Chinese smokers perceive smoking cessation apps and their roles in supporting quitting. Objective: This study aims to explore Chinese smokers’ experience of using smoking cessation apps to support smoking cessation. Methods: Chinese smokers with experience using smoking cessation apps were recruited via purposive sampling through social media. In total, 24 semistructured interviews were conducted online in Mandarin, audio-recorded, and transcribed verbatim. Interview questions explored participants’ experiences of using smoking cessation apps, including their perceptions of different app features, factors influencing their engagement, and how these features supported or hindered their quit attempts. Qualitative analysis was conducted to identify themes related to participants’ experiences regarding smoking cessation apps. Results: Ten themes were identified through qualitative analysis. Smoking cessation apps were perceived as most effective for users who were motivated to quit and believed in the usefulness of the apps. Features such as progress tracking and feedback enhanced extrinsic motivation and self-efficacy, with potential to foster intrinsic motivation over time. However, engagement with apps could decrease as users became more confident in maintaining abstinence. Social support functions provided emotional and informational support, and interactions with other quitters generated positive competition, particularly for users experiencing social isolation, although engagement with these features varied. Relapse prevention components, such as withdrawal symptoms education and recording features, were infrequently used when support was perceived as generic, low intensity, or insufficiently actionable. Good usability and user experience design were key drivers of sustained engagement. Participants valued apps that were simple and intuitive while offering different content formats, although preferences varied between users. Participants also described generic and nonpersonalized support as a limitation, despite rarely explicitly requesting greater personalization. Conclusions: Smoking cessation apps may support quitting through multiple mechanisms, including enhancing motivation and self-efficacy and facilitating social support, but their perceived value and use depend on users’ needs, beliefs, and contexts. The findings highlight broader considerations for mHealth intervention design and evaluation, including interpreting engagement in relation to changing support needs, recognizing that social features may generate additional motivational mechanisms through peer interaction, providing actionable and responsive behavioral support, accommodating diverse user preferences while maintaining usability, and using co-design to identify underlying user needs that may not be explicitly articulated. These considerations may inform the development of more responsive and user-centered mHealth interventions for smoking cessation and other behavior change contexts.
title: Chinese Smokers’ Perspectives on Smoking Cessation Apps: Qualitative Descriptive Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Retrieval over clinical free text underpins record search, cohort identification, and retrieval-augmented language systems. Performance is usually summarized by a single corpus-level mean, which can obscure systematic heterogeneity across patients. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study tests whether known-item retrieval performance varies across an early acute physiological derangement composite measured independently of the text, whether it reproduces under a validated severity-of-illness score, and whether it is robust to alternative outcome, retrieval, and explanatory specifications. <strong>Methods:</strong> We linked 4078 MIMIC-IV (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV) discharge summaries to an adult medical intensive care unit (ICU) cohort and built a pooled, length-matched index of 2956 documents drawn equally from 4 strata of a prespecified composite of early acute physiological derangement, comprising vital signs and Glasgow Coma Scale, mechanical ventilation, and age. A held-out 2-sentence passage had to retrieve its originating summary after removal. Eight contrastively trained dense retrievers, 5 masked language model controls, and BM25 were evaluated. Reciprocal rank at 10 (RR@10) was regressed on exposure stratum with patient-clustered SEs and Holm correction. The analysis was repeated under the Oxford Acute Severity of Illness Score (OASIS), a validated first-day score. Additional analyses examined categorical exposure shape, untruncated target rank, hit@10 (hit at 10), lexical representation, query characteristics, age removal, organ dysfunction, and measured covariates. <strong>Results:</strong> Mean RR@10 across dense retrievers fell from 0.127 to 0.080 between the lowest and highest composite stratum (−0.047; mean relative decline 37.2%), with Holm-significant negative slopes in all 8; a pooled model gave −0.0145 per stratum (95% CI −0.0207 to −0.0082; <i>P</i><.001; 23,648 observations). Under OASIS, it fell from 0.127 to 0.078 (−0.049; mean relative decline 38.7%); again, 8 of 8 were Holm-significant. The geometric mean rank of the correct document worsened by a factor of 1.17 per stratum under the composite and 1.24 under OASIS, 8 of 8 significant. BM25 also deteriorated, although from a higher baseline. It persisted across alternative query, indexing, rank, and hit@10 specifications; joint covariate adjustment attenuated the mean coefficient by 21.6%. Removing age attenuated but did not eliminate the pattern: all 8 retained negative slopes, the mean decline fell to 29.7%, and 3 of 8 remained Holm-significant. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Clinical free-text retrievability declined systematically with worsening early acute physiological derangement. The association held under an externally defined and validated severity-of-illness score as well as the study-specific composite and in lexical as well as dense retrieval. Corpus-level averages can therefore conceal clinically ordered heterogeneity, and clinical retrieval systems should be evaluated across patient strata rather than overall performance alone.
title: Clinical Free-Text Retrieval Across an Acute Physiological Derangement Composite in Intensive Care Unit Discharge Summaries: Stratified Evaluation Study

summary: Background: Patients with traumatic injuries present with heterogeneous injury patterns that are difficult to represent in statistical models. Common approaches either retain individual injury codes in high-dimensional sparse representations, such as one-hot encoding, or aggregate injuries into summary scores, reducing dimensionality at the cost of patient-specific detail. Objective: This study aimed to develop low-dimensional data-driven ICD-10 embeddings for traumatic injuries and compare their downstream discriminatory performance with one-hot encoding of the same injury codes. Methods: We conducted a retrospective study using National Trauma Data Bank (NTDB) records from 2018 and 2019. International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification diagnoses were mapped to World Health Organization ICD-10 codes, retaining traumatic-injury codes S00-S99 and T15-T34. A denoising autoencoder was developed on 2018 data and temporally evaluated on 2019 data. Representations with 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 dimensions were compared with one-hot encoding across 16 downstream tasks using logistic regression and LightGBM. Performance was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for binary tasks and macro one-vs-rest AUC for multiclass tasks. Models were trained and evaluated within individual hospitals and separately on the full NTDB. Hospitals were stratified into volume categories, from small (≤500) to major (2500 patients/year). CIs were obtained from 1000 nonparametric bootstrap samples. Results: The development cohort included 1,041,021 eligible patients from 2018, and the temporal evaluation cohort included 1,094,933 patients from 2019. At the hospital level, embeddings outperformed one-hot encoding. With LightGBM at 16 dimensions, the mean paired AUC difference across tasks was 0.054 (95% CI 0.048-0.060) in small hospitals (n=120) vs 0.023 (95% CI 0.020-0.025) in major hospitals (n=99). With logistic regression, differences were 0.056 (95% CI 0.050-0.063) and 0.041 (95% CI 0.039-0.043), respectively. In the full NTDB, 803-indicator one-hot encoding outperformed embeddings. Mean differences were –0.004 (95% CI –0.004 to –0.003) with LightGBM and –0.030 (95% CI –0.030 to –0.029) with logistic regression. At 64 dimensions, these differences narrowed to –0.001 and –0.016, respectively. Conclusions: Embeddings with as few as 8 dimensions achieved predictive performance comparable to or better than one-hot encoding, with up to a 100-fold reduction in dimensionality. Compared to one-hot encoding, embeddings improved performance in models trained at individual hospitals, particularly lower-volume hospitals. These gains may reflect reduced dimensionality, parameter sharing across codes, and representation of codes absent from hospital-specific training data, enabled by embeddings learned from the larger development cohort. In models trained on the full registry, one-hot encoding achieved higher mean AUC with both estimators, although the differences were minor (<0.005 AUC difference) for LightGBM with 16- to 64-dimensional embeddings. The embeddings and software are openly available.
title: Development and Evaluation of Embeddings for Representing Injuries in Patients With Traumatic Injuries: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary: Longitudinal clinical records capture health changes, but most models reduce them to endpoint risks or single-time biological-age estimates. We developed VitaFlux, a representation-learning framework that uses next-visit forecasting to encode clinical encounters as latent health states. Applied to 178,970 individuals with 4,439,390 aligned visits from the Zhejiang Population Health Cohort, VitaFlux learned a reproducible representation organized by age-associated, disease-burden and multisystem physiological variation. Forecast instability measured predicted health-state change at the next visit and was associated with observed one- and three-year mortality. Continuous trajectory measures captured heterogeneous progression, while current and forecast states improved the prediction of multiple clinical outcomes compared with a comprehensive clinical baseline. After cohort-specific adaptation, future-state forecasting outperformed a no-change persistence baseline in two independent aging cohorts. VitaFlux provides a unified framework for representing health-state position, forecasting near-term dynamics and quantifying longer-term progression from longitudinal clinical records.
title: Health-state instability and progression in longitudinal clinical records reveal heterogeneous ageing trajectories

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in clinical text processing, but their role in emergency departments (EDs) and ED-adjacent emergency care remains unclear because ED electronic health records (EHRs) are heterogeneous, time-critical, and safety-sensitive. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aims to synthesize peer-reviewed evidence on LLM applications to real-world ED EHR data and ED-adjacent emergency care data, focusing on clinical tasks, technical strategies, evaluation practices, and workflow integration. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)–guided systematic review of PubMed and Web of Science (January 1, 2022, to November 14, 2025). We included peer-reviewed English-language studies applying LLM strategies to ED and ED-adjacent EHR data. We extracted dataset characteristics, model families, task formulations (classification, summarization, and information extraction), adaptation strategies (prompting, fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic/hybrid workflows), evaluation metrics, and ED workflow phase. Two reviewers also independently completed a design-matched methodological quality and risk-of-bias appraisal. <strong>Results:</strong> Thirty-one studies met our inclusion criteria. Many relied on single-center datasets (n=12), relatively small sample sizes (<10,000 encounters; n=20), and English-language unstructured text alone or mixed EHR inputs combining text with structured or semistructured fields. Prompt engineering was the dominant adaptation strategy (n=27), while fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, and hybrid/agentic pipelines were less common. Postencounter studies frequently demonstrated task-specific retrospective technical feasibility, while triage, diagnostic-support, and disposition studies evaluated heterogeneous tasks and outcomes; these nonequivalent measures were not compared as indicators of workflow maturity. Workflow-phase assignment did not imply real-time integration, particularly when model inputs were available only after the relevant clinical decision point. Overall, 22 (71%) studies were classified as technical-performance-only evaluations; clinical utility was empirically assessed in only 3 (9.7%) studies, and prospective deployment in 4 (12.9%). No study directly measured patient outcomes or downstream patient-safety outcomes attributable to LLM use. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Current LLM applications across ED and ED-adjacent emergency care primarily function as documentation, surveillance, and auditing assistants rather than autonomous decision engines. Progress toward safe, deployable systems will require larger multicenter datasets, external and prospective validation, safety- and fairness-centered evaluation, and governance mechanisms that support responsible clinical integration. However, most evidence remains technical or retrospective, while prospective workflow integration, empirically demonstrated clinical utility, patient safety, and patient benefit remain insufficiently evaluated.
title: Large Language Models for Electronic Health Records in Emergency Department (ED) and ED-Adjacent Emergency Care—Technical Strategies, Clinical Tasks, and Workflow Integration: Systematic Review

summary: Lung adenocarcinoma is a highly heterogeneous disease, highlighting the need for more accurate prognosis prediction. We developed a multimodal deep learning model combining preoperative computed tomography (CT) and postoperative whole slide image (WSI) to predict the disease-free survival (DFS) of resected stage I lung adenocarcinoma. Based on a cohort of 1078 patients from multiple centers, our dual-information instance neural network achieved superior performance over unimodal approaches. The risk stratification defined by the model effectively distinguished DFS in both validation cohorts and served as an independent predictor, suggesting the complementary value of the model beyond clinicopathological factors. An exploratory scoring system integrating the model-derived risk stratification with key clinicopathological factors was developed, identifying patients with significantly different prognostic outcomes. Further analyses suggested that patients with high-risk stage IB disease or high scores might derive DFS benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy, warranting prospective validation. Beyond its predictive capacity, the model also provided morphological insights, identifying prognostically significant structures such as tertiary lymphoid structures and stroma barriers, while RNA-sequencing analysis revealed distinct oncogenic pathway activation and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments in high-risk patients. By leveraging routinely acquired clinical images, this multimodal approach offers a practical tool for improving prognostic stratification, with potential implications for informing patient selection for adjuvant chemotherapy in resected stage I lung adenocarcinoma.
title: Multimodal CT-pathology imaging deep learning model for risk stratification in resected stage I lung adenocarcinoma

summary: Background: Sarcopenia is an age-related syndrome characterized by muscle loss and functional decline, increasing fall risks. Early identification is crucial, yet convenient and accurate screening tools remain limited in routine practice. Machine learning (ML) models show promise for early sarcopenia detection, but their diagnostic performance and methodological quality have not been systematically quantified. Objective: This review aimed to quantitatively evaluate the diagnostic performance of ML models for sarcopenia prediction, compare performance across ML algorithms, and identify key sources of heterogeneity and methodological limitations. Methods: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched from inception to April 15, 2026. Eligible studies developed or validated at least one ML model for sarcopenia and provided sufficient data to reconstruct a 2×2 contingency table. Risk of bias was assessed using PROBAST (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool) developed by Moons et al. The primary analysis used a bivariate random‑effects (Reitsma) model to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values were pooled using a univariate random‑effects model with the Hartung‑Knapp‑Sidik‑Jonkman (HKSJ) method, and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were estimated. A secondary analysis incorporated all models using cluster-robust variance estimation (RVE). Subgroup analyses and meta‑regression explored heterogeneity. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). Results: Twenty studies (20 prespecified index models) were included. The pooled AUROC was 0.89 (95% CI 0.82-0.93; 95% PI 0.54-0.98), with pooled sensitivity of 0.77 (95% CI 0.68-0.83; 95% PI 0.37-0.95) and specificity of 0.88 (95% CI 0.83-0.91; 95% PI 0.62-0.97). Gradient boosting had the highest pooled AUROC (0.92), but CIs overlapped across algorithms. Externally validated models had a pooled AUROC of 0.85, lower than that of internal ones (0.91). The secondary analysis of all 115 models yielded consistent results. Meta‑regression identified no significant covariates. PROBAST assessment revealed that half of the studies were at high risk of bias. Conclusions: This review provides the first quantitative synthesis of ML‑based sarcopenia prediction models, with several innovations: (1) it provides algorithm‑stratified pooled estimates of diagnostic accuracy, (2) it formally quantifies performance across algorithms and addresses the unit‑of‑analysis issue through a 2‑tier approach, and (3) it quantifies the performance gap between externally and internally validated models. By identifying specific weaknesses—insufficient external validation, poor calibration reporting, and high risk of bias—this review offers a roadmap for improving future studies. Practically, these models may serve as cost‑effective prescreening tools. However, GRADE certainty was very low, with substantial heterogeneity, insufficient external validation, and high risk of bias, indicating that current models are not yet ready for routine deployment. Future research should prioritize rigorous external validation, transparent reporting, calibration assessment, and clinically implementable design. summary: Background: AI is increasingly applied across health care domains, yet public trust in AI across racial and ethnic groups and across health domains is poorly understood. Objective: This study examined trust in AI relative to trust in human professionals and identified sociodemographic characteristics associated with this comparative trust. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 10,506 US adults from the Understanding America Study (UAS), a probability-based internet panel, with poststratification survey weights applied to descriptive estimates to characterize the US adult population. Data were analyzed using multinomial logistic regression, adjusted for the sociodemographic characteristics used in poststratification survey weights. Trust in AI relative to human professionals was assessed for mental health counseling (the primary outcome), health diagnoses, and diet and exercise planning. Responses were categorized as “less trust than in a human professional,” “the same level of trust as in a human professional” (parity trust), “more trust than in a human professional” (superiority trust), or “not sure.” Results: Among the 10,506 participants (n=6385, 51.3% [percentage weighted using poststratification survey weights] female; mean age 49.3, SD 17.0 years), most trusted AI less than they trusted human professionals for health diagnosis and mental health counseling. Trust was lowest for mental health counseling (1136/10,469, 11.9% reported parity or superiority trust) and highest for diet and exercise planning (4773/10,460, 43.2%). For mental health counseling, non-Hispanic (NH) Black, Hispanic, and NH Asian adults were more likely than NH White adults to endorse parity trust, and these groups and NH multiracial adults were more likely to endorse superiority trust. NH Asian adults were 2.5 times more likely to endorse parity trust (relative risk ratio [RRR] 2.58, 95% CI 2.04-3.25; <i>P</i><.001) and nearly 6 times more likely to endorse superiority trust (RRR 5.95, 95% CI 3.79-9.35; <i>P</i><.001) for mental health counseling. NH Black (RRR 3.32, 95% CI 2.19-5.05; <i>P</i><.001), Hispanic (RRR 2.41, 95% CI 1.60-3.65; <i>P</i><.001), and NH multiracial (RRR 3.57, 95% CI 2.06-6.19; <i>P</i><.001) adults also showed elevated superiority trust. For mental health counseling, all racial and ethnic minority groups were more likely than NH White adults to select “not sure.” Generative AI use for general purposes was associated with higher trust, whereas higher education levels were associated with lower trust. Conclusions: NH Black, Hispanic, NH Asian, and NH multiracial adults were more likely than NH White adults to trust AI more than human professionals for mental health counseling. These data cannot show whether higher trust leads to greater use, and higher trust should not be interpreted as a preference for AI over human-delivered care. Nonetheless, this pattern informs how mental health AI tools can be designed, evaluated, and governed, as individuals with the greatest trust in these tools may be most affected if the tools perform poorly.
title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Trust in AI Relative to Human Professionals for Health Care: Nationally Representative Cross-Sectional Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with poorer adult health, but the behavioral and informational pathways underlying these associations, and whether digital environments condition them, remain unclear. Clarifying whether these pathways vary across contemporary digital contexts may help explain heterogeneity in the long-term health correlates of early adversity. <strong>Objective:</strong> Guided by the life course perspective, this study examined whether ACE exposure was indirectly associated with adverse adult health through tobacco and alcohol use risk (TAUR) and health literacy (HL), and whether social media use (SMU) moderated these pathways. <strong>Methods:</strong> We analyzed data from 30,054 adults in the 2023 Psychology and Behavior Investigation of Chinese Residents. A moderated dual-mediation structural equation model specified TAUR and HL as parallel mediators and SMU as a first-stage moderator. Robust maximum likelihood estimation was used. Conditional indirect associations at the SMU mean and at ±1 SD were estimated using 100,000-draw Monte Carlo 95% CIs. <strong>Results:</strong> Greater ACE exposure was associated with higher TAUR (B=0.118, 95% CI 0.101-0.135; <i>P</i><.001) and lower HL (B=–0.028, 95% CI –0.036 to –0.020; <i>P</i><.001). At mean SMU, indirect associations were positive through TAUR (B=0.020, 95% CI 0.014-0.027; <i>P</i><.001) and HL (B=0.004, 95% CI 0.003-0.006; <i>P</i><.001). For TAUR, the ACE association was smaller at higher levels of SMU (interaction B=–0.034, 95% CI –0.042 to –0.025; <i>P</i><.001). The conditional indirect association was B=0.026 at low SMU and B=0.015 at high SMU, with an index of moderated mediation of –0.006 (95% CI –0.008 to –0.004; <i>P</i><.001). For HL, the interaction was also negative (B=–0.043, 95% CI –0.051 to –0.035; <i>P</i><.001), and the indirect association through HL was negative at low SMU (B=–0.002, 95% CI –0.004 to –0.001; <i>P</i>=.002) but positive at high SMU (B=0.011, 95% CI 0.008-0.013; <i>P</i><.001), with an index of moderated mediation of 0.006 (95% CI 0.005-0.008; <i>P</i><.001). Johnson-Neyman analyses showed that the ACE to TAUR association remained statistically significant across the observed SMU range, whereas the ACE to HL association was positive below –0.855 SD, nonsignificant between –0.855 and –0.472 SD, and negative above –0.472 SD. The conditional indirect associations were statistically significant but small in magnitude. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> ACE exposure was associated with adult health through distinct behavioral and informational pathways that varied across SMU levels. These findings may inform the development and evaluation of interventions addressing TAUR and health information use in social media–rich environments.
title: Social Media Use as a Moderator of Behavioral and Health Literacy Pathways Between Adverse Childhood Experiences and Adult Health: Nationwide Cross-Sectional Study

summary: Background: Hospital clinical data warehouses (CDWs) contain longitudinal patient-level information distributed across heterogeneous clinical domains and require strict governance, privacy protection, and controlled data access. Although disease-specific registries facilitate structured clinical research, routine hospital CDW workflows often require repeated technical intervention when clinicians iteratively refine cohorts or integrate additional variables. At Samsung Medical Center (Seoul, Republic of Korea), an operational audit revealed a mean turnaround time of 2.7 (SD 1.6) weeks for clinical data extraction requests, highlighting a workflow gap between clinicians’ research questions and engineer-mediated database query development. Objective: This study describes the development and single-center implementation of IDEA (intersection, difference, expansion, attribution), an informatics abstraction framework designed to support authorized clinicians in performing iterative cohort construction and variable integration within a governed hospital CDW. Methods: IDEA implements 4 user-facing operations: intersection (I), difference (D), expansion (E), and attribution (A). Attribution enables dynamic integration of variables from multiple predefined clinical data domains into an active cohort. IDEA was implemented within the Samsung Medical Center CDW, containing longitudinal electronic health records from 1995 to 2025 and 12 cancer registries. The implementation was evaluated using oncology cross-registry scenarios, descriptive analysis of user actions recorded between January 2024 and December 2025, including 11,460 IDEA operator events, and analysis of 349 user-defined cohorts (“My Registries”) established from 2022 to 2025. Results: IDEA supported interactive cohort construction, refinement, and attribute-based stratification across 12 cancer registries without manual SQL authoring. Clinical end users generated the majority of the 11,460 operator interactions: research nurses accounted for 7918 (69.1%), physicians for 2871 (25.1%), and IT personnel for 619 (5.4%). Attribution was the most frequent operation (8726, 76.1%), suggesting that iterative variable integration into established cohorts was a major use case. Additionally, 349 user-defined cohorts were registered as reusable baseline populations for subsequent cohort curation. Conclusions: IDEA serves as a complementary pathway for clinician-led data curation within a governed hospital CDW, integrating cohort refinement, variable integration, and reusable cohort management into a single workflow. This approach may support selected routine curation tasks for authorized users working with quality-validated data, while complex requests continue to require analyst support. Multicenter evaluations are needed to independently assess dataset accuracy, completeness, and institutional transferability.
title: The IDEA Framework for Clinician-Led Data Curation in a Hospital Clinical Data Warehouse: Single-Center Implementation Study
